utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Douglas Stringer, appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. I am accompanied this morning by my colleagues - moving from my left to right - Matthew Cross, Laurel Baig, Helen Brady and Saeeda Verrall. Our Case Manager is Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. [Microphone not activated] Mr. Gotovina, and Mr. Markac, appeal from the Trial Judgement, rendered in this case on 15 April 2011 by Trial Chamber I. According to the Scheduling Order issued on 4 April 2012, the Appeals Chamber will presently hear the appeals in this case. I will first briefly summarise the appeals and the manner in which we will proceed today. This case concerns the responsibility of Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac for crimes committed in the Krajina region of Croatia, around the time of the military action referred to as Operation Storm, which took place in August 1995. During the indictment period, Mr. Gotovina served as colonel general in the Croatian army and was commander of the Split Military District. Mr. Markac was assistant minister of the interior and commander of the special police in Croatia. The Trial Chamber found that both Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac were members of a joint criminal enterprise for JC -- or JCE, whose common purpose was to permanently remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina region by force or threat of force. Both Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac were convicted under the first form of JCE for persecution and deportation as crimes against humanity, and under the third form of JCE for persecution and local detentions, murder, inhumane acts as crimes against humanity and for plunder of public and private property, wanton destruction, murder and cruel treatment as violations of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Gotovina to a single term of 24 years of imprisonment. Mr. Markac was sentenced to a single term of 18 years imprisonment. Mr. Gotovina advances four grounds of appeal, challenging his convictions, and requests that the Appeals Chamber overturn his convictions in their entirety. In ground 1, he challenges the Trial Chamber's finding that unlawful artillery attacks on civilians and civilian objects took place. In ground 2, he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings that unlawful attacks forcibly displaced Serb civilians. In grounds 3 and 4, he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings that a JCE existed and that he was individually liable for the crimes attributed to the JCE. The Prosecution response that all grounds of Mr. Gotovina's appeal should be dismissed. Mr. Markac presents eight grounds of appeal, challenging his convictions, and requests that the Appeals Chamber overturn his convictions in their entirety or, in the alternative, that his sentence be reduced. In ground 1, he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings that the JCE existed and that he was a member of, and individually liable for the crimes attributed to the JCE. In grounds 2, 3, 5, and 6 he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings with respect to the role of the special police in the destruction and plunder of Gracac, in the destruction of Donji Lapac and for scheduled killing number 10. In ground 8 he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings concerning deportation and forcible displacement. In ground 9 he challenges the Trial Chamber's finding that an international armed conflict existed throughout the indictment period, inter alia. Finally in ground 12, he challenges his sentence. The Prosecution responds that all grounds of Mr. Markac's appeal should be dismissed in its addendum to the Scheduling Order for appeal hearing issued on 24 April 2012. The Appeals Chamber invited the parties to discuss with references to the record: 1, whether the Trial Chamber erred in applying a 200-metre range of error in analysing the lawfulness of artillery shelling. 2, whether the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding impact sites should be upheld if its application of the 200-metre range of error is deemed erroneous. 3, whether the Trial Chamber's finding that illegal artillery attacks took place should be upheld in its conclusions with respect to impact sites are deemed erroneous and/or whether the Trial Chamber's finding that the JCE existed should be upheld if its finding that illegal artillery attacks took place is deemed erroneous. Throughout the hearing counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentations. However, I would urge counsel not to repeat verbatim or to summarise extensively the arguments presented in their briefs. The Appeals Chamber is familiar with these arguments. Furthermore, the parties are obliged to provide precise references to materials supporting their oral arguments. I note that there remains evidence in this case whose admission on appeal has yet to be decided. I would discourage the parties from referring to these materials. If such references are made, I ask that the parties clearly indicate that they're referring to materials whose admission has not yet been decided. Finally, I reiterate that the appeal process is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their case as presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to alleged errors of law, which invalidate the Trial Chamber Judgement or alleged errors of fact which occasion a miscarriage a justice. As set out in the Scheduling Order, this hearing will proceed as follows: First we will hear submissions from counsel for Mr. Gotovina for one hour, 30 minutes. After a pause of 15 minutes, the Prosecution will respond for one hour and 30 minutes. Following another pause of 15 minutes, counsel for Mr. Gotovina will have 30 minutes to reply. In the afternoon, starting at 10 minutes past 2.00, we will hear the submissions from the parties of Mr. Markac's appeal, followed by optional personal statements from Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac. Parties will present their submissions in a precise, clear and concise manner. The Judges, of course, may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each parties 'submissions or at the end of the hearing. Having now stated the manner in which we will proceed, I would like to invite counsel for Mr. Gotovina to present his appeal. And let me remind the parties that we have a very tight schedule, and I would be grateful to the parties if they will adhere to the time allocated to them. So counsel for Mr. Gotovina, please do start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Once again, my name is Gregory Kehoe. I will be presenting the initial argument on behalf of General Gotovina, basically address two points, 1 and 2, the questions asked by the Chamber. I will then turn the floor to my colleague -- floor over to my colleague, Mr. Misetic, who will discuss questions 3 and 4. And then, lastly, Mr. Akhavan will finish our presentation with some brief remarks. Your Honour, with regard -- before we answer the questions presented by the Trial Chamber, and -- the Appeals Chamber we will like to give a brief overview of the case and exactly what the Trial Chamber's findings were with regard to the Serb civilians who left the Krajina area. The Trial Chamber concluded, Your Honours, that the Serb civilians left for reasons unrelated to unlawful contact by the HV in all places but the four towns at issue. Those towns being Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. The reasons the Trial Chamber cited for the departure of those civilians in places other than those four towns can be found in paragraphs 1754, 1755, and 1762 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement. They include information such as information provided by local committees or SVK unit, Army of Serb Krajina units, the departure of others and fears of what would happen when the Croats and the HV arrived, fear of violence commonly associated with armed conflict and general fears of Croatian forces and distrust of Croatian authority. The last reason presented by the Chamber was, in fact, the RSK officials telling habitants to leave on 4 August 1995. However, the Trial Chamber found that the reasons for departure from all other places could not have been a reasonable explanation for why they left the four towns at issue. Why? Because of alleged unlawful artillery attacks which deliberately targeted civilian areas from which the Trial Chamber concluded that General Gotovina ordered indiscriminate attacks on the four towns. Was this finding of unlawful attacks really the only reasonable explanation of the evidence? Let's briefly touch on a few items. The Trial Chamber had evidence before it that 95 per cent of all projectiles fired in Knin were deliberately fired at military objectives. I direct the Chamber to Annex 1 of the Appellant's response to the Prosecution's motion to strike Appellant's reply brief filed with this -- filed with the Appeals Chamber 7 October 2011. The actual final statistics are on page 2. International investigations by the United Nations Military Observers in August 1995, the United States government investigators found that the attacks -- that were highly professional and concentrated on military targets. No investigation on the ground made any contrary conclusion that would suggest an unlawful attack. I direct Your Honours to Prosecution Exhibit P64, which is the provisional assessment by the UNMOs, the UN -- the United Nations Military Observers, who after their preliminary assessment or provisional assessment was followed up by a final assessment. This final assessment proved to be consistent what the provisional assessment has confirmed by Prosecution witness, Alun Roberts, the chief information officer of the UN. And this confirmation is located at trial transcripts pages 7081 to 7082. The United Nations Secretary-General, the European Community Monitoring Mission and other international leaders made no mention of an unlawful attack when reporting the events in the Krajina on 4/5 August 1995. More importantly, no finding that any civilian was killed or injured and no Serb civilian has ever been identified who claimed to have left the Krajina due to the fear of shelling when the lawful or unlawful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, my colleague Judge Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to take you back to that part of your statement, that you asked the question whether that was the only reasonable finding that the Trial Chamber could have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Implying that if there are other reasonable findings, then the Appeals Chamber should find that the Trial Chamber erred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. If there is a reasonable explanation of the evidence consistent with innocence, then the -- the Appeals Chamber should find our clients not guilty and overturn the Judgement of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Even if the finding by the Trial Chamber is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The law is, Judge Robinson, that if there is a reasonable explanation of the evidence, in this instances consistent with innocence, then the Appeals Chamber must find our clients not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you will direct us to the other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will during the course of our presentation, Judge Robinson, go through some of those items seriatim which will actually play into the questions that the Appeals Chamber asked, questions 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Robinson. Mr. Kehoe, you may continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I noted, more importantly no finding that any civilian was killed or injured and no Serb civilian has ever been identified who claimed to have left the Krajina due to fear of shelling, be it lawful or unlawful. Conclusion. Let us talk about what we can conclude from these matters. For these reasons and those which we will lay out later, the Trial Chamber acted unreasonably in concluding that the reasons for the departure which the Chamber found in all other areas of the Krajina which were not caused by any alleged unlawful conduct by the Croatian army could not have been a reasonable explanation of the evidence in the four towns at issue here. Your Honours, we welcome the four questions posed by the Chamber which we consider to be at the core of the Trial Judgement, whether there is any sufficient basis other than the arbitrary 200-metre rule that could establish and unlawful attack by HV forces directed against the Serb civilian population. I will now turn to the first question that was presented by the Chamber. Question 1: Whether the Trial Chamber erred in applying a 200-metre range of error in analysing the lawfulness of artillery shelling. The answer quite simply is yes. I think it is important before we discuss range of error to discuss exactly what the Trial Chamber concluded and what they noted the 200-metre rule was. It simply says that any shell falling within 200 metres of a known military objective will be presumed to have intended to strike that military objective because that would be "a reasonable interpretation of the evidence." Your Honours, this is not a margin of error standard. There was no establishment of any margin of error standard. This was simply a rule established by the Trial Chamber. Had we had expert testimony on the specific margin of error we would have to take many different items into account when going into that margin of error, not the least of which is, for instance, rounds falling outside that margin of error, outliers, and then discussing why, in fact, a round for whatever reason, be it human error, wrong -- improper information, et cetera, would cause a rounds to fall outside that margin of error. Well, suffice it to say that the 200-metre rule is not a margin of error. Why was this 200-metre rule an erroneous standard by which to analyse the artillery fire? And how and why did the Trial Chamber err in using this -- this standard? Well, first and most importantly, the Trial Chamber's first error is in failing to explain why it even needed to do an analysis of shell impact locations at all to determine the intent behind General Gotovina's attack order. As I noted just briefly in my earlier comments, the Trial Chamber had evidence before it on the basis of HV documentation that at least 95 per cent of all rounds fired were fired with the intent to strike lawful objectives. This should have been sufficient in itself for the Chamber to determine that there was a reasonable explanation of the evidence consistent with the Defence's assertion that General Gotovina's order was not for an unlawful attack but, rather, was interpreted and implemented as an order for an unlawful attack -- as a lawful attack. Excuse me. This is exactly what chief of artillery, Marko Rajcic, testified. He testified that he received General Gotovina's order and he implemented it as an order for a lawful attack directed on military objectives. And his testimony was corroborated by the HV artillery records. And how about deaths or destruction? There was no finding by the Chamber of any civilian deaths or injuries in any of the four towns as a result of the shelling. There was likewise no evidence of extensive destruction of civilian objectives either. Therefore, it is left unexplained by the Trial Chamber why in view of these conclusive facts it needed to even look at impact sites to determine the intend of General Gotovina's order or, further, why it needed to even devise a methodology, the 200-metre rule, based on measuring the distance between impact sites and known military objectives. That leads into the second error by the Trial Chamber, and that has a -- directed to the 200-metre rule itself. This 200-metre rule has no evidentiary basis in the record whatsoever. It was never discussed during trial. It was never brought up during trial. It was never a matter that was briefed during trial. Nothing. The Trial Chamber established its 200-metre rule at the end of a very long analysis of evidence of margin of error of HV weapon systems. At paragraph 1898 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement, by placing the -- this discussion of the 200-metre rule in the context of margin of error suggests that the Trial Chamber was trying to tie its 200-metre finding to its analysis of margin of error, but ultimately did not. If we go back to this discussion in paragraph 1898 where the Trial Chamber wrestles with this margin of error standard, it ultimately could come to no conclusion as to the margin of error. For instance, the Trial Chamber cited Prosecution witness Konings who testified that for 155 metre shell fired at a distance of 14.5 kilometres, the margin of error would be 55 metres in range, plus up to 60 metres for each of the four factors cited: Muzzle velocity, wind speed, air temperature, density. Those, of course, wouldn't be the only four but those are the four that are listed. Now, first on a foremost, we have to look at the actual weapon that Mr. Konings was talking about. There was no 155-metre Howitzer cannon used in this particular case. The particular gun at issue was a T-130. In any event, had the Trial Chamber accepted the Konings test, Konings would have placed the margin of error at up to 295 metres for a 155-metre shell fired at a distance of 14 and a half kilometres. Those are the general comments that were made by Konings with regard to this 155. The firing distance in this case for the T-130 was at 26 kilometres. Clearly at a 26 kilometre any margin of error would have clearly been grater. Thus, the Trial Chamber did not rely on Konings's testimony to establish the 200-metre rule because Konings at a significantly reduced distance had a margin of error of almost 300 metres. Ultimately, the Trial Chamber recognised that the Prosecution had failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt what the ranges of error of the HV weapon systems were. This was a failure of proof by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber recognised that failure and I direct the Chamber to the screen to footnote 932 on page 965 of the Trial Judgement where the Chamber noted as follows - thank you - the Trial Chamber had noted that: "Had these impacts which were at a distance of up to 700 metres from artillery attacks been the result of the inaccuracy of the artillery weapons used, that would require further consideration of whether such inaccurate weaponry can be used in the context of an artillery attack on specific targets within a town." Clearly this finding demonstrates that the Trial Chamber did not know what the margin of errors were for the HV weapon systems. At this point, because there was a failure of proof by the Prosecution as to the margin of error, the Trial Chamber should have found that the Prosecution had failed, simply failed, to meet its burden of proof. Instead, the Trial Chamber decided to simply ignore the issue of the proper range of error in establishing its 200-metre rule. This is quite clear. As I just noted for Your Honours, footnote 932, the Chamber admits that it did not know the proper margin of error. Let's turn our attention to paragraph 1906 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement which, likewise, is now on the screen. And it begins at the bottom of the page and then carries over where the Trial Chamber notes: "In conclusion, the Trial Chamber finds that too many projectiles impacted in areas which were too far away from identified artillery targets and which were located around Knin for the artillery projectiles to have impacted in these areas incidentally as a result of errors or inaccuracies in the HV artillery fire." Clearly, Your Honours, if the Trial Chamber believed that the margin of error had been established as less than 200 metres, it would have simply stated that as a basis for excluding the possibility of the shells landing more than 200 metres away. Is there some special significance to this 200-metre rule? We can search the record, Your Honours. The Trial Chamber never explained why the 200 metres had any specific significance. There 's no evidence in the record to justify the selection of 200 metres as a standard. Accordingly, it thus appears that the Trial Chamber chose this 200-metre standard arbitrarily. Finally, it appears that the parties, including the Prosecution, now agree that the 200-metre margin of error, to the extent that it is a margin of error, is overly narrow. Clearly the Trial Chamber erred in establishing the 200-metre rule. It could not account for the proper margin of error. The third reason why this was an error by the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, is this: There was no notice of this standard given to the accused. Appellant's grounds of appeal 1.1.3. notes that the Chamber's adoption of a 200-metre radius around military objectives was an assertion, as I noted previously, that was never discussed at trial. So, as we direct our attention to this first question, Your Honours, whether the Trial Chamber erred in applying a 200-metre range of error in analysing the lawfulness of artillery shelling, given that the evidence demonstrated that fire was concentrated on military targets, given that the 200-metre rule has no relation to margin of error, given that the 200-metre rule is clearly an arbitrary standard not discussed at trial for which no notice was given, on behalf of General Gotovina, we submit that the Trial Chamber did in fact err in establishing this 200-metre rule as a basis upon which to render a decision. Let us now turn to question 2. Whether the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding impact sites should be upheld if its application of the 200-metre range of error is deemed erroneous. Clearly the answer is no. And let us go through the analysis step by step. If the 200-metre rule is deemed erroneous, then the Trial Chamber's conclusions concerning impact sites must also be reversed. The Trial Chamber drew several unreasonable inferences which all rest on the erroneous application of the 200-metre rule. First, the Trial Chamber used its 200-metre rule to establish the civilian character of "civilian areas in which it said certain shells fell." The jurisprudence of this Chamber is clear. That the Prosecution in a criminal case bears the burden of establishing beyond a reasonable doubt that "an object was indeed dedicate to civilian purposes." And I cite to Your Honours the Blaskic Appeals Judgement paragraphs 111 and 145. Here, Your Honours, the Prosecution failed to introduce any evidence of the presence of civilians or civilian objects in any of the Chamber's so-called civilian areas and failed to introduce any evidence to establish that any of the Chamber's civilian areas were, in fact, per Blaskic, dedicated to civilian purposes. In fact, the Prosecution could not establish that any civilians had been killed or injured by shells and very few civilian objects were hit by shells in the four towns combined. Finally, in violation of the Blaskic standard the Trial Chamber itself failed to make findings that any of these civilian areas were in fact dedicated to civilian purposes. Your Honours must think, Well, how did this happen? Why was there no evidence of this? The reason the Prosecution failed to establish the civilian character of particular objects or areas is because the Prosecution's case was that there were "few, or in almost all cases, no identifiable military targets." That was the Prosecution's case as we move into trial, and I cite for Your Honours the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at paragraph 31. The Prosecution's case was that the HV fire on the town was per se unlawful -- excuse me, was a per se unlawful attack against civilians because there were no military objectives in the towns. Accordingly, once the Trial Chamber found that the Defence had, indeed, established the existence of many military objectives, the Trial Chamber should have found that the Prosecution had simply failed to prove its case. Instead they did something very different. Instead, the Trial Chamber altered the Prosecution's case to the Prosecution's benefit. Where the Prosecution had failed to introduce any evidence to prove the civilian nature of specific objects or areas in Knin, frankly because it took the position that the entire town was a civilian zone due to the alleged absence of military objectives, the Trial Chamber proceeded to use its 200-metre rule to do two things. It chose to arbitrarily treat all areas outside 200 metres of known HV military -- artillery targets as being civilian in character. What did this do? First and foremost, it circumvented the need under Articles 51 and 52 of protocol 1 to establish that civilian or civilian objects were attacked. Instead the Trial Chamber invented the concept of civilian areas, I quote, "by which the Chamber created zones of presumed civilian character." What was the net effect of this decision? The net effect was that the Trial Chamber created a presumption of criminal intent for all shells falling in a civilian area without regard to whether the civilian or civilian object was actually targeted. The Trial Chamber thus used the 200-metre rule to fill in huge gaps in the Prosecution's case as pleaded and tried and had already been rebutted by the Defence. That rebuttal is that there were many military objectives in the four towns. As a result, the Trial Chamber afforded civilian status to any area more than 200 metres from a known military objective. And let us just talk about some of those now described military areas -- excuse me, civilian areas; for example, the cross-roads in Obrovac was found to be a civilian area merely because it was more than 200 metres from a known military objective. The railway fuel storage in Knin was found to be a civilian area even though the railway station itself was found to be a legitimate military objective strictly because it was too far away from a known military objective. Whether -- per Blaskic, whether the railway fuel storage was actually dedicated to civilian purposes as required by Blaskic is a question that the Trial Chamber didn't even try to answer. Why? Because the Prosecution had failed to introduce any evidence on that point. Let us visualise this a little bit more specifically and examine how this -- this reversed the burden of proof. We can go up on Sanction on the screen for one moment. Map A. This would be Map A in the -- in the maps that you have. If we look at this, this is the practical application of the Trial Chamber's Judgement. And this is a 200-metre radius around military targets as identified by the Trial Chamber. And unilaterally, anything that landed within this area was presumed to be directed on a military target, and anything that landed outside this area landed in this so-called civilian area, and, thus, was presumed to be improper. That was a conclusion reached with no actual evidence of what was outside these 200 -- this 200-metre radius as set forth in Map A and without any evidence that the particular areas that were then designated as civilian areas were in fact dedicated to civilian purposes per Blaskic. What was the net effect of this? Well, first, this -- as you can see, it doesn't establish or doesn't satisfy the Prosecution's burden of proof. As I just noted, the Prosecution had to establish that any object struck by a shell was dedicated to civilian purposes. Again, the Trial Chamber made no finding that these areas were dedicated to civilian purposes and could not do so in the absence of any evidence advanced by the Prosecution. But more importantly, the 200-metre rule was used to reverse the burden of proof. It required the accused to bring forward evidence of military objectives near impact areas. If the accused failed to bring forward evidence of such military objectives, then the Trial Chamber applied the 200 metre standard to establish the civilian character of its civilian areas even where no evidence was submitted by the Prosecution to identify whether civilians or objects dedicated to civilian purposes were, in fact, present in these areas. At this point, Your Honour, we would like to take this a little bit more closely and examine one of the examples advanced by the Trial Chamber and how it was actually employed in this Judgement. And I direct your attentions -- of the Chamber to a map on the screen that we're going to be talking about an impact area that was discussed in paragraph 1904 of the Judgement. Before we do that, if I can just take the Chamber through this particular map, the area at question is the area in front of the UN headquarters. If can you see the area circled in yellow, there are three circles in that area. There's a field in front of the headquarters. Those impact areas were identified by Prosecution witnesses Dijkstra, Berikoff and Williams during trial. The red are military targets that were fired upon by the HV per Marko Rajcic. What we have in 25 and 26 are two military targets that in fact Mr. Rajcic said they did not fire upon. Using this map -- mis -- classic example and this is the use of the 200-metre rule, the Trial Chamber analysed the three shells falling into the empty field in front of the UN barracks and found that the field was more than 200 metres from a known HV target but less than 200 metres from other military targets -- objective, excuse me. The Chamber found that because there was no evidence that the HV fired upon these military facilities within 200 metres of the empty field, the field was civilian. Again, this is on 1904. My colleague reminded me this is on 1904 of the Judgement. It appears that the Trial Chamber found if the HV had targeted these additional military facilities closer to the 200 metres to the field, it would have found the field to have been of military character. Let us direct ourselves a little bit more specifically and go to the next map, which is Map 4. This is directed towards a 25 -- which is the Ante monastery but was in fact a headquarters of the special police for the ARSK. And this was a target that was not fired upon by the HV per Marko Rajcic. However, in analysing this, had the HV decided to fire on this particular objective at 25, we can see from the calculation be it at 200 metres or 400 metres, at virtually half of this field would immediately be transformed into a place where any -- any round landing in that would not have been improper. So you have the rather incongruous conclusion as a result of this decision made by HV where half this field, any rounds following in half this field were proper and any rounds falling outside either 200 or 400 metres fell in civilian areas and were thus improper. If we go back to the next slide which shows it again coming from the other direction, in paragraph -- in number 7, this is -- 26 is another HV facility -- excuse me, I'm sorry, RSK facility. It is their barracks which is just adjacent to the UN building. If you can see 26 where the RSK barracks are, just south of that on this photograph is the UN facility. Again, this was not fired upon by the HV per Marko Rajcic. As a practical matter, however, had the HV fired upon number 26, the RSK southern barracks, what do we have once again? We have once again the transformation of this field as a proper place upon which rounds could -- rounds could land and there would be no negative criminal consequences. We can expand this out yet further and turn this to paragraph 17 -- excuse me, Map 17. And before we get to that, we can note that paragraph 1904 demonstrates how the civilian status of a particular object or area depended exclusively on whether it was in the 200 metres of a military objective actually targeted. Moreover, it is important to note that the 200-metre rule is not based on any margin of error. We have included this 200-metre standard here because presumably if the margin of error had been established as 400 metres per Andrew Leslie, a Prosecution witness and a Canadian officer, it would have created a 400 metre-rule. This, the civilian status of areas and objects under the Trial Chamber's methodology depends on either the 200-metre rule or the margin of error of the weapon systems firing near the locations. Now look at the -- the Map 17 that's on the screen. This is the practical application of what the Trial Chamber did. What we have done is put circles on there for 200-metre radius and circles around the targets for a 400-metre radius, and again, depending on what the HV targeted or didn't target, transformed this field into what could have been a civilian area or could have been completely proper because it was under 200 or 400 metres of a military objective. This completely puts aside any analysis as required by Blaskic that these particular areas are dedicated to civilian purposes. Obviously when we analyse a chart such as this, this is an absurd result because it tells us nothing about whether the object was dedicated to civilian purposes. But, frankly, Your Honours, this is the nature of the methodology employed by the Trial Chamber. Accordingly before I turn my -- this matter over to Mr. Misetic, let us conclude with regard to question 2, again, whether the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding the impact sites should be upheld if its application of the 200-metre range of error is deemed erroneous. Clearly, it should not. Civilian areas based on impacts alone and not whether the area was dedicated to civilian purposes, improper. The reversal of the burden of proof by the Trial Chamber, clearly improper. Any decision whether an area was civilian based on an arbitrary 200-metre standard as opposed to the character itself was clearly improper. For all the reasons set fourth above, the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding impact sites should not be upheld and should be reversed in its application -- even if its application of the 200-metre range of error is erroneous. At this juncture, Your Honours, I would like to turn the floor over to my colleague, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, could I just ask you a question before your colleague takes over. You say something about the question whether the Trial Chamber erred in discounting the possibility of targets of opportunity given the determination by the Trial Chamber that the evidence did not establish whether Croatian forces had the ability to monitor areas where roadblocks, police and military vehicles were present in the relevant towns. So my question pertains to targets of opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there was, in fact, evidence presented that there was the capability to examine targets of opportunity. Clearly on the 5th as they moved into town, there was more than enough time to hit targets of opportunity and to examine targets of opportunity. So the premise that there was no ability to see impact sites was simply improper and I believe that the citations set forth in our brief established that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- distinguished members of the Appeals Chamber, good morning. My name is Luka Misetic. I will be addressing questions 3 and 4. Mr. President, first if I could just supplement my colleague's response to your last question. We would also draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that witnesses Leslie, and I believe Dawes, testified that the HV -- that they witnessed bracketing fire in Knin on the 4th, and from that they drew the conclusion that the HV could in fact observe Knin because bracketing fire requires the ability to observe what your fire is doing. I don't have the citations with me but I know we have cited that in our briefs, Mr. President. Mr. President and Your Honours, I will be addressing questions 3 and 4. Question 3 from the Appeals Chamber is: Whether the Trial Chamber's finding that illegal artillery attacks took place should be upheld if its conclusions with respect to impact sites are deemed erroneous. The simple answer obviously is no. The finding of illegal artillery attack cannot be sustained if the conclusions with respect to impact sites are deemed erroneous because the 200-metre rule was the necessary precondition to each of the inferences drawn by the Trial Chamber to establish the alleged illegality of the shelling. The Trial Chamber concluded that the shelling operation was unlawful based on the following inferences. All but one of which are derived from the Trial Chamber's erroneous 200-metre rule and its subsequent erroneous conclusions about "shells falling in civilian areas" described by my colleague, Mr. Kehoe. The six erroneous inferences drawn are as follows: First, that the HV deliberately fired artillery projectiles at areas devoid of military targets, i.e., civilian areas; 2, that projectiles could not have landed in the civilian areas as a result of errors or inaccuracies in the HV's artillery fire; 3, that General Gotovina's artillery order was an illegal order to treat whole towns as targets; 4, that reports of HV artillery units indicated that whole towns were treated as targets; 5, that the general impression of eye-witnesses was that "the shelling impacted all over Knin and was indiscriminate"; and, 6, there was a disproportionate attack against Milan Martic. All but one of these inferences are derived from the 200-metre rule. If the 200-metre rule was erroneous, then the findings just cited must also be reversed because they rest on the Trial Chamber's erroneous conclusion that shells impacted in civilian areas. With respect to the first inference, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the HV deliberately targeted civilian areas is based on its conclusions that projectiles had landed in civilian areas. And that's at Trial Judgement paragraph 1911. However, as just explained, without the 200-metre rule the Prosecution failed to prove that any of these areas in the four towns were "civilian areas," and therefore there was no evidence that the HV deliberately targeted civilian areas. Therefore, there can be no inference of unlawful intent drawn from a projectile falling in any particular place in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, or Gracac. Second, the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that shells could not have impacted more than 200 metres from a military objective due to the margin of error of the weapon systems. Because the Trial Chamber erred in establishing a 200-metre rule, it erroneously excluded margin of error as a basis for reasonable doubt explaining why shells fell more than 200 metres from military objectives. This finding is at paragraph 1906, which, again, will be up on your screen and was shown to you previously. It says: "In conclusion, the Trial Chamber finds that too many projectiles impacted in areas which were too far away from identified artillery targets and which were located around Knin, for the artillery projectiles to have impacted in these areas incidentally as a result of errors or inaccuracies in the HV's artillery fire. Thus, the Trial Chamber finds that the HV deliberately fired the artillery projectiles targeting these areas in Knin." For Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac, it is the same finding, except without relying on a finding of too many shells falling. Had the Trial Chamber not made this error, it would have had to conclude that because it did not have sufficient evidence of the margin of error, it could not exclude the reasonable possibility that shells fell more than 200 metres from military objectives due to the unknown margin of error. Alternatively, had the Trial Chamber accepted Leslie's 400-metre standard as the margin of error it would have concluded that only 13 of 1200 projectiles fired, or 1 per cent, fell beyond the margin of error of the HV weapons systems. And we have this on a chart in front of you, Your Honours, on the screen in front of you. We have broken down the Trial Chamber's findings by the four towns and you have in the four towns exactly five incidents for a total of 13 total projectiles that fell beyond 400 metres, beyond what Leslie said was the HV margin of error. In Knin, if we focus on Knin, the Trial Chamber found 5 out of 900 rounds fell beyond what Leslie said was the margin of error. That means that .05 per cent of the shells of the projectiles that were fired in Knin fell outside the margin of error. Your Honours, we submit that 99.5 of projectiles falling within -- within the range of error of HV weapons systems is powerful evidence that General Gotovina's orders were in fact interpreted and implemented to mean that military objectives should be targeted. Moreover, this finding of five projectiles is remarkably consistent with the subsequent investigation of the shelling of Knin conducted by the United Nations military observers, and that is, again, at Trial Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P64. The United Nations Military Observers found that only three to five shells were found or were observed outside the immediate vicinity of military objectives. In other words, the Trial Chamber's own findings are consistent with the conclusions of the United Nations military observers whose conclusion was that there was no evidence of an unlawful artillery attack. Had the Trial Chamber used these numbers or applied a 400-metre margin of error it could not have reasonably concluded that the only explanation of the evidence is that the HV was shelling towns indiscriminately. We note however that even with the statistics as they were before the Trial Chamber, i.e., that only 5 per cent of all rounds fell beyond 200 metres, this was sufficient to demonstrate that whole towns were not treated as targets. The third inference of the Trial Chamber is, in fact, that General Gotovina's artillery order was unlawful but this inference cannot be sustained if the 200-metre rule is overturned. The following must be noted: Marko Rajcic was General Gotovina's chief of artillery and, as such, was the person who both interpreted and implemented General Gotovina's order. He was the Prosecution's witness, not the Defence's. And he was the only witness with personal knowledge who testified about how General Gotovina's orders was implemented and interpreted. Marko Rajcic testified explicitly that General Gotovina's order was interpreted as an order only to strike only lawful military objectives. This testimony was powerfully corroborated by the evidence before the Trial Chamber that 95 per cent of all rounds fired were fired at military objectives. Rajcic's testimony was also corroborated by the subsequent investigations of the shelling of Knin conducted by, amongst others, the UNMO investigators and the United State's investigators who did not conclude that there was an unlawful artillery attack. Again, that is trial exhibit P64. Accordingly, even with the 200-metre rule Rajcic's explanation of Gotovina's order was confirmed by other corroborating evidence in the record. Yet the Trial Chamber ultimately concluded that Gotovina's order was unlawful. It first stated at paragraph 1893 of the Trial Judgement that it would assess the legality of Gotovina's order based on whether it found Rajcic's testimony to be credible. The Trial Chamber then proceeded to apply its invented 200-metre rule to conclude that Rajcic's explanation could not possibly be credible because - and this is at Trial Judgement paragraph 1911: "The Trial Chamber considers that the deliberate firing at areas in Knin which are devoid of military targets, i.e., civilian areas, is inconsistent with Rajcic's explanation of the HV artillery orders. Instead, it is consistent with the plain text of those orders to put towns under artillery fire, meaning to treat whole towns, including Knin, as targets." In other words, the Trial Chamber used its conclusion that 5 per cent of projectiles fell in civilian areas to disregards Rajcic's evidence and to conclude that Gotovina issued an illegal order. If the Chamber were wrong in its conclusions about the civilian character of these "civilian areas," and therefore wrong to conclude that the HV "deliberately targeted civilian areas" then the Trial Chamber had no basis to discount Rajcic's corroborated testimony. Even with the 200-metre rule, the fact that the implementation of General Gotovina's order resulted in at least 95 per cent of all rounds fired at military objectives was more than sufficient to establish that General Gotovina's order was lawful and interpreted by his subordinates as such. Without the 200-metre rule and thus without the finding that the HV deliberately targeted civilian areas, Rajcic's testimony is unassailable. Next we turn to the inference about HV artillery reports. Without the 200-metre margin of error the reports of HV artillery units do not prove that whole towns were treated as targets. From contemporaneous reports at HV artillery units, the Trial Chamber had evidence before it that at least 95 per cent of all projectiles were fired at military objectives per General Gotovina's order. At paragraphs 1895 and 1896, the Trial Chamber noted that there were some entries in HV reports which might be interpreted as evidence that whole towns were treated as targets. The Trial Chamber also found, however, that these entries were oftentimes a coded account of the targets fired at and may have been the result of "lack of details, errors, or other inaccuracies in the reports." In order to determine whether these entries were evidence of indiscriminate attack or simply inaccuracies in the reports, Trial Chamber said that it: "... will further evaluate these reports in light of the findings on the locations of impacts in Knin." Again, that's Trial Judgement paragraphs 1895 and 1896. Thus, because the Trial Chamber's conclusions based on the impact areas were wrong as a result of the mistaken 200-metre rule, the innocent interpretations of HV reports also cannot be concluded as reasonable explanations of the evidence. Even the Trial Chamber stated as much. Without the 200-metre margin of error, the general impression of eye-witnesses that the "shelling impacted all over Knin" is actually consistent with the Chamber's finds that the HV lawfully targeted military objectives in Knin. The Trial Chamber relied on the testimony of witnesses in Knin who said that "the shelling was all over Knin and was indiscriminate." That's at Trial Judgement paragraph 1911. However, we'd like to put back on the screen which are Maps A and B, which the -- Your Honours, you have already had distributed to you. This is, again, the map with the military objectives in Knin and the 200-metre circles around it. Now the witnesses -- many of the witnesses, indeed most of the witnesses, relied on were in the extreme right portion of this map, in the UN compound. The Trial Chamber found that any shells landing in these areas were presumed to have been intended to strike military objectives. Now, if a shell landed in these areas, it would both be lawfully fired and from the perspective of witnesses on the grounds, be perceived as falling all over Knin. Indeed, that is because military objectives were all over Knin. The Trial Chamber had evidence that at least 850 projectiles landed in these areas. Had the Trial Chamber assumed Leslie's 400-metre margin of error - if we can move to the next line, please - the circles become even larger. This is where shells would have impacted in Knin which the Trial Chamber would have considered lawfully fired because they fell within the margin of error of HV weapons systems. The witnesses' perception that the shells were falling all over Knin is consistent with the fact that legitimate military objectives were targeted all over Knin. The UN Military Observer's conclusion that the artillery fire was concentrated against military objectives also confirms this. Eye-witness testimony is thus of little significance, particularly - and we emphasise - that there is not a single witness in this case who was aware of every military target in Knin. And therefore what basis they would have as to whether a shell could or should be falling in a particular part of Knin is unexplained. Finally, with respect to the alleged disproportionate attack on Martic. Although this finding would not be impacted by overturning the Trial Chamber's finding on the 200-metre rule for reasons explained more fully in the Appellant's brief, the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that the attack on Martic was disproportionate. There was no evidence of the presence of any civilians at his residence and no evidence whatsoever that Gotovina had "knowledge of circumstances giving rise to the expectation of excessive civilian casualties." There is no evidence of any harm to any civilians as a result of the targeting of Martic. Martic as the Commander-in-Chief of SVK forces was prepares the highest value military objective possible. Moreover, the Trial Chamber did not conclude that the alleged disproportionate attack was evidence of a direct attack against civilians, meaning that the Trial Chamber did not say that the real object of this attack was not Martic but the civilians around Martic. Instead, it concluded this was evidence of a general disregard for civilian safety, but the Trial Chamber did not call into question that Martic was indeed the intended objective of this attack. Accordingly, the Martic incident does not on its own provide evidence of an attack to target the civilian population. Thus, all but one of the factors that the Trial Chamber considered in arriving at its conclusions rest on the 200-metre rule and the incorrect inferences drawn from impact locations. The Chamber's finding of indiscriminate attack must fail. If there is no proof beyond a reasonable doubt that shells impacted in civilian areas there is no evidence of any unlawful attack. Even if there were proof of impacts in civilian areas there is no proof that this was not the result of errors or inaccuracies in the HV weapons systems, i.e., the margin of error, human error, or intelligence errors. Indeed without the 200-metre rule, the Trial Chamber could have establish that: 1, Gotovina ordered that previously identified military objectives be targeted with artillery in the four towns; 2, of the 900 rounds of artillery fired in Knin, at least 850 were demonstrably fired with the intent to strike military objectives; 3, in Knin only five rounds out of 900 fell beyond the 400-metre margin of error established by Leslie for HV weapons systems; 4, no civilians were killed or injured in the shelling in the four towns; 5, the damage to civilian structures was minimal and confined to the vicinity of military objectives; 6, there is no evidence that any civilian was targeted by artillery fire; and, 7, there is no evidence that any civilian structure was targeted by artillery fire. Given all of these factors, let us turn our attention to whether there is any evidence of an actus reus or mens rea of the crime of unlawful attack. There is no unlawful attack, first, because there is no proof of an actus reus. There is no evidence that civilians were made the object of the attack, no evidence that the HV artillery fire was of such nature to strike military objectives and civilians or civilian objects without distinction, and no evidence that the HV used inherently indiscriminate weapons during the artillery operation. Therefore, the actus reus of unlawful attack does not exist without the 200-metre rule. Second, the Trial Chamber conclusion that there was the relevant mens rea to commit an unlawful attack as the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity must also fail. The Chamber expressly found that its conclusions about the existence of such unlawful intent was based upon, 1, the language of HV artillery orders, and, 2, the inference that these orders were unlawful based on the deliberate shelling of areas devoid of military targets. That's at Trial Judgement paragraph 1912. Because both of these rest on the erroneous 200-metre finding, the finding concerning intent to commit unlawful attack must also be reversed. Your Honours, I will now turn to question 4 posed by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that 95 per cent of the projectiles, there was evidence that 95 per cent of the projectiles were aimed at military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that mean that you accept that there was evidence that 5 per cent --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- was aimed at civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is the remaining shells that I discussed in terms of the ambiguity in HV military artillery reports. We do not accept that. And, as a matter of fact, the Trial Chamber itself, as I discussed, said that those entries are ambiguous and would be evaluated in light of its findings on the locations of impact areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So they don't help at all in relation to establishing indiscriminate attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In answers to the Appeals Chamber's questions and now yours, if you overturn, in questions 1 and 2, the findings of the 200-metre rule and the subsequent inferences drawn about impact locations, then the Trial Chamber itself said that it was going to only draw criminal intent from those entries based on where it found shells to have back impacted. So if those conclusions about impact areas are wrong, then the Trial Chamber itself said explicitly, I believe in paragraph 1895 and 1896 of the Trial Judgement, that the Trial Chamber said that these entries could have been the result of lack of details, errors, or other inaccuracy in the reports, but then said it would evaluate whether they were in fact the result of such errors on the basis of its findings on the location of impacts on Knin. So we would argue, Your Honours that those remaining 5 per cent in fact were directed at military objectives and that the only question about them has been resolved and that there is a basis to conclude that they were in fact simply coded language and language -- they were poor record-keeping which the Chamber itself found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Question 4 from the Appeals Chamber asks: Whether the Trial Chamber's finding that a joint criminal enterprise existed should be upheld if its finding that illegal artillery attacks took place is deemed erroneous. The answer is no. Without an illegal artillery attack, the necessary precondition for the existence of a JCE namely, the "commission of a crime provided for under the Statute" does not exist. There is no commission if there is no unlawful attack. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 2314 of the Trial Judgement defined the common criminal purpose of the alleged JCE. It said that the common criminal purpose -- excuse me, that the members of the Croatian political and military leadership shared the common objectives of the permanent removal of the Serb civilian population from the Krajina by force or threat of force which amounted to and involved persecution through the crimes of deportation, forcible transfer, unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects and discriminatory and restrictive measures, as well as the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer. The purpose of the joint criminal enterprise required that the number of Serbs remaining in the Krajina be reduced to a minimum but not that the Serb civilian population be removed in its entirety. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber found that the common criminal purpose was the permanent removal of the Serb civilian population but not that the Serb civilian population be removed in its entirety. A few paragraphs earlier the Trial Chamber found that this common criminal purpose was to be achieved through an unlawful artillery attack. This is paragraph 2311, via Sanction. It says: "The minutes of the Brioni meeting show that the participants were aware of the difficulty situation for the Krajina Serbs, in particular in Knin, and that they knew that it would not require much effort to force them out. Under these circumstances, members of the Croatian political and military leadership took the decision to treat whole towns as target for the initial artillery attack. Deportation of the Krajina Serb population was, to a large extent, achieved through the unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, which the Trial Chamber has found were carried out on discriminatory grounds." At paragraph 2321 of the Judgement, the Trial Chamber also made clear what was not in the common criminal purpose. It said: "The Trial Chamber finds that the common objective did not amount to, or involve, the commission of the crimes of persecution, through disappearances, wanton destruction, plunder, murder, inhumane acts, cruel treatment and unlawful detentions. And also did not involve the crimes the destruction, plunder, murder and inhumane and cruel treatment." Accordingly, the Trial Chamber found that the common criminal objective did not involve deporting Krajina Serb civilians through crimes such as murder, destruction, plunder, inhumane acts and cruel treatment. Instead, the Trial Chamber found a common criminal purpose of deporting Krajina Serb civilians through an unlawful shelling attack on the four towns and then imposing discriminatory measure to prevent these civilians from returning. Accordingly, if the Appeals Chamber were to rule that the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that there were unlawful shelling attacks on the four towns for the reasons we have previously addressed this morning, then there would be no actus reus left that could be used to support the claim that any intent to deport the Krajina Serb population was actually implemented. In short, the 200-metre margin of error and the resulting erroneous finding of unlawful attack, without that, the Trial Chamber could not have identified any actual cause of departure of Krajina Serbs from the four towns. Just as importantly, it would not have had any basis to differentiate between the causes of departure of the Krajina Serb civilians from the rest of the Krajina which the Chamber found in paragraph 1754, 1755 and 1762 were not caused by any unlawful conduct by the HV and the causes of the departure from the four towns. It should be emphasised, however, that without the finding of actual unlawful attacks the Trial Chamber would not have established any criminal mens rea to deport the Krajina Serb population and thus would not have been able to establish the existence of any common criminal purpose. Indeed the Trial Chamber's findings concerning the Brioni meeting and the discriminatory housing policy all rest on the Trial Chamber's finds that an unlawful artillery attack actually took place. Let us turn our attention for a moment to the Brioni meeting findings. Concerning the Brioni meeting both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution have conceded that there is no single statement at the Brioni meeting from which the unlawful agreement to shell civilian towns can be inferred. Instead, both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution explain that the alleged unlawful intent of the Brioni participants is to be inferred from the subsequent unlawful artillery attack which allegedly took place. On your screens, Your Honours, via Sanction this is paragraph 2310 of the Trial Judgement: "The Trial Chamber considers that the discussion at the Brioni meeting, at which the participants discussed the importance of the Krajina Serbs leaving as a result and part of the imminent attack. Further, it infers from the mass exodus of the Krajina Serb population within days of the launching of Operation Storm and the immediate efforts, on a policy and legislative level, to prevent the population from returning that members of the Croatian military and political leadership intended to force the Krajina Serbs from their homes." We note the juxtaposition there between the first sentence which says they discussed the importance of leaving and then drawing the inference that the conversation was about forcing based on subsequent events. At paragraph 2305, five paragraphs earlier, the Trial Chamber has carefully considered the minutes of the Brioni meeting in chapter 6.2.2. It here further considers them in light of subsequent events as found by the Trial Chamber. Within days of the discussion at Brioni, Gotovina's words became a reality. It goes on and says: "The Trial Chamber has found at chapters 4.4 and 5.8.2 (i) in at least some of the these attacks the entire towns were treated as targets for the artillery. These attacks therefore constituted unlawful attacks and civilians and civilian objects." Now, the Prosecution has itself argued to the Appeals Chamber that the Trial Chamber did not look at the Brioni transcript itself to draw its inference that the discussion at Brioni was about forcing Krajina Serbs from their homes. We'll show on the screen now portions of the Prosecution's respondent's brief. This is respondent's brief paragraph 234. The Prosecution says: "The Trial Chamber correctly found that an unlawful attack against civilians and civilian objects was intended and within the purpose of the JCE. This conclusion was based on many considerations, not just on four factors as Gotovina claims. "For example, Gotovina's repeated suggestion that the JCE shared intent must be found in the words of the Brioni meeting alone should be rejected; the Chamber properly made this finding on the totality of the evidence." We turn to paragraph 239: "Gotovina appears to suggest that the Chamber found the existence of a formal decision at the Brioni meeting by the JCE members to target whole towns. But there is no such finding. Nor would a formal decision be required to find the existence of the JCE. The Chamber concluded based on the evidence that under these circumstances a general decision was taken at Brioni to subject whole towns to the initial artillery attack. Given the discussions at the meeting where Gotovina and Tudjman made explicit reference to the shelling and potential destruction of Knin, the express terms of Gotovina's attack order, and the indiscriminate shelling of the four towns which occurred shortly thereafter, the Chamber reasonably found that the JCE members at Brioni decided to target these towns." We turn to paragraph 268: "Gotovina's references to the accuracy of his comments are beside the point. The Chamber's focus was appropriately directed at the meaning of Gotovina's statements and those of the other participants in the context of the meeting and subsequent events." And, finally, at paragraph 271: "The Chamber's finding that Gotovina intended to target ... civilians to force them to leave the Krajina and to use artillery for this purpose, was based on the totality of the evidence, not a single statement at the Brioni meeting." Accordingly, the Trial Chamber clearly made its findings on Brioni contingent upon its finding that an unlawful artillery attack actually took place after Storm and that Gotovina's order was unlawful. The Prosecution concedes in its respondent's brief that the Brioni transcript, on its own, does not contain evidence of a formal decision to target towns with artillery nor a single statement in which targeting civilians with artillery to force them to leave was discussed. Therefore, if you overturn the Trial Chamber's finding of unlawful attack you must also overturn its reasoning establishing that a criminal intent existed at Brioni to target the four towns with indiscriminate artillery fire. With respect to discriminatory measures, the second element of the criminal mens rea to permanently remove the Krajina Serb population, concerns the Trial Chamber's findings about discriminatory housing laws. This is issue cannot form the basis of a JCE involving Appellants Gotovina and Markac absent of finding of unlawful artillery attack because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I just wanted to make sure that in your remaining time you will address us of the question of the evacuation orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber made express findings that Appellants Gotovina and Markac, and this is at Trial Judgement paragraph 2325-26 concerning General Gotovina and 2562 to 63 concerning General Markac, the Trial Chamber found that neither Appellant had any involvement whatsoever in the housing policies or any other allegedly discriminatory policies. Accordingly, even if the Appeals Chamber were to confirm that there existed a JCE to impose discriminatory measures, it is clear that the Trial Chamber found that neither Gotovina nor Markac had any involvement in the core crime of any such JCE, i.e., a discriminatory measures JCE. Moreover, the Trial Chamber made its findings that these housing laws were discriminatory contingent upon its findings that the Krajina Serbs had been unlawful expelled through shelling in the first place, thus making any obstacles to return unlawful. The Appellant expressly at trial noted that states have the right to deny the immediate return of nationals of an enemy state in times of armed conflict, citing a decision of the Ethiopia-Eritrea Claims Commission, and this is at Trial Judgement paragraphs 1748 and 1749. The Gotovina Defence expressly noted that this right to prevent immediate return only existed if the state did not unlawfully expel the civilians in the first place. The Trial Chamber distinguished this precedent on the basis that civilians in this case had been subjected to an unlawful attack against civilians. Thus, if there is no unlawful attack, then the Trial Chamber's basis for distinguishing this authority disappears and we are left with the question of whether a state has the right to prevent the immediate return to its territory of aliens of an enemy state in an armed conflict. The Trial Chamber avoided this question when it concluded that it was irrelevant because civilians had allegedly been unlawfully expelled. Your Honours, in conclusion on the Appeals Chamber's four questions, as is evident from your questions -- from the answers to your question, the finding of joint criminal enterprise rests fundamentally on the Chamber's erroneous 200-metre rule from which the Trial Chamber ultimately drew erroneous conclusions about the civilian nature of impact areas, about the lawful or unlawful nature of the artillery attack and about the presence of culpable intent on the part of General Gotovina and about the existence of a JCE. Should you overturn the 200-metre margin of error the Appeals Chamber must necessarily overturn General Gotovina's conviction on all counts because there is no JCE liability any longer. Mr. President, now in answer to your question about the Martic evacuation order. Mr. Kehoe and I have laid out for you this morning that the Trial Chamber itself made explicit find in three paragraphs of the Judgement, 1754, 1755, and 1762, that the Krajina Serb civilian population left areas outside of the four towns for reasons that did not relate to any unlawful conduct by the HV. The Trial Chamber, as Mr. Kehoe pointed out, itemised several factor from which it drew that conclusion. One of those factors -- in fact, the last fact that Mr. Kehoe mentioned, and this is at a Trial Judgement paragraph 1762, is "RSK officials telling inhabitants to leave on 4 August." Now, Your Honour, we submit and you have seen ground 2 of our appeal. Ground 2 of our appeal, in detail itemises how and why the Krajina Serb population left en masse and left from the Krajina. The issue of deportation here, as we know, the crime of deportation involves forcefully expelling people across a de jure or de facto border. There is no evidence in this case of any identifiable Serb civilian that the Prosecution can give you a name of any such person who claimed to have decided to leave the Krajina in fear of unlawful artillery attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, counsel, just for a second. The Trial Chamber concluded the evacuation orders were not the primary cause of civilian departure. You believe that the Trial Chamber in this respect acted outside the scope of discretion. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, first and foremost, I think the -- as -- I think we would all agree the key issue isn't for the Defence to explain why they did leave. It's for us to explain why they didn't leave, and they didn't leave because of artillery shelling. But second -- second, we laid out in our Defence final brief that the Trial Chamber had more than sufficient evidence before it of all of the steps taken by the RSK authorities to trigger the civilian flight. There is a problem between the Trial Chamber's approach to the Martic evacuation order and what we contend actually happened. The Trial Chamber seems to have been looking at the narrow issue of whether the evacuation order was implemented in the sense of they were able to organise fuel and trucks, et cetera, and there was some sort of a systemic departure from the Krajina. Our position is that once it was made known to the civilian population that an evacuation order had, in fact, been issued, people decided to leave. Whether they left organised or unorganised, in a systematic manner or not, is of little relevance to the ultimate issue. Our objective is ground 2 is to explain what the evidence was. Moreover, there was plenty of evidence, including from the commander of Sector South of the United Nations in Knin who filed a report which is in evidence in which he analysed what happened in Operation Storm, and he, himself, came to the conclusion that once the evacuation order was issued everybody decided to leave, civilians and military. And so we do believe that the Trial Chamber failed to address key evidence; for example, the Trial Chamber doesn't address that evidence from the commander of the UN Sector South. There is other evidence that we have identified in our briefs that the Trial Chamber simply failed to address, and as we noted the Trial Chamber on critical issues has a duty to address key evidence in the case. The -- the other factor, Your Honours, to consider is that the Trial Chamber's basis for excluding the evidence concerning Martic rests on the testimony of Kosta Novakovic, who testified that civilians were already on the move prior to the evacuation order and who also said that they issued the evacuation order in order to put some order into a process that was already taking place. We suggest, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber committed an error when it failed to do any assessment of the credibility of a person -- a military person in the ARSK -- or SVK who in fact participated in the issuance of the order and had a motive to downplay the importance of that order. So, Your Honours, we believe there were several errors committed by the Trial Chamber in failing to address that evidence. But again I would emphasise that for purposes of this case, what is important is what didn't cause the departure and we would argue that there is no basis for the Trial Chamber to conclude that all of the reasons outside of the four towns could not have been a reasonable explanation for why civilians left the four towns. Now I will -- unless there are any other questions, Mr. President, I will turn the floor over for a five-minute submission by my colleague, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, distinguished members of the Appeals Chamber, I'm honoured to make some brief concluded remarks on this appeal and its wider implications for humanitarian law. This case is simple and straightforward. The Trial Judgement's fundamental finding is that HV violations of Article 51, paragraph 2 of protocol 1 was of such an exceptional scale and gravity that it constitutes crimes against humanity. It finds in particular that the deliberate targeting of whole towns was so extreme that it was the direct and primary cause of the mass exodus of 20.000 civilians. In this context, the persecutory attack of unlawful attack is not merely one act among other; rather, it is helped to constitute the very essence of the widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. What is the proof in support of this far-reaching conclusion? Quite simply, the totality of the evidence is that 1.200 artillery projectiles were fired in urban areas but without a finding of even a single civilian death or injury and without any proof of extensive destruction of civilian objects under such circumstances is a massive deliberate attack against a civilian population the only reasonable inference. The conclusion would have to be that despite a criminal policy the HV forces were so exceptionally incompetent that none of their 1.200 projectiles succeeded in hitting a single civilian. Needless to say, such a conclusion would be manifestly absurd and no amount of creative legal reasoning can compensate for this fundamental lack of proof. This case, we submit, is as simple and straightforward as that. General Gotovina's conviction on these facts is a miscarriage of justice, but there is a wider consideration here. The Judgement establishes a precedent that would make lawful warfare practically impossible. Throughout modern history, humanitarian law has been relevant to military commander because it has struck a realistic balance between humanitarian protection and military necessity. The former ICRC legal adviser Louise Doswald-Beck observes that states negotiating protocol 1 intended to "codify a law that was acceptable to their military staff." Eminent publicists have noted however that courts and tribunals have frequently ignored operational or battlefield practice. In order to remain credible and relevant the jurisprudence of this Tribunal must apply humanitarian law consistent with the operational realities of warfare and not an impossible standard. Consider, for instance, the observation of Professor Michael Schmitt in the International Review of the Red Cross, and I quote: "That there is no foundation to claims of the emergence of the customary norm on the use of precision weaponry in urban settings or that states which possess precision weapons must always use them." That's in the 2005 issue of the International Review of the Red Cross at page 460. If General Gotovina is convicted of large-scale unlawful attacks on these facts, what is the practical standard for urban warfare applicable to the most advanced armed forces of the world? Surely if General Gotovina is guilty of attacks against whole towns without a single finding of civilian death or injury then military forces with precision weapons must be held to an even higher standard. It is evident that despite feasible precautions even the military operations of the most advanced forces have resulted in thousands of civilian casualties. Indeed, it is difficult to image any urban combat in recent history that compares favourably with the HV artillery operations in terms of civilian impact. Mr. President, distinguished members of the Appeals Chamber, like Tadic almost two decades ago, this is a landmark case for the Tribunal that will be widely scrutinised, especially by military experts on the laws of war. By applying a reasonable standard, informed by operational and battlefield practice, the Appeals Chamber will ensure a lasting contribution to the viability of humanity law. Applying such a standard, we respectfully submit, clearly requires this Chamber to enter a Judgement of acquittal against General Gotovina. I thank the Chamber for its patience. That conclude our remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akhavan, and thank the counsel for Mr. Gotovina for adhering to the timetable and for their arguments. We will now -- yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't want to interrupt counsel during their submissions, but in the course of the submissions we were looking at the maps, and it just appears to us that the legend that appears at the bottom of a couple of these doesn't correspond to the size of the circles, the 2- or 400 metres. I don't know if it means anything. I don't know if the Chamber is going to have these, but it is something that we notice. I'm looking at Map A here. The 200 doesn't appear to correspond to the 1.000-metre scale that is at the bottom but I just wanted to note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We just looked at these without prejudice. I will -- we will now -- unless there is it an answer to that, that you ... we will now adjourn for a -- until 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Response by the Prosecutor. An hour and 30 minutes. Mr. Stringer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, again, and Your Honours. Counsel. This morning, together with my colleague Matthew Cross, I will address General Gotovina's arguments in his ground 1 on the unlawful shelling attack which the Chamber found was directed against the four towns of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, and Obrovac on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995. In the course of our submissions, Mr. Cross and I will address the first three questions that the parties received from Your Honours. After Mr. Cross and I have concluded, my colleague Ms. Baig will address the Chamber's fourth question. And after that, my colleague Ms. Verrall will address the deportation and evacuation order issue. As an overview, Your Honours, our submissions on the unlawful attack can be summarised as follows. The Trial Chamber correctly found that the Croatian Army, HV, shelling attack of the 4th and 5th of August was an unlawful, indiscriminate attack on the towns. The unlawful attack was not a singular event, unconnected to others, but, rather, was part of a common criminal plan to permanently remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina region of Croatia. Its findings on unlawful attack are amply supported by various sources of evidence, all of which consistently point to the fact that the towns themselves were targeted in the attack.
