This includes the discussion among Gotovina, Markac, and others, with President Franjo Tudjman at Brioni on the 31st of July, 1995, four days before the attack. The Chamber correctly concluded that this discussion was "about civilians being forced out." Secondly, the plain language of the attack order issued by General Gotovina on the 2nd of August to "put the four towns under artillery fire," as well as the orders of Gotovina's subordinates to the same effect. Thirdly, the numerous eye-witness accounts and conclusions of UN military personnel in Knin as part of the UN peacekeeping forces there who observed that the shelling attack hit all over the town and was indiscriminate. Also, the finding on lawful attack, the Chamber's finding was informed by the total disregard of the civilian population in Knin when the HV shelled several locations, hoping to hit RSK President Milan Martic, even though they knew the chances of hitting him were very slight. I will refer in greater detail to each of these. The only reasonable conclusion to be drawn from all of this evidence is that an unlawful shelling attack on the four towns was planned, ordered and executed. In regard to the issues of margin of error and the significance of the Trial Chamber's findings on specific impact locations as raised in the Chamber's questions 1, 2, and 3, this is the Prosecution's position. First, this goes to question 1, if you consider the evidence available to the Chamber at trial, its use of a 200-metre margin of error in its analysis of the shelling case was not unreasonable. Our answer to question 2 is that any error involving the 200-metre margin of error does not affect the Trial Chamber's findings on impact sites. The 200-metre margin of error was used primarily to assess the testimony of Gotovina's chief of artillery, Rajcic, who claimed that the HV had precise weapons that targeted only lawful targets. The Chamber's exacting analysis of specific impact sites shows first and foremost that projectiles hit all over the towns, including on or near homes, a hospital, a health clinic. The Chamber correctly found that the location and the spread of known impact sites across the towns was inconsistent with Rajcic's claims of precise, lawful targeting. This holds true even if the margin of error was greater than 200 metres. In question 3, the Chamber asks whether the overall finding of unlawful attack should be upheld if the Trial Chamber's conclusions on impact sites are found to be erroneous. Again, the answer is yes. Based on the wide range of evidence which I'll refer to in these submissions, such as the criminal plan discussed at Brioni, and the attack orders themselves, the use of the 200-metre margin of error in connection with findings on the limited number of known impact locations does not affect the overall finding of unlawful attack. Even setting aside margin of error, you can find that the towns themselves were deliberately targeted based on all the other evidence. This Chamber should reject the Defence's attempt to elevate any single item, including margin of error, to such a status that that item alone determines the lawfulness, or not, of an artillery attack. Judges must consider the commander's intent based on all the evidence. Intent is determined by considering all his acts and his omissions, not just by calculating the margin of error of his weapons. The Chamber's consideration of the shelling attack cannot begin with the first shells that hit the four towns, beginning at about 5.00 in the morning on 4th of August. We must first go back to a consideration of the common criminal plan. Although the unlawful attack on the towns of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, and Obrovac formed a significant part of the common plan, it was not the only part. The plan was wider in scope and wider in its implementation. Its precisely this wider scope and how the unlawful attack fits into the overall common criminal plan that support the Trial Chamber's findings on unlawful attack. Like the Trial Chamber, this Chamber must consider the discussion and the agreements made four days earlier at Brioni. There, Gotovina, Markac, and other high-level advisors joined Croatian president Tudjman to discuss the retaking of the Krajina in what was to become known as Operation Storm. As the transcript of this meeting - it's in evidence as Exhibit P461 - makes clear, the Brioni discussion was not confined to legitimate military aspects and goals of the operation. Rather, it reveals that the objective was to ensure that the civilian population itself would be driven from the region as part of the military operation. It is no accident that the removal of the Serb civilian population was a part of the operation. President Tudjman viewed the Serb population in Croatia as a strategic threat. Peter Galbraith, the United States ambassador to Croatia from 1993 to 1998 had frequent meetings and contacts with President Tudjman. In his evidence, Ambassador Galbraith stated: "President Tudjman preferred a reasonably or basically homogenous Croatia. He believed that states ought to be ethnically homogenous or close to it. He believed and stated that the Serbs in Croatia were too numerous and constituted a strategic threat to Croatia. He very much approved the population transfers." That's Exhibit P44 [sic], paragraph 31, referred to in the Judgement, paragraph 1999. Indeed, civilians were one of the issues on which President Tudjman focussed at Brioni, saying: "But as I've said, and we've said it here, that they should be given a way out here ... because it is important that the civilians set out, and then the army will follow them, and when the columns set out, they will have a psychological impact on each other." That's the transcript Brioni, P461, at page 15. In response to this statement, General Gotovina stated that if the Croatian forces continued to exert pressure, the only civilians left would be the ones who were incapable of leaving. And you have the General's remarks on the screens in front of you. "If we continue the pressure possibly for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay." Now, Your Honours, are these the statements that you would expect from military leaders who intend to honour their obligation to protect the civilian population during the attack? "It is important that they set out ... if we continue the pressure ... there won't be so many civilians left?" The Trial Chamber correctly concluded that the discussion of civilians at Brioni was not about protecting them but was, rather, about civilians being forced out. That's paragraph 1995 of the Judgement. The artillery attack that followed four days later must be viewed in this light. That the Serbian population, viewed as a strategic threat, was to be forced out as part of the military operation. Other aspects of the criminal plan that occurred after the shelling attack nonetheless furthered the goal of driving the Serbs out. This sheds light on the nature of the attack itself. We know that on completion of the artillery attack, Gotovina and Markac's ground forces entered the four towns. Gotovina's prediction at Brioni proved to be true. The few Serb civilians who remained after the shelling attack were, for the most part, those who had been too old or weak to flee. For the next two months, these unfortunate individuals were the target of an unrestrained wave of crime and retribution at the hands of Gotovina and Markac's subordinates. Through it all, Gotovina and Markac took no serious measures to put an end to the crimes. The lack of concern for the protection of civilians that manifested itself in General Gotovina's remarks at Brioni was all too apparent in the aftermath of the shelling attack. Another aspect of the overall plan sheds light on the objective of the attack itself. Once the Serbian population was removed from the Krajina after Operation Storm, Croatian government officials took steps to ensure that the Serb civilians who fled would not be able to return. Ethnic Croats were encouraged to move into the houses abandoned by the Serbs. Discriminatory laws were enacted that made it much more difficult for the Serbs to return and claim their homes. Gotovina and Markac themselves were not personally involved in developing these policies. They contributed to the common plan in other ways. However, the policies on preventing Serb returns do tell us about the overall objective of Operation Storm. Thus, as I have said, the unlawful attack cannot be viewed in isolation as a singular event, unconnected to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, in connection with your last point, are you suggesting that your case does not rest on the occurrence of unlawful military attacks?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that at all. What I'm suggesting, Mr. President, is that the lawfulness of the attack has to be assessed in light of all of the events not only that occurred before the attack but also after. The attack is a reflection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But if the attacks are not unlawful --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If the attacks are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- are not unlawful, you still have a case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, we do have a case. My colleague, Ms. Baig, and later today Ms. Brady, are going to address that issue which, as I understand, goes largely to question 4. My submissions, Mr. President, are assuming and, if I may say adamantly, advocate the position based on the evidence that the attack is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The 200-metres question is sort of overarching in this case. Now should the Appeals Chambers - and I'm not indicating in any way that it might or might not - but if the Appeals Chamber were to reverse the finding of the Trial Chamber regarding the 200-metres range of error, how is evidence from the impact sites determined by the Trial Chamber helpful, given that the Trial Chamber itself found that each of the four towns also contained lawful military targets? Couldn't the impacts far from those military targets be simply an error? Is there any significance to be attached to the argument made earlier today by the Defence, pertaining to virtual absence of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try to move through your questions as briefly -- or as succinctly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 200 metres, as I'm going to say, or as I had hoped to say a bit later in my submissions, the 200-metre margin was correct based on the evidence at trial. Now, if it's not correct, this is what we know and how the 200-metre rule was applied. And I'll bring this back to the 95 per cent figure that my colleagues continue to rely on. At the trial, the Chamber was only able to determine the specific location, specific impact sites for about 10 per cent of all the shells that were fired. We know that at least 1200 shells were fired in the four towns during the operation, 900 at least were fired into Knin. When the Trial Chamber talks about specific impact locations, it is only talking about those that it was able to fix, which is only about 10 per cent of the total. If you look at the annex that we attached to our brief, when you look at the known impact locations, the known impact locations, 50 per cent of those fall outside 200 metres, roughly. Half fall in; half fall out. Now, in order to get us to the 95 per cent figure that my learned colleagues refer to, what they've done is to take the other 90 per cent, the unknown impact locations, they've assumed that all of those unknowns actually landed inside 200 metres. There's no basis for making that assumption. So we know that if 5 per cent of the knowns landed within 200 metres, they've added 90 per cent, which are the total number of unknowns to get to their figure. Actually, the number that matters is the spread, the proportion of the known ones. Because if the known shells fall evenly, roughly evenly across the towns, as the Chamber found, and as the witnesses testified to, then there's no basis for assuming that the 90 per cent of the unknown impacts all fell within 200 metres. That's especially the case if you now expand the margin of error out to 400 metres, assume that the weapons they used were twice as inaccurate as the Trial Chamber gave them credit for. So, what we know about the impacts, the known ones, which are the only ones that matter for the purposes of the 200-metre rule because the 200-metre rule was only applied to the known impact locations, that means that roughly half, 50 per cent, fell within 200. Not 95 per cent, as counsel have stated. If I could just respond to your other question, Mr. President, on the presence of military targets in the towns. We've done a number of unlawful shelling cases at this Tribunal, Mr. President, as you and the Judges well know. The fact that there are lawful targets during the course of what's found to be an unlawful attack is not remarkable. And it certainly does not distinguish this case from any of the unlawful shelling cases that we've had here before. Yes, there are lawful targets. But in determining the intent of the shelling operation, you can't simply look at a limited number of places where you know shells fell. You have to look at all the evidence. And with your permission, Mr. President, if I could return to my submissions, I would like to talk about some of the other evidence on this. Apart from the discussion at Brioni, we know that Gotovina issued his attack order on the 2nd of August, two days later. That's in evidence at P1125. And I want to draw the Chamber's attention to the language that the Chamber had at the trial on this point. You've got it in front of you now, Your Honours. What the General has done here was to direct in his order that specific lawful targets, military targets be hit, strikes against the enemy's front line, command posts, communications, and by putting the towns, Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, under artillery fire. This was added in addition to the other targets specified by the General in his order. I should note Drvar, Your Honours, is located outside the scope of the indictment in this case. It's in Bosnia and Herzegovina and was not considered by the Trial Chamber. So, what we see here is language that, as the Trial Chamber sensibly noted, was based on a plain reading of the text of this order. The Trial Chamber found this indicates an order to the HV to treat whole towns in Knin as targets. That's paragraph 1893 of the Judgement. Now, Your Honours, this order and this specific direction was passed down the chain of command. We see it again in the order issued by the General's chief of artillery, Chief of Staff of artillery, Marko Rajic, who, in his order, and you've got the language in front of you now, directed that, in addition to doing all of these other things, neutralising, hitting communications centres, command posts, et cetera, he ordered put the towns under artillery fire. The same language. That's Exhibit D97. Your Honour, the same language moves down the further down the chain of command, closer to the people who are going to be firing these guns. Exhibit P1263 is the order of Zadar Operative Group chief of artillery, Marijan First. He ordered put the following -- excuse me, let me -- I skipped over Mladen Fuzul, OG Zadar commander, who in language virtually identical to Gotovina's ordered his subordinate artillery groups to "lay down fire on the towns of Benkovac and Obrovac." Lay down fire on the towns. The same thing appears in the order issued by OG -- chief of artillery, Marijan First who again orders: "Put the following towns under artillery fire: Benkovac, Gracac, Obrovac." Now, the Defence in their submissions made a lot of statements about firing into civilian areas. Well, these are civilian -- the towns themselves are civilian areas. We know that in addition to the orders themselves emanating from General Gotovina, moving down the chain of command, that contemporaneous reports referred to my colleagues of -- who were actually -- who were made by the people firing the artillery, also support the view that they were, indeed, firing on the towns. This Exhibit P1268 is a report of the TS-4 artillery group that was firing on Knin. Here, in their report, they say that at 1500 hours, in irregular intervals, they fired a total of 18 projectiles from a T-130 - that's one of the artillery guns - at the general area, the general area of Knin. This is perfectly consistent with the language that we see in the orders of the superiors. Now, at trial, Mr. President, I'd like to draw your attention to the testimony of the Prosecution's artillery expert witness, Colonel Konings. Konings was present in Sarajevo during the conflict, and he led UN investigations of shelling incidents there. At trial, this is what he said in reviewing the artillery report we just looked at about the shells fired into Knin. He told the Trial Chamber in this case: "And I have to go back to my experience being six months inside the city of Sarajevo. There was no military purpose. The only purpose of using artillery in this way was harassing a civilian population with the objective to make them flee." He continues: "I have to say it in this clear way because that is the connection that I find in using the word 'irregular intervals,' 18 projectiles in the general area of Knin, and then the connection with the OP order that we discussed before." And the OP order he refers to there is the artillery -- or the attack order issued by General Gotovina. There are more reports issued by different groups, different soldiers in different places who are also reporting the same thing. Exhibit P2385 comes from a log of the special police. At 8.55 in the morning and then again at 11.30 in the morning, Your Honours have it, they say that they are shooting artillery fire. References to artillery fire targeting Gracac and Medak. 11.30, "artillery fire targeting Gracac." Again, targeting towns. The towns themselves being the objects of attack. Another is Exhibit P1200, Your Honours. I'm not going to talk about it in detail. I'll draw your attention to it. These and other reports that the Trial Chamber had supported its finding, its correct finding in our view, that the reporting of the artillery units is consistent with the other evidence indicating that the HV was treating the towns themselves as targets. Paragraphs 1911, 1923, 1935, and 1943. We submit that this interpretation was reasonable given the plain language of the General's attack order, the language of his subordinates' attack orders, and the view that Gotovina expressed at Brioni, that with continued pressure the civilian population would depart. What other explanation can there be for simply shooting projectiles into towns? There's only one reasonable conclusion to be reached. In addition to the attack orders and the reports of the HV's artillery, the Trial Chamber justifiably relied on the testimony of experienced military personnel present in Knin on the 4th and 5th. One of them was UN Sector South commander Forand. He told the Trial Chamber that the shelling of Knin was "indiscriminate and was directed against the civilian population to create mass panic." Another one of these observers was Leslie, who I will talk about further in my submissions. Finally, the Trial Chamber had evidence and rightfully considered evidence of the disproportionate attack on RSK President Milan Martic. The Chamber correctly observed that the manner in which Gotovina's subordinates attempted to shell him in his apartment building revealed its attitude toward the civilian population living in Knin. They fired shells at his presumed location on three occasions on the 4th. The first of these attacks occurred between 7.30 and 8.00 in the morning on the 4th. The HV fired 12, 130-millimetre artillery shells at his apartment building. The Trial Chamber found that this was an otherwise civilian apartment building located in a predominantly civilian area of town. Gotovina's artillery commander, Rajcic, testified that they did this even though they knew the chance of hitting or injuring Martic was very slight. It's at Judgement paragraph 1910. The Trial Chamber found that in this attack there was a significant risk of a high number of civilian casualties and injuries. Its finding was undoubtedly based in part on testimony of Konings. I direct Your Honours to his testimony at page 14316 of the transcript where he talked about what happens when one of these projectiles impacts a civilian area, when a shell -- the -- I should say the -- what he called the "absolute lethal distance" within which a shell will kill everyone in its range. So just to work backward from where I am at this point. During the morning of the 4th of August, while the HV was firing its 130-millimetre shells at Martic's apartment building knowing that they had little opportunity to hit him, Forand and others were experiencing what they concluded was an unlawful attack. The same attack was being directed against the three other towns at the same time. The artillery personnel delivering these projectiles were writing down in their reports that they were firing on the towns, or in the general area of the towns. This is what they've been ordered to do. Their orders lead directly up the chain of command back to General Gotovina. And Gotovina himself had issued this order because, as we know from Brioni, it was necessary that the civilians set out, that they leave. Let me respond to the General's arguments, as well as the Chamber's questions. This brings us down to Gotovina's challenges based on margin of error of the weapons systems he fired. He misunderstands the role that the 200-metre margin played in the Chamber's analysis. In question 1, Your Honours ask whether the Trial Chamber erred in applying the 200-metre margin of error. The answer is no. Based on the record, based on the evidence available at the time, it was reasonable. If you look at Judgement paragraphs 1893 to 1911, you'll find that the primary purpose of the Chamber's margin of error analysis was not to determine conclusively whether the attacks as a whole were unlawful. Rather, the margin of error analysis formed part of the Chamber's assessment of Rajcic's claim that the attack orders, despite their plain text, were interpreted as only pertaining to lawful targets. After considering the number and location of the known impacts that fell more than 200 metres from a lawful target, the Chamber determined that Rajcic's interpretation of the plain language of the orders issued by General Gotovina himself and the others was not credible in light of all the other evidence that I've just summarised. Such as the attack orders, the artillery logs. The Trial Chamber said that it considers that the deliberate firing at areas in Knin which were devoid of military targets is inconsistent with Rajcic's explanation of the HV artillery orders, and the Chamber had every reason to conclude that they were firing deliberately at Knin without respect or without regard to military targets because we see it in the attack orders, and we see it in the reports of the HV's artillery, who were delivering the projectiles into the towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is how the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- if the attacks were, as you are suggesting, deliberate, or even if they were merely indiscriminate, in contrast to Sarajevo which you mentioned a few moments ago, where there were plenty of casualties, could you give me a simple explanation as to how to explain that even if the Defence was not quite accurate in suggesting there were no casualties whatsoever, how do you explain there were so very few?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: There were hundreds and hundreds of shells fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Cross is going to address the issue of civilian casualties in greater detail. I will say this. The unlawful attack that's charged in this case was charged as a persecutory act not as an unlawful attack itself. So that the -- it wasn't required, first and foremost, to prove civilian death. We don't have an annex attached to this indictment in which deaths -- specific victims were identified and whose deaths were proved at trial. It wasn't required because of how the unlawful attack is charged in this case as part of the persecution. Now, as Your Honour, I believe, indicated, you seem to be aware of the evidence in the record about the many witnesses who saw the many casualties, injuries, people lying in the streets of Knin, during the course of the attack on the 4th and the 5th. It bears noting that the HV's infantrymen, their ground forces did not enter these towns, until Knin, midday, on the 5th. So if the witnesses, many of them who have testified about the casualties, the bodies that they've seen on the 4th, there can only be one cause of that. So we see the issue of casualties as somewhat of a red herring, Mr. President. It wasn't required to be proved, and it certainly ignores the fact that the witnesses provide a lot of evidence about the existence of casualties, and, worse, during the course of a shelling attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just ask for my time. Mr. President, my colleagues were going to start throwing things at me if I go over 40 minutes and I'm at 40 minutes now. Let me try to quickly wrap up because I don't believe I have actually gotten to all of your questions and I would like to do that. Question 1 I've answered. It was reasonable based on the evidence. We draw Your Honours' attention to the testimony of Gotovina's artillery Chief of Staff, Rajcic, who spoke about the margin of error of the 130-millimetre guns that were fired on Knin. The Chamber did have the testimony, as was pointed out in the Defence submissions, of Konings about the 155-millimetre weapon, which is a different weapon but which is -- the Trial Chamber considered in factoring in where it was going to come down on margin of error. On the 400-metre margin of error, Mr. President, if I could just add this because now the Defence wants to embrace the testimony of Mr. Leslie who testified about a 400-metre margin of error on a first shot. He did not testify at trial as an expert under Rule 94 bis, and the Defence actually objected to his evidence on that basis at trial. The fact that the Defence now embraces a 400-metre margin of error is notable because this accepts generally that the weapons fired into the four towns were substantially less accurate, less precise than the Trial Chamber gave them credit for. It is also noted because, as Leslie testified, he concluded that the attack was indiscriminate. I refer Your Honours to pages 1990 to 1991 of the Judgement, in which Leslie testified that the fire was all over the place. If, as General Leslie observed, Gotovina's men were firing all over the place, then the margin of error is of little consequence. If they were targeting the towns themselves, based on the attack orders, as reflected in the artillery reports that are being written contemporaneously, then the margin of error doesn't matter. It doesn't affect any findings on the deliberateness of the attack. Your Honours, I'm going to now summarise, and this goes to question 3, going to conclude, I should say. In his report, Colonel Konings described how the artillerymen calculate margin of error. It's mathematics. You refer to firing tables. You factor in the weather. It gives you a range of error, how likely you are to hit the target. He never suggested, nor did the Trial Chamber, that margin of error is the beginning or the end of the analysis. This case does not rise or fall based solely on whether the known impact locations are within or without a margin of error, whatever the margin might be. Your Honours must determine the intent of the commander and his intent is ascertained by considering all the evidence, not simply by calculating margin of error of the weapons the commander deployed. Intent must be determined by considering the commander's behaviour. Not just the behaviour of his weapons, as expressed in margins of error. All of his acts, his orders, his statements, his omissions must be examined. In this case, Your Honours, the Chamber did just that, whether the margin of error of Gotovina's artillery is 200, 400, or 1200 metres, and whether any given projectile impacted 200 metres from a target, 450 or 700, and there's evidence of all of those, it does not change what Gotovina said at Brioni. It doesn't change what he put in his attack order. It doesn't change what's reflected in the attack orders of his subordinates. It doesn't change the fact that, as reflected in the HV's own reports, they were firing into the towns themselves. And it's for those reasons, Mr. President, and this is in response to the Chamber' question 3, any error, any flaws in the Chamber's analysis of the 200-metre rule or on specific impact locations of which only 10 per cent is known does not affect the overall finding of unlawful attack which was justifiably and amply based on all the evidence in the case. Now, unless Your Honours have any more questions, I am going to turn the floor over to my colleague, Mr. Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, may I perhaps ask you a clarification on your position, just to understand it well. Are you pushing your line of reasoning up to the point that even if technically the targets, the targets of the attack, would have been only the military attacks -- or the military targets, the attack itself would have been unlawful because it was a part of a means of committing the crime of forced transfer of the population. Is that your theory?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And you're going to hear more about that in the submissions from my colleagues, Ms. Baig and also Ms. Brady. But if the attack was carried out with the intent to forcibly remove the civilian population, then the -- even if -- and if they were counting on collateral damage, if you will, to bring that about as -- as the result of shelling only lawful targets, then if they possessed the intent, it would, indeed, constitute the criminal -- the triggering event for the deportation. So in this respect, the lawfulness of the attack or not would not affect the overall finding on terms of JCE or deportation. Again, it's our position that the unlawful attack itself was intended and that the towns were deliberately targeted to bring about that very result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So your position is that the attack, even if they have acted against military targets, if they had the purpose of -- not of getting military advantage simply from the attack by destroying the targets, the military targets, but in order to commit a crime, the crime of forced transfer, that would make it unlawful? Even if technically, in theory, justified -- justifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows, the crime of forcible transfer, deportation, can be carried out by means that are lawful or unlawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I get your position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is the Chamber ready for me to pass now to Mr. Cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CROSS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. To answer the second question on the addendum, I shall now address the evidence and findings concerning particular impact locations. And my submissions shall address three points. First, that pursuant to Gotovina and Markac's orders, the HV and special police fired indiscriminately on the towns of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, and Obrovac. They hit both lawful targets and civilian objects alike. Second, That the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the towns themselves were targeted remains reasonable. If all of the impact locations throughout the towns can be explained by a margin of error which is greater than 200 metres, then Your Honours can, and should, draw an inference from that finding of the weapons' very inaccuracy. And given the other evidence in the Judgement, the use of such inaccurate weapons would still support the plain text of Gotovina's order to attack the towns. And, third, Your Honours, this was far from a victimless crime. The unlawful attack on Knin alone dispossessed 14.000 Krajina Serbs from their homes. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for rising. This was an issue that arose in briefing with the parties. I did want to note for the record our objection because it appears that the Prosecution is now arguing disproportionate attack and this was an issue we had raised before and we'd note our objection to it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CROSS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may briefly respond to Mr. Misetic. As Your Honours may recall, the Prosecution made a filing at the end of last week setting out its position with regard to the centrality of proportionality to the case at trial. Given the shortage of time, Your Honours, I do not propose to go through those salient points at this moment unless it would assist Your Honours at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I suggest that we let the counsel for the Prosecution to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CROSS
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honours. And the Prosecution adopts its position set out in the filing to which I referred. And thirdly, as I was saying Your Honour, this was far from a victimless crime. 14.000 Krajina Serbs were dispossessed from Knin alone. Civilian bodies were seen by witnesses lying in the streets and in the hospital, and widespread damage was done to civilian objects. Turning to my first point in detail, I shall use Knin as an example, and the Prosecution relies on its written submissions with respect to the other three towns. In the artillery attack on Knin, the HV did not discriminate between the lawful targets and the multitude of civilian objects which surrounded them. The emphasise in the Judgement on particular impact locations does not mean that the Judgement must be read as saying, These were the only places that were struck. In fact, the even distribution of artillery rounds across Knin is implied by the Chamber's analysis and it supports its conclusion. First of all, the evidence in the trial record is clear that there was no part of Knin which was not under the umbrella of the HV's guns and rockets. And in that respect, Your Honours can see Judgement paragraph 1906, which refers to rounds striking in the north, the south, and the east. And indeed, Your Honours, those findings of particular impact locations support that distribution of rounds hitting all over the town. Thus, rounds hit in the northern borders in a cemetery, and that's in the Judgement at paragraph 1905; in the southern borders of the town, in the field near the UN compound of which the Defence has discussed, that's paragraph 1904; to the very east of the town, by the ECMM HQ, the hospital, and a house known as "marking J," and that's in the Judgement at paragraphs 1903 and 1905; and also in the centre and to the west of town, and that's Judgement paragraphs 1899 and 1900, hitting both lawful targets, civilian objects and residential areas. Now the Chamber reasonably considered that these impacts were not accidents. For example, the cemetery was at least 700 metres from a lawful target. The hospital was at least 450 metres from a lawful target. And that's in the Judgement at paragraph 1905. Likewise, the ECMM HQ was 300 metres from a lawful target. 1903. Nothing in this appeal affects the findings by the Chamber about those particular impact locations. And they remain significant, whatever method is used to evaluate them. Given all of the evidence considered by the Chamber, neither Rajcic's evidence, nor any other evidence in the record, raised a reasonable doubt about the meaning of Gotovina's attack order. Second, Your Honours, turning to the point raised by my learned friends about ratios and statistics. The ratio, as Mr. Stringer said, of impacts on lawful targets or within 200 metres of lawful targets compared to impacts on civilian objects or outside 200 metres from lawful targets also demands the conclusion that the HV fired indiscriminately. Of course, no Chamber could attempt to identify all of the impact locations in an attack of this scale, but the fact that almost 50 per cent of the impact locations are more than 200 metres from a lawful target is significant. This is consistent with all the other evidence, bearing in mind the incomplete nature of the artillery logs. And that fact is referred to in the Judgement at paragraphs 1267, 1367, and 1368. Moreover, Your Honours, the findings in the Judgement supporting the 50 per cent analysis are set out in the annex to our response brief. Now, Gotovina has said, in his brief at paragraph 3, that the Chamber presumed that about 95 per cent of the artillery fire hit lawful targets, but there is no justification for that view in the Judgement. And given the weight of other evidence which supports the indiscriminate nature of the attack, the presumption of innocence did not require the Chamber to make such a finding. Thirdly, Your Honour, the particular impact locations are only part of the story. The reality of the situation in Knin was graver than these individual episodes imply. More widespread. More hazardous for the civilian population. Sergeant Dreyer, who marked Exhibits P78 and P79 to where he had seen artillery impacts, said this: "What I should have done is I should have taken a big pen and drawn a circle right around Knin and not specify and say: This is the area of impact. Because that was the area of impact. Knin itself, in all directions ..." And that's in the transcript at page 1741. As Mr. Stringer briefly mentioned, eye-witnesses in Knin agreed that artillery fire was evenly spread across the town and not especially concentrated on those military targets of which the witnesses were aware, and the Chamber reasonably took this evidence into account. These witnesses included at least six either serving or retired professional military officers. And Your Honours can find that in the Judgement at paragraphs 1278, 1287, 1295 to 1297, 1311, and 1336. Colonel Leslie said, at page 1979 of the transcript: "The fire was, to put it in laymen's terms, all over the place." Moreover, even when the two-day long attack was in its relatively early stages, its indiscriminate nature was patently obvious. And I refer Your Honours on that point to Exhibit P331. Your Honours, may I continue? I'm obliged. The artillery fire itself prompted General Forand immediately to send a letter of protest to Gotovina and the HV commanders, which is in evidence at P83. Your Honours, I shall now turn to address the second question from the addendum more directly. Your Honours asked whether the Chamber's conclusion about impact locations should be upheld if the 200-metre margin was erroneous. And our answer simply is: Yes. The 200-metre margin did form part of the Chamber's analysis, as described by Mr. Stringer, but even so, although the margin was relevant to the Chamber's finding of unlawful attack, it was not necessary to it. Therefore, even if the 200-metre margin of error is removed from the Chamber's analysis, Your Honours can still uphold the finding of unlawful attack. First, on the basis of the comprehensive body of evidence described by Mr. Stringer. Second, on the basis that if Gotovina can show all of the impact locations are explained by the margin of error, then those weapons were inherently unsuitable for use in an urban environment. And, thirdly, on the basis of the disproportionate nature of the HV artillery fire. Since Mr. Stringer has already addressed the first point, I will confine my submissions to the second and briefly also to the third. Your Honours have heard Gotovina assert today that a 400-metre margin of error would have been a reasonable finding for the Chamber rather than 200 metres. But even such a margin of error would not undermine the Chamber's finding. For example, the impacts by the cemetery, 700 metres from a lawful target, and the hospital, 450 metres from a lawful target, still could not be explained as accidental, collateral damage. Indeed, to undermine the Chamber's findings that the impact locations could not have been accidental, Your Honours would need to be satisfied that a 700-metre margin of error was applicable. And Gotovina has pointed to nothing in the record which supports such a margin, much less that the Chamber was unreasonable for not considering it. Moreover, even if the evidence were to show that the HV artillery, in fact, had a 700-metre margin of error or even a greater margin of error still, then that factor should be taken into account in assessing the intent behind the attack. The HV gunners were trained and experienced - that's in the Judgement at paragraph 1183 - and they and their commanders would have known the error of their weapons. Use of such inaccurate weapons in the context of these four towns would strongly indicate the intent to treat the whole towns as targets. And, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber has expressly recognised such an approach in the case of Martic, and that's in the Martic Appeals Judgement at paragraphs 260 to 261; in the Strugar Appeal Judgement at paragraph 275; and in the Galic Appeal Judgement at paragraph 132. Further still, in the footnote to which my learned friend's referred, the Chamber itself recognised the application of this approach. So in footnote 932 of its Judgement, volume 2, the Chamber said of its findings about particular impact locations: "Had these impacts which were at a distance of up to 700 metres from artillery targets been the result of the inaccuracy of the weapons ... that would require a further consideration of whether such inaccurate weaponry can be used in the context of an artillery attack on specific targets within a town." This footnote, Your Honours, was not an acknowledgment that the Chamber could not determine the proper margin of error, but, rather, an acknowledgment that if the margin of error was much greater than it appreciated it to be, then it would also have taken that into account in its analysis. Finally, Your Honours, the Chamber's approach to proportionality would also support its overall finding even if the 200-metre margin was unreasonable. The Chamber expressly regarded the three separate attacks on Martic's location, which it found to be disproportionate, as "an indicative example." And that's at footnote 935 of volume 2 of the Judgement. The Chamber also made all the necessary findings to show that the other attacks on Knin could also have been disproportionate. Since all of the targets were in the vicinity of civilians and civilian objects, the Chamber's finding of, and I quote, "a significant risk of a high number of civilian casualties," and that's in paragraph 1910 of the Judgement, "related equally to them all." As for the limited military advantage, the Chamber expressly noted that the targets themselves were physical structures, they were buildings, and the number of troops present in Knin was only about 150. And that's in the Judgement at paragraphs 1225 and 1397. And also, Your Honour, in the context of Judge Meron's question earlier about targets of opportunity, in paragraph 1908 where the Chamber considered this with respect to Knin, they again noted that even if there were observers, such that they could have been engaged, the number of those targets within the city on the evidence was not sufficient for such action. These targets taken together certainly did not require at least 900 rounds of artillery fire, fired for 26 hours out of a 31-hour period, using both rockets and guns. Such attacks were disproportionate. And for some of the relevant factors in this analysis, Your Honours can see, for example, the Judgement at paragraph 1184, and also the report of Prosecution expert witness Konings, which is Exhibit P1260. That's in fact the addendum to his report. Your Honours, in the interests of time, I will now touch very briefly on the aspect of victims and then I shall defer to my learned friend Ms. Baig. As I have already said, the town of Knin contained approximately 15.000 civilians on the morning of the 4th of August, and that's in the Judgement at paragraphs 1233, 1577, and 1747. But by the time the HV troops arrived on the 5th of August, just a day and a half later, during which time the shelling attack was in progress, approximately 14.000 of these 15.000 people had fled their homes in terror as result of the attack. And that's in the Judgement at paragraph 1743 and 1747. And all of these individuals are victims in the sense that they're affected by the shelling. With regard to findings about civilian deaths or injury or damage to particular civilian objects, as Mr. Stringer has said, Gotovina and Markac were charged with persecution by way of unlawful attack, which has no results requirement, rather than unlawful attack itself. But the fact that the Chamber didn't make findings on the point doesn't mean that it did not hear evidence on the point. At least seven eye-witnesses referred to seeing what they thought were the bodies of civilians killed in Knin in that period. And Your Honours can find those references at paragraphs 1287, 1291 to 1292, 1302, 1307, 1333, 1336, and 1390 of the Judgement. Likewise, Your Honours, at least nine eye-witnesses testified about the widespread damage done to civilian objects in the town. And Your Honours can find that in the Judgement also, roughly between 1276 and 1349. Many of these witnesses did note that the damage done was less than they might have expected from the violence of the shelling that they had experienced, but this is consistent with the evidence of Prosecution expert witness Konings as to the effects of the kinds of munitions that were used. And Your Honours can find that in Exhibits P1259 and P1260. Lieutenant Liborius, who was an eye-witness, also noted that the use of rockets against Knin would have very limited effect against targets such as buildings. He said: "The use of especially multiple rocket systems of modest calibre appeared to me to terrify people as this weapon has no real effect on hard targets." And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly requested to slow down in order to facilitate the simultaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CROSS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, rockets accounted for almost 45 per cent of the rounds fired in the unlawful attack. And that's in the Judgement at paragraphs 1263 to 1265. On my very final point, Your Honours, the damage assessments carried out by some international observers, as Mr. Gotovina referred, were in many cases significantly underestimating the extent of the damage. These matters were fully and reasonably addressed in the Judgement and the Prosecution relies in that respect on the arguments set out in its response brief at paragraphs 46 to 49. Your Honours, unless Your Honours have any further questions, this concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm responding to question 4. In doing so, I will touch very briefly on a few points raised by the Appellant in grounds 2, 3, and 4, concerning deportation and joint criminal enterprise. Unless you have specific questions on these issues, the Prosecution would rely on its brief. In question 4, the Appeals Chamber has asked whether the Trial Chamber's findings that a JCE existed should be upheld if its findings -- that illegal artillery attacks took place is deemed erroneous because of errors resulting from the application of the margin of error. Your Honours, the Prosecution's short response to this is: Yes. Because the JCE members intended these artillery attacks to cause the deportation of the Serb civilian population from the Krajina. Before I go on to explain this position in more detail, I'd like first to clarify that the Prosecution is not suggesting the criminalisation of legitimate warfare. Nor is it upsetting the balance between human protection and military necessity as was suggested this morning. In the hypothetical situation of a military commander who to achieve a military objective launches an artillery attack against military targets and this results in unforeseen and incidental civilian flight, there could in that situation be no basis for a conviction for deportation as a crime against humanity. Such a commander would not have the necessary intention required for that crime, nor would the action form part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population. But I must emphasise, Your Honours, that as much as the Defence attempts to spin the Judgement towards that hypothetical, Gotovina is not in the position of this hypothetical and innocent commander. Instead, Gotovina and his fellow JCE members shared the direct intention to deport using the artillery attack as the means to achieve this end, and that's found at paragraph 2314 of the Judgement. As a result of the shelling, 20.000 Serb civilians fled from the Krajina in a sudden and mass exodus. Croatian forces didn't just seek to defeat their military opposition to take control of the region. They also aimed at a crime - emptying the land of its Serb habitants. Harming the civilian population was an objective of the military operation. Gotovina's criminal convictions, including the Trial Chamber's findings that a JCE existed, should therefore be upheld even if the artillery attack findings are invalidated. Overall, the operation was still unlawful under the laws and customs of war because it was aimed at achieving the expulsion of the civilian population. This purpose is expressly prohibited by basic principles of international humanitarian law which undoubtedly form part of custom. And I'll briefly touch on the principles of distinction and humanity as well as the international humanitarian provisions on deportation. At its most basic, the principle of distinction requires the parties to direct their military actions against military rather than civilian objectives. Examples of this provision can be found in Articles 48, 51(2), 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, and Article 13(2) of AP 2, as well as many others. As the preamble of the St. Petersburg Declaration of 1867 states: "The only legitimate object which States should endeavour to accomplish during war is to weaken the military forces of the enemy." This principle is codified in Article 48 of Additional Protocol I, the basic rule concerning protection of the civilian population. The parties to the conflict shall "direct their operations only against military objectives." Operation Storm in contrast was directed against a civilian objective - to achieve the removal of the civilian population. International humanitarian law, of course, also encompasses the principle of humanity which demands that the parties limit, as much as possible, the effects of war on the civilian population. Common Article 3 to the Geneva Convention, for example, prohibits deportations and transfers as violence to life and person and outrages upon personal dignity. Again, Operation Storm violated this principle by intentionally subjecting the civilian population to these harms through deportation. Moreover, forcible movement of civilians is strictly regulated by international humanitarian law, for example, Article 49 of Geneva Convention 4 and Article 17 of AP 2, and allowed only under the most stringent conditions, none of which were satisfied in this case. Generally speaking, the population can only be moved to ensure its security or for imperative military reasons. The move can only be temporary, provision must be made for the safety and care of the civilians. Violent or arbitrary means or a lack of provision for health and safety would in themselves make such transfers unlawful under IHL. Thus, under IHL, the shelling in this operation was illegal not only because it targeted whole towns as explained by my colleagues. It was also illegal under IHL because it was aimed at causing the deportation of the Serb civilian population. A further violation of the principles of distinction and humanity. In sum, it wasn't only the means that was illegal. So too was the intended result. More importantly for this case, there can be no question that this amounted to deportation as a crime against humanity, which I will move to shortly. In many cases, Your Honour, if it turns out that the accused targeted military objectives, then it might be very difficult to infer any criminal intention. In this case, however, the JCE members illegal objective for the military operation was clear. We have a transcript of the JCE members planning their criminal operation. The JCE members then committed the crime of deportation by shelling the towns and causing the mass exodus of 20.000 Krajina Serbs. Immediately afterwards, Tudjman, the president and supreme commander of the armed forces and a key member of the JCE, bragged publicly about the efficiency of the criminal expulsion. Gotovina and others encouraged a crime wave against Serbs -- remaining Serbs and their property, causing further deportations. Finally, to ensure that the Serbs who had left could not return to the Krajina, members of the JCE instituted discriminatory laws and policies aimed at preventing their return to Croatia and transferring their property to Croats in accordance with the Croatian leadership's demographic re-colonisation policy. Taking these findings as a whole, it's clear that the JCE member, including Gotovina, shared the intent to deport the civilian population and then executed this common criminal purpose. This was not a military attack that led to an unintended consequence as Gotovina would have you believe. It was a crime committed purposefully, in tandem with a military operation. Let me briefly take you to a few of the details, turning first to the Brioni meeting. The Trial Chamber found that in the context of a long ethnic struggle between Serbs and Croats in the Krajina region, JCE members were planning an attack aimed at expelling the Serb population from the Krajina and then keeping them out. This is supported by the transcript of the meeting. As Mr. Stringer has already mentioned, Gotovina suggests that if the HV continued pressure, then "for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving." And that's at P461, page 15, discussed in the Judgement at paragraph 2304. Gotovina's comments confirm that he knew that an artillery attack would cause civilian flight and keep civilians out. Gotovina's attempt to isolate this comment as an innocent prediction is untenable in the context of the transcript of the whole -- as a whole, and in the context of the rest of the evidential record which shows that this was the intent behind the operation. Equally, his repeated claims that he was not talking specifically about Serbs must be rejected in light of the ethnically charged context. Moreover, the Chamber properly rejected the Defence argument that this exchange concerned moving civilians out of harm's way, explicitly finding that this was not a reasonable interpretation. It noted that the participants made no reference whatsoever as to how the military operation could be carried out in a way to minimise civilian harm. Instead the focus of the discussion was on creating a pretext for using the artillery and engaging artillery for "complete demoralisation." Gotovina confirmed that Knin could be destroyed in its entirety in a few hours. Statements of the other participants demonstrate that the JCE members shared this intent to deport, that the objective of the operation was to cleanse the area. For example, Tudjman proposed using propaganda to increase civilian chaos and encourage additional civilian departures. Leaflets in which they would pretend to encourage Serbs to stay, by "ostensibly" guaranteeing their rights. The Chamber gave very detailed consideration to the parties' submissions, particularly concerning the translation and the correct interpretation of this particular exchange, finding that it was an "expression of the true intent to show Serbs out but at the same time giving them the impression that they could stay." And that's at paragraph 1994 of the Judgement. The Chamber found that within days of this discussion, Gotovina's comments that the only remaining Serbs would be the ones who couldn't leave became a reality. Gotovina planned, ordered and conducted the artillery attack aimed at cleansing the area of its Serb population. Whether or not the artillery attack also targeted military objectives, the Chamber found that as a result of Operation Storm shelling, "large parts of the civilian population of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, amounting to at least 20.000 people, were forcibly displaced from their homes and fled across the border to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia." At 2305 of the Judgement. This was exactly the result that was planned during the meeting. Gotovina's contributions to the common criminal purpose do not depend on the artillery attack being found unlawful in and of itself, and I remind you that a JCE contribution need not be criminal per se. And you can find that at the Krajisnik Appeals Judgement, paragraph 215. I should point out here that the issue of lawful or unlawful targeting has no effect on the causation of the mass exodus. Deportation as a crime against humanity does not require that the underlying means of carrying out the deportation is unlawful in and of itself. For example, forcible displacement crimes have been carried out through hate speech, propaganda, and the driving of buses, which may not be criminal per se. In this case, the evidence proves that the shelling was the cause of the mass exodus. Witness after witness confirmed that the civilians left the Krajina because of the shelling. And to take up the issue raised by my colleagues this morning, I would point you briefly to Witnesses 6 and 54 as examples of witnesses who said specifically that they left because of the shelling. There are many more in the transcripts. And they left because of the shelling, Your Honours, not because of any evacuation order. My colleague Ingrid Elliott will discuss the evacuation in more detail in relation to Markac's appeal this afternoon. But the evacuation order came far too late in the afternoon, once the civilians were also already fleeing, if it was even distributed. And there is considerable evidence and findings about the evacuation order coming far too late and questions about its dissemination that Ms. Elliott will discuss. Regardless of the legal characterization of the shellings, Your Honour, it was still the actus reus of the deportation. And what of the few Serbs that Gotovina mentioned at Brioni who had no possibility of leaving? Well, they were subjected to further abuse, including additional persecutions, murders, inhumane acts, cruel treatment, unlawful detentions, wanton destruction, and plunder. These crimes caused further deportations. The Chamber found that in addition to ordering and commanding Operation Storm, Gotovina also contributed to the JCE by failing to make a serious effort to prevent and follow up on crimes committed by his subordinates against the Serb civilians and Serb property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You might be going a bit too fast for our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have -- I didn't hear that. I apologise. So the Chamber found that Gotovina also contributed to the JCE by failing to make a serious effort to prevent and follow up on crimes committed by his subordinates against the Serb civilians and Serb property after Operation Storm. This failure further confirms Gotovina's intentions. Instead of taking the available measures to prevent or punish, Gotovina excused his subordinates' crimes by claiming that these were acts of understandable revenge. These actions are inconsistent with Gotovina's claims of innocent conduct or innocent intention. Finally, Your Honours, before I conclude, I should emphasise that if the Chamber were to find that the JCE conviction was unsustainable, this would require the Chamber to make further findings on the other modes of liability as the Appeals Chamber did in the Dragomir Milosevic case. For example, for the reasons that I've just discussed, Gotovina would in any event be guilty of aiding and abetting the crimes of the JCE because he knowingly made a substantial contribution to them. Likewise, the Chamber would have to consider Gotovina's criminal responsibility as an aider and abettor or instigator and under the doctrine of superior responsibility for the follow-on crimes committed after Operation Storm. To wrap up the Prosecution's response on question 4, Your Honours, even if the Appeals Chamber finds, first, that the Trial Chamber erred applying the margin of error, then that this affects the Trial Chamber's conclusion about impact sites and that this leads to a reversal of the Chamber's findings concerning the illegality of the artillery attacks themselves, the Chamber's finding that Gotovina is guilty of participating in a JCE to permanently remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina should be upheld. Gotovina and his fellow JCE members shared the common criminal purpose to deport of civilian -- the Serb civilian population from the Krajina and carried out that purpose through the shelling attack aimed at harming the civilian population. Moreover, Your Honours, once one looks at Gotovina's illegal order to target the whole towns, his subordinates' orders that repeat this down -- down the chain of command in similar terms, the HV reports back up the chain of command that towns in general had been shelled, the eye-witness accounts of the attack on those towns, and the effect of the shelling, this provides additional confirmation of the Trial Chamber's convictions. Your Honours, may I just wrap up with a final paragraph? Your Honours, Gotovina shared the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise to permanently remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina. To fulfil this common criminal objective, he ordered the forces under his command to treat whole towns as military targets and followed through with an illegal attack against civilians and civilian objects. Subsequently, he failed to prevent or punish his subordinates for committing crimes against the remaining Serbs and their property. As a result of their concerted efforts, some 20.000 Krajina Serbs were forcibly displaced. Many others were killed, injured, and suffered damage to their -- and suffered damage to their homes and property in the aftermath of the operation. Gotovina was properly convicted by the Trial Chamber. He has failed to show any legal error invalidating the verdict or any factual error occasioning a miscarriage of justice, and his appeal should be dismissed in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry, I have an objection. I waited until Ms. Baig had finished, but it's simply this, if I may. The Scheduling Order envisages that the Prosecution to our submissions, respond to our submissions in the afternoon.
