utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I take note of your point. Please do remember that I myself asked a question about evacuation orders, to which they had to respond --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but they won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- but your point --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Your point is well taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to mention also that the evacuation order is also raised by Markac's appeal more fully and it will be discussed there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But not our oral submissions. This is the chance to respond to oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think that we will let it go as it is. The Court has listened to the argument and will be fair in their evaluation and assessment, I can assure you. Okay. 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Reply for Mr. Gotovina. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In reply, let me start my remarks, Mr. President, by noting something that must be noted by the Appeals Chamber as well, and that is the dramatic change in the Prosecution's case from its pre-trial brief to its remarks today. We, as Defence counsel, we must admit, are a bit flabbergasted at how we have had to sometimes try this case as if we were trying to catch a butterfly, and that is trying to pin down the Prosecution on what its theory of the shelling case is. This started out in the pre-trial brief as a case of almost, per se, unlawfulness of shelling by the firing of artillery on towns that contained no military objectives, and today, after -- through all the years of shifting theories, it went to indiscriminate attacks and then use of weapons that did not respect the principle of distinction, and ultimately, today we are discussing whether the fire on lawful military objectives was the act of deportation that caused civilian flight. That should reveal something to the Appeals Chamber and I note that that is the first time the Prosecution has ever raised that argument in this case. That should tell you something about the evidence in this case and about the strength of the Prosecution's case. The second thing that you should note is that the Prosecution in its presentation virtually, although it made the pro forma defences of the Trial Judgement, spent most of its time abandoning the Trial Chamber's reasoning and adopting brand new reasoning. For example, whereas the Trial Chamber drew its inferences of criminal mens rea from the actus reus having been allegedly proven, the Prosecution now says, well, if we haven't proven the actus reus, then we ask you to infer from the proven criminal mens rea that there was an intent to deport and therefore you should start looking at whether the targeting of lawful military objectives constitutes the crime of deportation. This morning we went item by item, and we will not repeat ourselves, about how the Trial Chamber inferred criminal intent into HV artillery reports, how it infer -- how it rejected Marko Rajcic's testimony from its finding of the commission of an unlawful attack. The Prosecution did not address any of the arguments we raised this morning. The second issue is the Prosecution now argues disproportionate attack and that that somehow is consistent with the Trial Chamber's findings, despite the fact that the Trial Chamber in footnotes 932 and 935 expressly said that it would not consider the proportionality of the overall attack except for the Martic incident. Third, the Prosecution now argues that MBRLs were improper to use on the towns, despite the express finding of the Trial Chamber to the contrary at paragraph 1897 of the Judgement. Fourth, and perhaps most importantly, although all of these points are important, this argument about firing on military objectives with an unlawful purpose is inconsistent with the Trial Chamber's own findings. And I draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to paragraphs 1899 and 1900, 1901, 1902, and that's just for Knin. The last sentence of all those paragraphs say: "In light of these findings, the Trial Chamber considers that the evidence allows for the reasonable interpretation that the HV may have determined in good faith that firing," in this case, "at the railway station and post office would have offered a definite military advantage." The Trial Chamber then in the subsequent paragraphs again says that the identification of these targets in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, the Trial Chamber found there was sufficient basis in the evidence to conclude that they were selected in good faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My colleague Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's no interpretation. We don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You probably have to change the channel? No, you are okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The LiveNote also doesn't have it, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Can we try again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Are you having interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. And the court reporter is not either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we stop for a second and address this issue Just wait one second -- or you will ask in English? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat my question. I'd like to know to what extent it's been unreasonable for a Trial Chamber to infer the civilian character of areas where there were no military targets, since the civilian character seemed to have been -- may have been induced without any evidence to support it. Should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How, and in what was it unreasonable, for a Trial Chamber to infer the civilian character of areas where there were no military objectives, military targets? The civilian character may be -- may the civilian character be inferred from a general statement without any evidence to support it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was completely unreasonable for several reasons. First, as we noted this morning, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement says that the Prosecution bears the burden of proving that a "object was indeed dedicated to civilian purposes." And the Appeals Chamber there rejected the -- what otherwise in Additional Protocol I is a presumption of civilian-ness unless the military nature of a target has been established. In a criminal case, the Prosecution bears the burden of proofing that fact. The second reason it's unreasonable is the Trial Chamber itself at Trial Judgement paragraph 1267 said that the -- concludes that the Croatian army fired on more targets in Knin than it is aware of based on the evidence available to the Chamber. The Trial Chamber thus assumed either that there couldn't have been additional military objectives in those "civilian areas" or else assumed that those targets, if they were within 200 metres, were civilian targets, i.e., unlawful targets of artillery fire. So by simply drawing inferences of civilian areas based exclusively on whether the area is 200 metres away from a military objective tells us nothing about that particular area. And we use the example of the railway fuel storage in Knin. The Trial Chamber found that the railway station was a legitimate military objective but then found that the fuel used for the railway system was civilian because the station was 200 metres away from an objective -- objective that the Chamber could find in the evidence. Whether the railway fuel was being used for a military purpose in support of the railway system that was a military objective is a question the Trial Chamber didn't even attempt to answer because the Prosecution never introduced any evidence of civilian purpose of any particular area because its proposition at the beginning of the trial was the entire town is a civilian zone and there are no military objectives in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To complete the point that I was making earlier, in terms of the Trial Chamber's findings that these targets were identified in good faith as offering a military advantage, the Prosecution's new case would require that the HV in fact identify those objectives in bad faith. Because if the targeting of an objective has as its real purpose to target the civilian population, then by definition that cannot be good faith and it is by definition bad faith identifying of military objectives. So the Prosecution is asking you to make a series of findings in conflict with the Trial Chamber's own. And, unfortunately, we do not have time in 30 minutes to go through each of the military objectives that was established at trial as to why they offered a significant military advantage to the Croatian army in its effort to liberate its own territory and to seize the capital of a break-away Serb entity. Next, in addressing some comments that were made about Mr. Galbraith and the Brioni transcript, the Prosecution talks about Mr. Galbraith's views of President Tudjman but ignores the more important issue of Ambassador Galbraith's conclusions about Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I am sorry, but the Bench had to consult and now you can proceed, say something about the procedure with regard to the point you have raised earlier with regard to the alleged novelty of the theory advanced today by the Prosecution and how we deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next issue to address is the attempt by the Prosecution to inject Ambassador Galbraith's views and whatever his views of President Tudjman were he had very specific views of what happened in Operation Storm, and I cite the Appeals Chamber to the trial transcript of his testimony at 5055 to 5056 under questioning by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber: "First of all, Mr. Galbraith, do you consider the purpose of operation form primarily to expel the Serbs?" Answer: "No, not all."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Do you consider that this was or could be a side-effect of militarily taking over the Krajina territory and have it within Croatia again?" His answer: "I did not consider that the expulsion of the Serbs would a side effect but I did consider that the departure of the Serbs would be a side-effect." And that is the distinction that we have consistently argued at trial and in our briefing here, and which the Prosecution conveniently ignores. The participants at the Brioni meeting, as noted in our brief, had 60 days prior the experience of the events of Western Slavonia where the entire Serb civilian population left and it was clear based on investigations and indeed the conclusions of the Secretary-General of the United Nations that they theft for reasons unrelated to any unlawful contact by the HV. The Brioni participants certainly would have been aware of that possibility, indeed likelihood, that a similar thing might take place if they try to liberate their territory in Sectors North and South as well. That is what the discussion at Brioni is about. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber itself, as we've noted several times today, found that the Serb civilians left everywhere but the four towns for reasons unrelated to any unlawful contact. So were the Brioni participants talking about all of those civilians leaving who did leave for reasons related to any unlawful contact as found by the Trial Chamber? Or were they talking about implying that they should target civilians in four towns to force them to leave? And the question arises: How reasonable is it that if Serb civilians had evacuated Western Slavonia 60 days earlier and had evacuated the entire Krajina except for four towns for reasons unrelated to any unlawful conduct by the HV, that they would have stayed in the four towns but for the illegal conduct of the HV, or, as we heard this morning, the lawful targeting by the HV intended to force them to flee. We submit to Your Honours there is no basis for that inference in the Brioni transcript. They mention General Gotovina's comment at Brioni, and, again, so I don't repeat myself, General Gotovina's comment was perfectly accurate as found by the Trial Chamber in all places but the four towns. And you have military commanders considering, What are we to do if the civilian population decides to leave en masse as they had done 60 days later? That is the discussion. And the conclusion is: Let the civilians leave. What is the alternative? To trap civilians in a war zone? To force their army to continue to fight for their civilians? Turning again to another issue regarding these 95 per cent of rounds. The Prosecution twists our position and we need to clarify this. We have pointed the Appeals Chamber to a chart that was submitted on the 7th of October to the Appeals Chamber in a filing. What we are saying is the Trial Chamber found that 95 per cent of all projectiles were fired at military objectives. The second question that then arises which the straw man that the Prosecution was addressing this morning is, where did those projectiles land and we only know where a certain number landed. The Prosecution -- it is the Prosecution's case, whether they acknowledge it or not, that every one of those rounds fired at a military objective, i.e., 850 out of the 900 rounds, must have landed within 200 metres. Why do we say that? Because they say and they are defending the 200-metre rule this morning. And the 200-metre rule says there can be no explanation for a shell falling outside of 200 metres except if the Croatian army intended to fire outside of that 200-metre radius. The Prosecution says there can be no inherently indiscriminate nature of the weapons if the 200-metre survives. Therefore, if the Croatian army intended to fire 850 rounds at military objectives, then the Trial Chamber's case and the Prosecution's defence of that case must mean that every one of those rounds fell within 200 metres. The Prosecution discusses General Gotovina's order as well as the fact that the order was repeated by subordinates. Again, the Trial Chamber's approach here was to reject Marko Rajcic's testimony on the basis of its conclusions about impact locations and we need not repeat our positions already argued this morning. But if Marko Rajcic's testimony was corroborated and correct and could not be excluded on the basis of findings on impact areas, then all we are left is a lawful order that was repeated down the chain of command. We noted and there was some discussion by my learned friend, Mr. Cross, this morning, about one shell that landed at 700 metres away. As I noted this morning, and Mr. Cross did not contest, five out of 900 landed beyond the margin of error of the weapons system. Why did one fall at 700 metres? We're not saying that margin of error is the only reason that a shell might fall beyond the margin of error of a weapons system. As I noted to Judge Guney there were additional targets in the town which the Trial Chamber confirmed at paragraph 1267. Was one of those targets by the cemetery which was 700 metes away from another military objectively? The Trial Chamber doesn't answer that question. Were there targets of opportunity? The Trial Chamber, again, found, no, but that conclusion, as we have noted in our briefs, was unreasonable. Concerning casualties -- excuse me, let me address one other point. The Prosecution says that the Trial Chamber considered Konings' testimony on range of error in establishing the 200-metre rule. We pointed out this morning that Mr. Konings, as stated by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 1898, would have set the margin of error at 295 metres for a weapon T-155 at 14 and a half kilometres. So how that could possibly corroborate the Trial Chamber's 200-metre finding is left unexplained by the Prosecution. Concerning casualties, there was a reason that the Trial Chamber made no finding that any person was killed by shelling. And it is certainly much more complex than was presented by Mr. Stringer this morning about if somebody sees a body in the street that person must have been killed by artillery. First, there is the question of the credibility of the witnesses and their statements, a fact that the Trial Chamber does not explore in the Judgement. Second, the Trial Chamber notes in paragraphs 1360 to 1364 that it only had forensics for three persons alleged to have been killed in Knin on 4 August and found that those forensics did not prove that anyone had been killed by shelling. Furthermore, and this is important, it is 18 years since Operation Storm. We don't have anecdotally hearsay-wise any news report of any family member or any human rights organisation or anyone who claims to have lost a loved one in the shelling of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. These alleged bodies that were seen in Knin, to this day, remain completely anonymous. Finally, we note that Witness -- Prosecution witness Mira Grubor, at trial transcript 1418 and 1419 noted that in the entire southern Krajina the only hospital with a surgical ward was in Knin. Whether bodies had been brought there from other locations is, of course, a question that was entirely possible and there was plenty evidence of ARSK forces moving wounded from front line positions into Knin town on that day, a finding that the Chamber made itself in the Trial Judgement. Accordingly, the Prosecution's assertion that if a body is seen, there can be no other explanation other than they were killed by shelling is simply false. Again, on this issue of disproportionate attack I also wish to make the following note, and I know, Mr. President, you have indicated you will address this or may address later, I'm not sure. There is no reference by the Prosecution of proportionality in any filing in this case prior to the commencement of trial. And to the extent that the Prosecution wishes to argue that they're entitled to draw or adduce evidence of proportionality in support of a theory of unlawful attack, that must be laid out in a pre-trial brief to give the accused proper notice and we cite the Appeals Chamber to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in the Galic case where they did exactly that. And they provided proper notice to Mr. Galic that he was being accused of direct attack, including, through disproportionate attack. That was not the case here. A comment was made this morning that Witness 6 and Witness 54 said they left because of shelling. That is completely inaccurate. We have pointed out in our reply brief in this case that the witnesses said, first of all, these witnesses lived in the immediate vicinity of what the Chamber found to be legitimate military objectives. So whether they were afraid of firing on a legitimate military objective, which is, we submit, a much more likely situation, or whether they were made afraid by three shells falling in an empty field more than a kilometre away from them was not explained by the Trial Chamber. Moreover, these individuals expressly said, and we've cited that in our reply brief, that they only left to outlying parts of Knin and other villages, intending to return, but then decided to leave, i.e., cross a de jure or de facto border, to leave the Krajina because others had started to depart after 6.00 p.m., i.e., after Martic issued the evacuation order. There is no person -- and then we were given the general sweeping statement "there are many other who testified to this," and of course that has never been cited in any brief by the Prosecution and nor is it identified in their comments today. Speaking of Knin now. Accordingly, we have no known victims, no hearsay reports of any dead or wounded in the shelling of Knin, and no even hearsay reports of persons saying, I decided to leave the Krajina because of a fear of shelling. Turning now to two additional issues. The Prosecution argues that General Gotovina committed to the JCE -- committed or contributed to the JCE by failing to take available measures to stop crime. As the Appeals Chamber is aware, that finding by the Trial Chamber is erroneous on many levels. First of all, as we noted in our remarks this morning, the Trial Chamber made an express finding that the common criminal purpose did not involve crimes like murder, burning, looting, inhumane conduct, et cetera. Therefore, as noted in our appeal, there is no substantial contribution to that crime, to those -- no substantial contribution to a JCE through those crimes. Furthermore, there can be no deportation of persons in furtherance of the common criminal objective if the Trial Chamber found that those means were not involved in achieving the common criminal purpose. Accordingly, that argument must fail by the Prosecution as well. Secondly, the Prosecution glosses over the Trial Chamber's findings about what measures General Gotovina was supposed to take. It is undisputed or at least it was accepted by the Trial Chamber that General Gotovina during this time immediately after Operation Storm was engaged in combat activities against the Bosnian Serb army in Bosnia when these crimes were taking place. The Trial Chamber found that General Gotovina, indeed, was allowed to presume that subordinates left in Croatia would be doing their jobs appropriately. However, the -- the Trial Chamber found that this presumption was rebutted when General Gotovina allegedly was put on notice that his subordinates were failing in their duties. First of all, there is no finding by the Trial Chamber that any subordinate failed in his duties, or any subordinate entity failed in its duties. So on what basis the Trial Chamber conclude that General Gotovina was required to return from Bosnia to address crime in Croatia is left unexplained because we still don't know who these subordinates were that were not doing their duties properly. As a matter of fact, the Trial Chamber concluded that, for example, the military police was working under difficult circumstances and that it was not proven that there was any intent to not investigate crimes against Serbs. Furthermore, the measures that the Trial Chamber said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Make sure, counsel, that you don't go too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise to the booths and the court reporter. Next, the measures that Trial Chamber says General Gotovina failed to take were completely invented in the Judgement. I say "invented" because they were never discussed at trial, never raised by the Prosecution. They include things like failing to make public statements. That issue was never addressed at trial, and in fact the Prosecution's case was that the Accused Cermak was the person who was supposed to be making public statements. The seconds issue is he failed to uses adequate resources. That issue, as well, is vague, because it's unknown what resources he allegedly failed to deploy. And, third, is that he failed to contact relevant people, period. Who these relevant people are and why General Gotovina was required to contact them is left completely unexplained. The Prosecution had a case on necessary and reasonable measures that General Gotovina should have taken. The Trial Chamber rejected all of those. At that point, the Trial Chamber should have found in favour of the accused. Instead, it came up with three more measures that were never discussed at trial to conclude that General Gotovina's failure to take these measures amounted to a substantial contribution to a JCE. We submit, Your Honours, that that is entirely unreasonable and that an accused, certainly in a trial, should be entitled to know what he is being accused of. Finally, with respect to other modes of liability, the Trial Chamber made express findings that it was not considering alternative modes of liability. It would be entirely inappropriate now for General Gotovina to be convicted of a case of which he has no notice, with no right of appeal, to challenge any finding convicting him of something of which he was not convicted in the first instance. It would be unfair to convict him or something that has not been fully litigated even in front of this Appeals Chamber; indeed these were comments made in passing in a footnote by the Prosecution in its respondent's brief without any further elaboration on why General Gotovina is liable under these alternative theories. Your Honour, if I may, I apologise, just two minutes. Mr. Akhavan wanted to address Judge Pocar's question that was posed to the Prosecution, if we may briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] this will bring our proceedings this morning to their conclusion. Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In response to Judge Pocar's question, the Prosecution clarified its view that lawful combat can be a modality for deportation. We would like to point out that this is in direct contradiction with the submissions at the Rule 72 hearings before the Pre-Trial Chamber where they argued that their case is not -- is not that unlawful -- that lawful combat can be a basis for deportation. We would like to as with as well that the chapeau requirement under Article 5 clearly requires that the civilian population be the primary object of the attack. The definition in customary law of deportation as recognised by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the ICC Statute is that deportation must be on grounds not permitted in international law, which evidently means unlawful means, unlawful means towards an unlawful end. Fourthly, the reference to Article 49 of Geneva Convention 4, which sets forth the customary law standard, is that deportation only applies to territories under the occupation of a belligerent, or the equivalent, in internal armed conflict. Clearly conduct of hostilities is a situation where the territory has not yet been placed under the authority of an adversary. And finally, we point that Article 51, paragraph 2, clearly indicates that with respect to, for example, paragraph 1940 of the ICRC commentary that it is foreseeable that civilians may be terrified of the consequence of combat operations but so long as there is a substantial military advantage, the foreseeability that they may be terrified and the foreseeability that they may even flee cannot be a violation of Article 51(2). So we submit that it would be an extraordinary result if this Appeals Chamber was to say that lawful combat can be transformed in the crime of deportation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akhavan. We will -- You will have this afternoon to reply, in any event, to the Defence of Mr. Markac. It seems to me that you perhaps could combine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, if it is allowable, if it's acceptable to the Chamber, we can [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Or would you like to speak three minutes now in a quick reply or combine it with your answer later to answer to Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think the first point is that we don't accept the characterisation that counsel has just been given of the position taken by the Prosecution at the hearing to which he referred. Beyond that, we'll combine it with our responses this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. The Bench will consider first further the possibility that we will ask both parties to present a short supplementary briefing on the question first raised by the counsel for the Defence regarding novel arguments raised here today for the first time. But we will work on that and we will talk about it this afternoon. Mr. Kehoe, do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just with regard to what is being suggested by the Prosecution, we, of course, object because what we were doing is rebutting the arguments advanced for the first time by the Prosecution. And to allow the Prosecution to then go back for another bite at the apple is simply improper and unfair and in violation of the Scheduling Order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will probably allow both parties to present a written brief on that and that will clarify it. I will not mind if the Prosecution includes a few sentences in its later reply. We will now stop till 1.30. I'm terribly sorry. 2.30, of course. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. I would like to start by reading a decision ordering supplemental briefing. The Judges of the panel have noted the comments made today by Gotovina's counsel, suggesting that the Prosecution has advanced new arguments on the merits of the case. The Appeals Chamber requests that Gotovina set out his objections in a supplemental brief, with a maximum of 3.000 words, submitted by 17 May. The Prosecution may respond within three days of the supplemental brief, with a 3.000-word submission. No reply will be allowed. Now I would like to read out a decision taken in my capacity as a Pre-Appeal Judge. It pertains to Rule 115. So in my capacity as a Pre-Appeal Judge, I note Gotovina's request that the deadline for submitting a reply to the Prosecution response to his second Rule 115 motion be extended to 18 May. I further note that the Prosecution has taken no position on this request, and in view of the full schedule of the last few days, I grant Gotovina's request. And now we will resume our proceedings and we will now hear submissions by Markac. One hour and 30 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly on the recent ruling that you have made about our filing of supplemental briefs, the parties filing supplemental briefs, his is to be submitted 17 May and ours --

utterances.text: 17 May, I think you said, with three days later our response.

utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: May I confirm that would be a Sunday, Your Honour. Can -- is that -- is that the day that it is due, the Sunday, or the following Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and outside the courtroom. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and I'm acting on behalf of Mr. Markac's Defence. After my brief introduction, I will turn over the floor to my learned colleagues Mr. John Jones and, afterwards, Mr. Tomislav Kuzmanovic. And by the end of our submissions, I will kindly request five minutes granted in a private session to address certain matter to the Appeals Chambers. Mr. President, Your Honours, at the very beginning of our oral submissions, we respectfully plea implementation of beneficium cohesionis principle. That is to say, that we gratefully adopt the submissions made on behalf of Ante Gotovina. Our submissions will be directed principally, if not exclusively, to the fourth question posed by the Chamber in its Scheduling Order; namely, whether the Trial Chamber's finding that a joint criminal enterprise existed should be upheld in its finding that illegal artillery attacks took place is deemed erroneous. We say that the answer to this question is plainly: No. There can be no JCE without a finding of unlawful shelling. This is plain from a close reading of the Judgement. The Trial Chamber's finding that there was unlawful shelling permitted, influenced, and indeed determined at its firing [sic] on every single aspect of the JCE. First, it led the Chamber to find that the discussions at the Brioni were about a JCE to remove Serbian population from the Krajina. Paragraphs 2305, 2316, and 2320 of the Judgement. Second, it led the Chamber to find that artillery strikes on Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac were carried out with the intent to deport Serbian populations. See also Judgement paragraphs 1745, 1746, and 1757. It thus led the Chamber to find that the crime of deportation was committed. Fourth, it led the Chamber to find that the crime of persecution was within the JCE and that persecution indeed occurred. Paragraph 1862, 1936, in relation to Gracac; 2310 and 2314 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement. Fifth, it led the Chamber to find that our client, General Markac, participated in an unlawful shelling. Paragraphs 2561 to 258 [sic], and 2583 of the Judgement. And sixth, this way it led to core findings against Markac; namely, that he was a member of the JCE, that he shared the objective of the JCE that he intended to contribute to the JCE, and that he substantially contributed to the JCE. The unlawful shelling attack is thus the linchpin of all of the Chamber's findings in relation to the JCE. If one removed that linchpin, and the notion of the JCE and of Markac's liability falls away. Now, I'm turning the floor to my colleague, Mr. John Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, as everyone knows, a picture is worth a thousand words and so we have prepared a simple visual aid, which should be in front of you, to help in answering Your Honours' fourth question, which I'll paraphrase thus. Assuming no unlawful artillery attacks, can the JCE be upheld? And we say clearly not, and we say that that is beyond argument. So to explain how the flow chart works, you should have it all in hard copy, and also on your screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Are you sure you are really simplifying matters by this not exactly simple picture that you have produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, Mr. President, I didn't want to blind you with science. However, at the same time, you will see, I hope, as I go through it, that this does simplify things and in fact taking it box by box ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just one second. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Hopefully all will, as they say, be revealed as I take you through it. So the bottom box is captured -- captioned "Unlawful artillery attack," and so that's the core finding which, ex hypothesi, for the purpose of answering the Chamber's question 4, is incorrect. And you have the paragraph references for that finding in relation to the four towns, and that's what's indications with the sections and the paragraph numbers. Section, or chapter, 5.8.2(i), and I ask you to remember that chapter because that comes up time and again in the Judgement, 5.8.2. It's the unlawful attack finding. And then for Knin, paragraph 1906, so all these numbers are all references to paragraphs in the Judgement and nothing else. Knin, 1906. Benkovac, 1923. Gracac, 1935. And Obrovac, 1943. So that's where the findings are. So this chart will show how everything, absolutely everything, depends on that finding. Every JCE finding and every finding of liability against Markac. So we have in this Judgement the proverbial pack of cards which if you pull away the bottom card falls down. And this chart shows how and why that is it the case. So first let's see what findings the Chamber directly derived from the unlawful artillery attack finding. I'll call it "the unlawful attack finding" for short. All the boxes on the next row, crimes, denote the findings by the Trial Chamber which derive directly from the unlawful attack finding. And I'll start with the box third from the right, the finding that the Brioni discussion was about a JCE to forcefully and permanently remove Serbs. I take it you can all see that. Third from the right. You have that finding in section 6.2.7, at paragraphs 2305 and 2315 of the Judgement. Now what the arrow below the box shows, pointing up to the box, is how that finding about Brioni and that it was the discussion of a JCE derives directly from and depends on the unlawful attack finding. And that's clear from paragraphs, as you see, 2305, 2316, and 2320 of the Judgement. Para 23305 reads, and we'll call it on the screen for everyone: "The Trial Chamber has carefully considered the minutes of the Brioni meeting in chapter 6.2.2. It here further considers them in light of subsequent events," and I would underline those words, "in light of subsequent events, as found by the Trial Chamber (see in particular chapters 4.4 and 5.8.2(i)." So those are the chapters, the sections on unlawful attacks. "Within days of the discussion at Brioni, Gotovina's words became a reality. Operation Storm was launched in the early morning of 4 August 1995 with artillery attacks on a number of towns and villages in the Krajina, including Knin. As the Trial Chamber has found in chapters 4.4 and 5.8.2(i), in at least some of these attacks the entire towns were treated as targets for the artillery. These attacks therefore constituted unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects. As a result, large parts of the civilian population of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, amounting to at least 20.000 people, were forcibly displaced from their homes and fled across the border to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. As the Trial Chamber has found in chapter 4.5 and 5.4.2 this constituted deportation." So the Trial Chamber used the unlawful attacks finding to find that the Brioni discussions was about a JCE forcibly to displace Serbs. Then we go to 2316, and 2316 - sorry - deals with President Tudjman, and it says, and I will just reads the beginning and end: "Franjo Tudjman was a leading participant at all important meetings at which matters relating to the joint criminal enterprise were discussed. He ensured that his ideas were transformed into policy and action, through his powerful position as President and Supreme Commander of the armed forces." So pausing there, the Trial Chamber sees Tudjman as the mastermind and principal architect of the JCE. So can we then turn the page and read three lines down: "Considering the discussions at the Brioni meeting and the events that subsequently took place," so again underline those words, please, "and the events that subsequently took place, the Trial Chamber finds that he," Tudjman, "for this purpose, intended to remove the Serb civilian population by force --" Ah, I was wondering how long it would be before the first injunction to slow down and it has arrived. I will do my best. "Considering the discussions at the Brioni meeting and the events that subsequently took place, the Trial Chamber finds that he," meaning, Tudjman, "for this purpose, intended to remove the Serb civilian population by force, including through the crimes within the purpose of the JCE." So Tudjman's intentions and thus the meaning of what was discussed at Brioni, which he led the discussions, is interpreted in light of the unlawful attack finding, through that prism. And then paragraph 2320, I'll just read three sentences down: "At the Brioni meeting, Tudjman and high ranking military officials discussed how the military forces should be used to ensure that not only the SVK but also the Serb civilian population would leave the Krajina. One of the means ultimately used was in itself a crime, namely, unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects in a number of towns in the Krajina." So we say it is crystal-clear that the Trial Chamber systematically interpreted the Brioni transcript, itself ambiguous at best regarding the existence of a JCE, interpreted the Brioni transcript "in light of subsequent events," namely, in light of its unlawful attack finding, and in light of its, ex hypothesi, erroneous finding that one of the means to carry out the JCE was itself a crime of unlawful attacks. Now just to digress, the Prosecution tacitly admit in their response to our appeals brief that Brioni is not indicative, certainly not beyond a reasonable doubt, of a JCE. And that's in paragraph 84 of their response to our appeals brief, where they say: "Third, Markac ignores the relevant context in which to assess his participation in the Brioni meeting. This includes the subsequent implementation of the JCE to remove the Krajina Serbs and Markac's contribution to it. Within days of the meeting, an unlawful artillery attack was unleashed on the Krajina Serb civilians. As a result, large parts of the population were displaced." And then it goes down, last sentence: "Given that the Brioni meeting provided the platform for the unlawful attack on the Krajina Serb civilians, Markac's attempt to artificially separate his participation at the Brioni meeting from the ensuing events should be rejected." So, in other words, you can't separate the Brioni assessment from the later unlawful attacks, which, ex hypothesi, are not unlawful at all. So Brioni alone, the Prosecution admits, does not reveal a JCE. And you have seen this morning the equivalent admissions by the Prosecution in paragraphs -- I think it was 234, 239, 268, and 271 of their response to the Gotovina brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Question to the French booth: Is it too fast for you? Is it okay, French booth?

utterances.text: It's a little fast.
