utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Too fast, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you will have to slow down a little bit or we will be without interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll take it at a snail's pace, then. So if you pick up the Brioni transcript, and it's an exhibit, P461, and read carefully through it, in its own context, you will not find a JCE. It was only by coupling the Brioni transcript with an alleged unlawful attack that the Chamber could find a JCE. And I refer to the transcript, the transcript, because, of course, not a single witness confirmed the Chamber's interpretation of the meeting. And isn't it extraordinary when two men are sent to prison for 23 years and 18 years on the basis of a JCE which allegedly crystallised at the Brioni meeting but not a witness in the world can be found to say that Brioni was about a JCE. It would be different if Brioni transcript on its face was clearly criminal, clearly, obviously criminal, but it isn't. So now, ex hypothesi, the unlawful attack finding was wrong, and therefore the Brioni transcript denuded of that incriminating context is innocuous, plain and simple, and that finding Brioni was about a JCE falls away. In fact, the discussions at Brioni are perfectly consistent with what the Trial Chamber found was a reasonable interpretation of what happened in every town and village apart from the four towns. Namely, a recognition by the Brioni participants of the well-known fact, well known, as you've heard, Ambassador Galbraith himself recognised it, that the Serbs would leave the Krajina out of a general fear of the HV, general fear of hostilities, general living conditions and other non-JCE-related factors. And on this subject, let's look at paragraph 1762 of the Judgement. And it should appear on the screen in a moment. Oh, I'm sorry, I'll just have to read it, then. The reference -- I imagine most parties have the Judgement in front of them. It starts five lines from the bottom: "The Trial Chamber recalls its finding ... that international armed conflict existed throughout the indictment period and area. The Trial Chamber considers that the commencement of the armed conflict may in itself have brought about fears of the violence associated with armed conflict, as a result of which civilians fled. In this respect, the tripe also considers the evidence of and its finding in chapter 4.5.3 ... on persons leaving the RSK in late July and early August 1995," i.e., before Storm, "in part because they believed a Croatian military operation was imminent. In the number of aforementioned incidents, the evidence indicates that the reasons for departure included the departure of others and a fear of violence associated with the expected imminent arrival of Croatian armed forces. For instance, Petar Colovic testified that his family left because many others were leaving. RSK officials told the inhabitants of Oton Polje to leave on 4 August 1995, because" so-called "'Ustashi' forces were approaching. Sovilj told his family to leave Kijani at 1 a.m. on 5 August 1995 for security reasons, because the HV might have entered the area." And then the important bit: "Considering that persons left the aforementioned locations prior to the commission of crimes or other threatening acts by members of Croatian military forces or special police in or near these locations, the Trial Chamber cannot conclusively determine that acts by members of Croatian military forces or special police created an environment in which those present had no choice but to leave. Instead, the Trial Chamber considers that the evidence allows for the reasonable interpretation that these persons left because of a fear of the violence commonly associated with armed conflict, or general fears of Croatian forces or distrust of Croatian authorities. Consequently, the Trial Chamber cannot conclude that these persons were forcibly deported [sic]." But in fact without the unlawful attack finding, the evidence allows for that interpretation in every case, including the four towns. So if you read the Brioni transcript, it is completely consistent with nothing more than the participants recognising the basic reality that the Trial Chamber itself outlined at paragraph 1762; namely, that Serbs would simply leave the Krajina when hostilities began. So I go back to the box and second from the left is captioned -- second from the left, yes, "Serbs were forcibly deported." Section 5.4.2, 1743 to 1745, and 1751. That finding directly derives from, is based on, and depends on the unlawful attack finding. As the arrow below indicates, this is clear from paragraphs 1745, 2305, and 2311 of the Judgement. 1745 is a short paragraph so I will take to you it: "The Trial Chamber considers that the fear of violence and duress caused by the shelling of the towns of Benkovac, Gracac, Knin, and Obrovac created an environment in which those present there had no choice but to leave. Consequently, the Trial Chamber finds that the shelling amounted to the forcible displacement of persons from ..." those four towns. 2305 we have looked at in another context, so we'll just look at the last three sentences. "These attacks therefore constituted unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects." As a result, large parts of the civilian population of the four towns were forcibly displaced. So here the Trial Chamber used unlawful attacks to find that the exodus of 20.000 people constituted deportation. And then 2311, again I'll just look at the last three sentences: "Deportation of the Krajina Serb population was to a large extent achieved through the unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects" in the four towns. Based on the foregoing, the Trial Chamber finds that unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects, as the crime against humanity of persecution, were also intended and within the purpose of the JCE." So the Trial Chamber found that deportation was achieved through unlawful attacks. In other words, the Trial Chamber used the finding of unlawful attacks to find that deportation occurred, and from that - and it is really double counting - the Chamber found it was done on discriminatory grounds, simply because the people there were overwhelmingly Serbs. And it then found intent based on nothing else, really, and thus crimes against humanity, persecution, unlawful attacks within the JCE. The Trial Chamber piled finding upon finding, spinning it all out of one finding, unlawful attacks which for our purposes we assume was erroneous. Now that's the box "Serbs were forcibly deported." You will see to the right of that box there is an arrow to the adjacent box, which says "1862." And that shows that the Trial Chamber derived the next finding, that Serbs were persecuted, both from the finding that Serbs were forcibly deported and principally from the unlawful attack finding. And I won't take you to paragraph 1862 as it's not crucial for our purposes. But what is most important for our purposes is that the Serbs were persecuted finding derives directly from unlawful attack. And that is shown by the two references in the arrow below to 1862 and 1936. 1936 relates to Gracac, which is most relevant to my client, so I will take you to that paragraph. "Considering the evidence on the ethnic composition of Gracac ... the Trial Chamber finds that the unlawful attack on civilians and civilian objects in Gracac discriminated in fact against the Krajina Serbs. In establishing the intention with which this unlawful attack was committed, the Trial Chamber has considered the language of the HV's artillery orders and the deliberate shelling of areas devoid of military targets." So again I would underline those words which are the unlawful attack finding. "The Trial Chamber has also considered its findings in chapters 5.2 [sic]," et cetera. Those are unlawful attack findings. "The Trial Chamber further considers that the unlawful attack against civilians and civilian objects was committed in the context of a wider discriminatory attack against Krajina Serbs ..." "The Trial Chamber finds that the unlawful attack on civilians and civilian objects in Gracac was carried out with the intention to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds." So you get two things there, two inferences by the Trial Chamber. Unlawful attack equals discrimination. Unlawful attack equals intention to discriminate, given that there were mostly Serbs in those areas because Croat civilians were ethnically cleansed in 1991. Or to put it the other way around, assuming as we do for the purposes of answering your question 4 unlawful attack is wrong, no unlawful attack means no unlawful attack qua crime, no unlawful attack as persecution, no unlawful attack as crime against humanity, no discriminatory attack and hence no discrimination, no intention to discriminate, no JCE involving unlawful attacks, and no JCE involving persecution. Because all the underlying core crimes fall away. So all the skittles get knocked down when you take away unlawful attack finding. It's extraordinary that the Prosecution should maintain otherwise. Now that analysis takes in some of the other boxes so I can deal with them more rapidly. To the right of the Brioni box, which we have already looked at, we have the box: "Those who ordered artillery strikes did so with the intent to deport," and you see the references in the box to where that finding is to be found. And that finding, too, is entirely dependant on the unlawful attack finding as are all the findings on this chart. And that's clear from paragraphs 1746 and 1757. 1746: "The Trial Chamber considered several factors in establishing whether the HV and special police forces who shelled these four towns on 4 and 5 August 1995 did so with the intent to forcibly displace persons from the towns. Firstly, the Trial Chamber recalls its findings in chapter 5.8.2(i)," and that's the magic chapter where unlawful attacks is dealt with, "that the HV and special police did not limit themselves to shelling areas containing military targets, but also deliberately targeted civilian areas in these towns and treated the towns themselves as targets for artillery fire. "In the same chapter, the Trial Chamber found that the unlawful attack on civilians," so it presumes an unlawful attack, "and civilian objects in these towns was carried out with the intention to discriminate against Krajina Serbs on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Trial Chamber further refers to the evidence reviewed in chapter 6.2.7 regarding the existence and objective of a JCE and particularly the evidence regarding the Brioni meeting" of 31st July. So the Brioni meeting too was interpreted in light of the unlawful attack finding. "Based on the aforementioned evidence and conclusions, the Trial Chamber finds that the HV and special police forces who shelled Benkovac, Gracac, Knin, and Obrovac did so within the intent to forcibly displace persons from these towns." Paragraph 1757 shows the Trial Chamber using the unlawful attack finding even to find that, what I call "non-artillery crimes" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- were committed with the intent to forcibly -- oh, I'm sorry. Even non-artillery crimes were committed with the intent forcibly to displace Serbs. 1757 you should have on your screens in a moment. "The Trial Chamber has considered several factors in establishing whether the members of Croatian military forces and special police who committed the crimes which resulted in the forcible displacement of the victims of and witnesses to the crimes did so with the intent to forcibly displace these persons." And then again the Trial Chamber goes back, as is its custom. "Firstly, the Trial Chamber recalls its conclusions in chapters 5.8.2, that the perpetrators committed these crimes with the intention to discriminate against Krajina Serbs ... the Trial Chamber further considered its findings in the same chapters that these crimes were committed as part of an attack against the civilian population. This attack includes deportation of Krajina Serbs from the towns of," and then we have the four towns again, "by means of unlawful attack ..." And incidentally, we do have a separate box on the far left of the row entitled "Non-shelling crimes were intended to deport," so that's that finding too. And we see from there how that is derived in 1757 from the unlawful attack finding. So we're mostly finished with this row concerned with the crimes. We just have a final box on the far right, captioned: "Those who carried out the artillery strikes did so with intent to persecute." And that finding is at paragraph 1936 of the judgement. And as you'll see from the arrow with the same paragraph number, that finding derives directly from the unlawful artillery attack finding. And we've already reviewed that paragraph, so I won't do it again. So to pause there, you will see how all of the key core findings relating to the core JCE crimes, deportation, persecution, crimes against the humanity, all the elements derive directly from the unlawful shelling finding. And even its findings on non-core crimes too. So no unlawful shelling means no JCE crimes, and in fact the unlawful shelling finding was so all-pervasive in the Judgement that it even led the Chamber to disbelieve President Tudjman's appeal to Serbs to stay in their homes. And you will find that at paragraph 2051, and I'll summarise it rather than reading it in whole. The Chamber said that it had to treat Tudjman's statement inviting Serbs to stay in their homes with great caution and the reason for that was because that had to be considered against the background of the discussions at Brioni, and then it further went on to say it has to be considered in light of the unlawful attack findings. And then it says: "Based on the foregoing, the Trial Chamber finds that the appeal was not a true reflection of the will and intention of Tudjman at the time." So without the unlawful attack finding, there's no reason to suppose that Tudjman's appeal was not a honest appeal to Serbs to stay in their homes. And certainly that's a reasonable interpretation of the evidence. So let's go to the next level on this flowchart, and that's the middle level where you will see just two boxes. Markac, that's obviously MM, participated in an unlawful attack and Markac participated in the discussions at Brioni. Now, we'll deal first with the box on the left, Markac participated in unlawful attack, and that finding was at paragraphs 2580 and 2583 of the Judgement. Now, it's obvious, isn't it, if there was no unlawful attack, Markac couldn't have participated in it. You can't participate in what doesn't exist. So we leave that box to one side. Markac participated in discussions at Brioni. Well, there is, of course, nothing criminal about simply participating in discussions. If Brioni was not about a JCE, then Markac's presence at Brioni and his participation in the discussions is completely innocuous. So for the Trial Chamber to use Markac's presence and participation in Brioni to derive JCE liability, it needs Brioni to be about a JCE. So that box, that finding's significance derives from the box below, Brioni was about a JCE, and in turn derives from the unlawful attack finding. Because Brioni was always interpreted by the Trial Chamber "in light of subsequent events," specifically in light of what the Chamber to be found to be unlawful shelling. See paras 2305, 2316, and 2320. And it is no coincidence that the Chamber took that approach. The reason why the Chamber had to go outside the Brioni meeting to subsequent events is because there is nothing in the minutes themselves, in the transcript, which shows a criminal enterprise. There is no mention of: Let's prevent the Serbs from coming back, for example, which is meant to be a core objective of the JCE. The JCE, of course, has to be a criminal enterprise, not an enterprise. The Wannsee Conference was a meeting about exterminating European Jews. In Argentina during the Galtieri regime there were meetings where the military junta explicitly said, Let's exterminate the Communists. A criminal enterprise. But Brioni has nothing at that. It's a military operational meeting to prepare for Operation Storm. A completely lawful operation, as the Chamber found Operation Storm and the Prosecution acknowledged. And it is worth remembering the Prosecution never claimed that there was anything wrong with Operation Storm, but they claimed there was a JCE wrapped up in Operation Storm. So now hopefully you begin to see how the Chamber's findings are built up from one finding at the bottom, and what we now need to look at is how the Chamber took all these building blocks, all based on the unlawful attack finding, and arrived at this top-most level, Markac's liability under the JCE. So this is the top level of our chart, four boxes. Markac substantially contributed to the JCE, including by failing to prevent/punish. Markac was a member of the JCE. Markac intended to contribute to the JCE, and Markac shared the JCE objective. We'll take those findings one at a time. Markac substantially contributed to the JCE. That finding derives directly from the Chamber's finding that Markac participated in the unlawful attack. So no unlawful attack means Markac didn't participate in an unlawful attack. And if Markac did not participate in an unlawful attack, then he didn't substantially contribute to the JCE. So that leaves our three last boxes. All of them are tied up with paragraph 2583, and it is a key paragraph so I will need to go through it line by line. "The Trial Chamber now turns to determining whether Markac shared the objective of the JCE, and whether with his acts and omissions Markac intended to contribute to it. Markac participated in the Brioni meeting and took active part in the planning of Operation Storm." Pausing there, there is nothing wrong with Operation Storm and being involved in the planning of Operation Storm. Even the Prosecution accepts that. And participation in Brioni is innocuous once you knock out the unlawful attack finding. Now then the Chamber discusses artillery orders and goes on. I'm going eight lines down: "The Trial Chamber found in chapter 5.8.2(i)," that's the chapter I've asked you to look out for because it is the key on unlawful attacks, "that these were orders to treat whole towns, including Gracac, as targets when firing artillery projectiles during Operation Storm." Pausing there, those orders were only found to be unlawful in light of the unlawful attack finding. See paragraphs 1911 for Knin; 1915, Benkovac; 1927, Gracac; and 1943 for Obrovac. I go on: "Considering that the purpose of the 3 August 1995 meeting in Zadar was the co-ordination of artillery, the Trial Chamber considers that the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence is that Markac, at the meeting, was aware of the nature of the planned artillery operations." I pause there. If the nature of the artillery operations was lawful, then there's nothing wrong with being aware of those operations. Then it goes on: "On this basis, the Trial Chamber finds that Markac was aware, when he ordered the artillery attack on Gracac, that it constituted an unlawful attack against civilians and civilian objects." Pausing there. No unlawful attack means no awareness of unlawful attack by Markac. "It thus shows his intent to contribute to the JCE objective." So then intent must fall away. Ex hypothesi, we assume no unlawful attack, intent to contribute must go. "In light of this finding," so "in light of this finding" means that as all those findings are, ex hypothesi, erroneous, that one is still nowhere. Almost the bottom of this paragraph. "In light of this finding, the Trial Chamber finds that Markac's omissions in relation to the crimes committed by the special police in both Gracac and Donji Lapac, as well as through his active role in covering up the crimes committed in Grubori and Ramljane, were also aimed at contributing to this objective. "On this basis," I underline that, on this basis, on this flawed basis if we say there is no unlawful attack, on this entirely flawed basis, "the Trial Chamber finds that Markac had the state of mind that the crimes forming part of the objective should be carried out. Considering all of the above," so all of the above is erroneous because each is built on the other, "the Trial Chamber accordingly finds that Markac was a member of the JCE." So that falls out. "The Trial Chamber finds that Markac thus intended that his actions contribute to JCE." That too has to fall away. It all falls away, all of 2583 you can strike a line through it if unlawful attacks is wrong, and everything of his JCE liability is in that paragraph. The "thus" in that last sentence means it follows from what went before, and all of what went before is false if unlawful attacks is false. So you have this tortured passage, with the greatest respect to the Chamber, but where element upon element of JCE liability is heaped on each other and in a totally circular, self-supporting way so that every element simultaneously proves and is proved by each of the other elements. And so the Chamber pulls itself by its own bootstraps into the ether. But as I said, it's a house of cards because once the unlawful attack finding goes, it all goes. It alls falls away, all collapses. Nothing is left when you take that away. So looking at the last three boxes on the table, Markac was a member of the JCE, intended to contribute to the JCE, shared the JCE objective, all our arrows show that the Chamber is, to use another metaphor, building bricks without straw. Each finding points to the other, but ultimately they're all founded on the unlawful attack finding. Now, another metaphor which might be helpful. The Judgement is like a knitted sweater. On one thread is the unlawful attack finding, but it's not just one thread which runs through the whole fabric of the Judgement. It's the first and central and omni-present thread. It's a thread which is wrapped in every other fibre of the argument -- of the garment, so that every bit of this Judgement, wherever you look, has got an unlawful attack thread wrapped around it. And wherever you cut this Judgement, there's an unlawful attack finding staring up at you. And it's no accident that the unlawful attack finding permeates everything, because the Trial Chamber liked its unlawful finding, if I can put it that way. It didn't shy away from making that finding the centrepiece of the Judgement. Based on this 200-metre rule, which the Prosecution described in its appeals brief as was generous, it's a generous rule to Gotovina and Markac, but which it now says is overly narrow. I don't know how they reconcile generosity and being overly narrow but they do, but if the Trial Chamber could be represented here today, I'm sure it would admit, as the Prosecution will not do, that if the unlawful attack finding goes, the JCE goes. And that the answer to Your Honours' fourth question is therefore a resounding no. I want to give -- I think I still have ample time. That was to explain the chart. There are a few questions raised earlier which I would appreciate dealing with -- having time to deal with. Firstly, this morning, Your Honour, Mr. President, asked a question about opportunistic targets. In essence, if the Trial Chamber thought that the evidence was inconclusive about opportunistic targets, what exactly is the position. This is the answer which I would give. If the Trial Chamber thought that the evidence was inconclusive as to opportunistic targets, to assume that they were no opportunistic targets is to fail to resolve any doubts in favour of the accused and therefore it's a breach of the presumption of innocence. That's the answer I would give to Your Honour. I will say one thing about the 200-metre rule. First if I could preface it by saying something by Rajcic because the Prosecution say that 200-metre rule is all about discrediting Rajcic. Rajcic was a Prosecution witness. It really is worth mentioning that. He was a Prosecution witness. And when he said that that -- the order to treat whole towns as targets was interpreted by him and by everyone down the level of command to mean fire on predetermined lawful targets, if he said that, but they say it's a -- in fact they were firing indiscriminately, he was a liar. Rajcic would be a liar. And it was their duty to say to Rajcic -- either have him declared hostile or to say to him: We put it to you, Mr. Rajcic, you are lying, that is not correct, that is not how you understood it. They never did it. In flagrant breach of Rule 90(H). And yet now that's their case. They say Rajcic implicitly must be a liar, and yet they rely on him as credible when he says that the chances of hitting Martic was slight. So when it suits them, Rajcic is credible; when it doesn't suit them, he is essentially a liar. So the unimpeached evidence of their witness is that this is how artillery orders were interpreted. And so saying that there is corroboration because this order putting towns under fire -- sorry. That this order which goes down the lines of command, showing how it is been sent down from one -- down the chain of command - sorry - that doesn't get them anywhere if, in fact, everyone interpreted the order as meaning fire on predetermined lawful targets. So then they link that to the 200-metre rule. Now we adopt Gotovina's submissions on the 200-metre rule. But can we just add this, and it is really more a point of logic. The 200-metre rule is only a rule about military targets. It says: Here is a military target. If you land within 200 metres, we presume you're aiming at that target. It doesn't tell you anything about whether civilian targets are being targeted. And so it does lead to these absurd results that a -- a missile which lands in a muddy swamp, lands in the middle of nowhere, in the middle of a desert, is against a civilian target, because it's a negative definition. That's the problem. If it's not military, it must be civilian. A muddy swamp is not a civilian object. A desert is not a civilian object, and yet their rule obliges them to say that it is. And it's also -- I don't want to be too -- using philosophical logic about this but I was a [indiscernible] at university. I did philosophy at university. But there is a fallacy, a well-known fallacy which is -- it's the fallacy of denying the antecedent, and it goes like this. Say if it is a cat, it's a mammal. It's not a cat, therefore it is not mammal. That is a fallacy because it could be a dog. It could be a horse. And the same fallacy is here. They say if it is within 200 metres, it's aimed at the targets. It is not within 200 metres, therefore it is not aimed at the target. Wrong. That's a straight logical fallacy. And the equivalent of it could be a dog is there are ample other explanations of why the target was outside 200 metres. And in paragraph 18 of Gotovina's appeals brief, it refers to these other explanations. And I quote: "The Trial Chamber failed to consider the following reasonable explanations for projectiles landing more than 200 metres from known artillery targets. 1, the range of error of the weapons system employed was beyond 200 metres; 2, the HV fire at a tactical level unknown to Rajcic would have provided additional military objectives; 3, there were other military targets not identified in evidence; 4, the shell's landing location may for some or all of these cases have been caused by errors, inaccuracies, or negligence; and 5, malfunctioning of weaponry or ammunition." I mean, it's obvious to the layman that artillery firing at 26 kilometres can be affected by wind, by whether it's on a flat piece of ground, whether one of the missiles has got a faulty fuse. It is obvious that there are a host of explanations. And it is a rule which utterly reverses the burden of proof because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel kindly slow down for the interpreters and the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'll simply adopt the submissions of Gotovina in that respect rather than repeating them. Now, Your Honour, Judge Pocar, asked the Prosecution what if the attack were -- were an attack only on military targets, would the Prosecution still say it was a crime. And the Prosecution said yes. And one of the things they said is, yes, if you're counting -- quote, if you're counting on collateral damage. Now you can't -- they can't count on collateral damage by definition. Collateral damage is what happens accidentally not deliberately, by definition. And where do they get that rule from? Where do they get the rule in IHL from, that it's criminal if you count on collateral damage. I have never seen that rule in the commentaries on the Geneva Conventions. So that it shows that really your question -- or, rather, the answer to your question, Your Honour, shows that the Prosecution will take any position and they will make up IHL on the hoof. And so they now postulate a JCE using lawful means, and only lawful means, and so then, firstly it would all depend on whether civilians leave or not. If they stay you're not committing one of the worst crimes -- and let's remember, that's what we're talking about, the worst crimes known to man. Crimes against humanity, JCE. If the civilians don't leave, whether they leave, that's what your liability depends on. Or it depends on what is floating around your mind. If when you man the guns and you pull the trigger you think, I hope those civilians will leave because of this lawful shelling, that transforms into a crime. A war crime, or a crime against humanity. What you are thinking becomes a thought crime. This is a thought crime. This is mens rea with no actus reus. And so they're making up the law and they're making up the case against Gotovina and Markac as they go along on the day of the appeal hearing. Their case at trial is that there were no targets, or almost no targets. Now they say even if there was but targets, they're still guilty. So 100 per cent different case and they're still guilty. It shows the Prosecution is willing to take any position. And it's not just they're moving the goal-posts around. They've taken the goal-posts from one side of the pitch and they've moved it to the other side of the pitch. And so they may be willing to move the goal-posts around 360 degrees, but I suggest Your Honours should not follow them down that sorry path. And Ms. Baig said, well, it's -- sorry, I'll pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I think there was a crime in old common law wishing the death of the sovereign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It is encompassing or something like that. Well, that is a particularly grievous offence so it's probably right that that's punishable. But it was also said that one would not have a criminal plan if -- if civilians leaving was unforeseen and incidental, was her phrase. Again, I don't know where in IHL they get that from, where is that test, the unforeseen and incidental test. So now you have to not foresee it. If you don't foresee it, you're not liable. So either you have to be wilfully blind, you have to close your eyes to what's foreseeable, but what if it is foreseeable? If you think, I want to conduct this lawful operation, I can foresee that civilians will leave, what do you do? Does that mean you can't launch a lawful attack because you foresee that? It's ludicrous, and that has no basis in IHL. As I say, in fact, creating thought crimes, no actus reus, but a crime if there's mens rea. That is not just contrary to IHL, that is contrary to every principle of criminal law, subject to Your Honours' example which I'll have to research. So I will leave it there and turn over to my learned friend Mr. Kuzmanovic unless there are any questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My presentation today, Your Honours, will concern mostly questions 2 and 3 in the addendum, whether the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding impact sites should be upheld if its application of the 200-metre margin of error is deemed erroneous; and number 3, whether the Trial Chamber's finding that illegal artillery attacks took place should be upheld if its conclusions with respect to impact sites are deemed erroneous. With respect to the first question, Your Honour, we won't have any other further submissions other than to answer that question a resounding yes. With respect to questions 2 and 3, the impact sites and the 200-metre rule, it's a resounding no. Judge Guney asked a very pressing question on page 89 of today's transcript in lines 3 through 7, which I will also endeavour to answer. His question was: Was it unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to infer the civilian character of areas where there were no military objectives? The answer to that question, yes, it was extremely unreasonable. I will explain why. The second portion of that question was: May the civilian character be inferred from a general statement without any evidence to support it? The answer to that is: No. The civilian character cannot and must not be inferred, as it turns reasonable doubt on its head and reverses the burden of proof. As the Court is well aware, in the Blaskic case, the Prosecution bears the burden of proving that an object was indeed dedicated to civilian purposes. The answer to Judge Guney's question can be vividly illustrated by the Trial Chamber's analysis of the artillery attack on the military targets in Gracac. Let's look at what the Trial Chamber did with respect to Gracac. Paragraphs 1927 through 1932 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement, in part, discuss Gracac. The Trial Chamber begins by explaining that: "No fewer than 150 projectiles fell on Gracac and its immediate vicinity on 4 August 1995." Paragraph 1928 of the Judgement. The Trial Chamber doesn't really explain how it got to that number but that's what we have and that's what I'm going to deal with. The Trial Chamber further explains that it has only been able to conclusively determine a small number of precise locations of impacts relative to a portion of those 150 projectiles. That's also at paragraph 1928. 150 projectiles, 150 impacts. I guess we can safely assume that that's what we have in relation to Gracac. How does the Trial Chamber conclude in paragraph 1934 that a considerable portion of the locations of those impacts were civilian objects or areas in Gracac? It does so by reviewing five target areas. Five. We submit that this in and of itself is unreasonable. However, it first qualifies this conclusion by stating in paragraph 1934: "... the number of civilian objects or areas in Gracac deliberately fired at by the HV," and it doesn't define what this means, "deliberately fired at," "may appear limited in view of the at least 150 projectiles fired at the town." The Trial Chamber further stated and repeated in paragraphs 1928 and 19234 of the Judgement that it was able to conclusively determine only a small number of precise locations of impact relating to some of those 150 projectiles. So keep in mind those two qualifications in relation to Gracac that the Trial Chamber made. One, that the civilian objects or areas were limited that they covered or were able to determine; and two, they conclusively determine only a small number of precise impact locations. Let's go through the steps of what the Trial Chamber did there and see what it did to determine whether or not the attack on Gracac was unlawful. The first impact area, at paragraph 1929, the Trial Chamber says there: "... artillery projectiles struck the police station in Gracac ..." It doesn't tell us how many projectiles, but it assumes that those projectiles hit their target. The second impact area, in 1929, is the Gracac Brigade command post. There's no discussion of number of impacts. Both were determined by the Trial Chamber to be military targets. So as far as the first two areas of impact are concerned, we don't have any issue relating to civilian targets or areas. The third area, in paragraph 1930 of the Judgement, a house located near a factory which served as a Serb military depot. It said that one or more, doesn't define how many, impacts. The Trial Chamber determined in that third area that firing at this depot would have offered a definite military advantage. The fourth impact area, at paragraph 1931, 10 to 20 impacts at an intersection, in which the Trial Chamber determined that firing there would have offered a definite military advantage. So we have four impact areas, all four either military targets, or areas that offer a definite military advantage. Let's look at the fifth impact area, at paragraph 1932. Several projectiles. Now, several can mean usually more than one. In common conversations, several to me means less than five. Six is a half a dozen, so we will say several is less than six. Near a witness who testified in this case, Gacesa, near her house, which the Trial Chamber determined was 300 metres from a target on the Jagoda list. The sixth area of impact were artillery projectiles. Again, how many, undeclared, undefined, near Witness Steenbergen's home - Witness Steenbergen was a UN military observer - that were within 450 metres or 800 metres of a targeted military target on both either the special police target list or the Jagoda list. So that is 150 impacts, projectiles. One to four of those impact areas -- one through four of those impact areas analysed were legitimate military targets or offered definite military advantage. The fifth area of one impact was within 300 metres - so it fits within the Leslie estimation range of error - of a target. And the sixth and final impact area concerning Gracac was within 450 to 800 metres of a target. So the conclusion the Trial Chamber drew from analysing those six impact areas out of 150 projectiles, that, in Gracac, civilian areas were deliberately targeted based on its findings in reviewing those six impact areas. That is unreasonable. The only witness to testify about targeting by the special police specifically was Josip Turkalj, a Prosecution witness, at paragraph 1437. Josip Turkalj's testimony regarding the special police targeting in and around Gracac was that the purpose was to neutralise the target and to minimise collateral damage. That's at paragraph 1435. In fact, Turkalj testified that he had a conversation with General Markac the day before Operation Storm began and Turkalj said General Markac told him: "When selecting targets, make sure that civilians would not come in harm's way." Turkalj testified not just about targets in and around Gracac, but about the entire area of special police access of attack, from the Velebit mountains all the way to Donji Lapac. Now, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that a considerable portion of the impact areas were civilian objects or areas, based on its own analysis of six impact areas is wrong. It's completely unreasonable and it is not supported by its own examples. Considering this flawed impact analysis, Turkalj's testimony about targeting and that military targets were targeted in and around Gracac, and the fact that there were no civilian deaths in or around Gracac, no evidence of civilian deaths as a result of artillery, or evidence of unreasonable collateral damage in Gracac due to artillery in the entire analysis of the Gracac artillery attack, the finding that an unlawful attack against civilians and civilian objects was widespread and systematic and an attack against the civilian population must be overturned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that both the special police, the Jagoda list, the special police targeting list found in four of those six areas were military targets, yes. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: To determine that the entire city of Gracac was unlawfully attacked by artillery, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I -- as a whole, as an entire town, without any selectivity between military and civilian areas. Correct. Based on one, that analysis; two, the number of impacts were analysed; three, the number of projectiles that were launched on Gracac; and four, the fact that four of the six areas that were attacked were military targets -- actually, five of the six, one -- one of which the range was in the acceptable, if you use Leslie's number, 400 metres, five of the six were with -- were legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that you can't extract from Gracac, say, four -- four impact areas and if those had been properly determined by the Trial Chamber as having been unlawfully attacked, that, you say, is not a sufficient basis for a finding that Gracac as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, because it's just not -- it is not enough. You have 150 artillery rounds. You have six areas of impact which, giving the Prosecution the benefit of the doubt, maybe have 20 total impacts, it is simply not enough to make a determination that the civilian areas, per se, were attacked intentionally by the special police and the HV, in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I just wanted to address one more issue on the JCE 3 issue as it pertains to General Markac. One particularly troubling aspect of the finding in JCE 3 as it relates to General Markac is this particular finding. And it's the finding in paragraph 2586 of the Trial Chamber Judgement. As the Court is well aware, if there is no JCE 1, there is no JCE 3, but I would be remiss if I did not address the Trial Chamber on this particular issue and essentially the main and almost sole finding of JCE 3 culpability in terms of mens rea for General Markac. The Chamber recognised that General Markac chose troops who were not local to the area in which operations were carried out so that revenge crimes could be avoided. So, in other words, if a unit was going into Gracac or Donji Lapac or in any other area of special police area of operations during Operation Storm, General Markac said, I don't want local guys to go there, even though it probably would have been better from the standpoint of knowing the terrain, he wanted someone from the Vukovar unit or the Osijek unit or some other unit to go because he wanted to even avoid the possibility that there might be revenge crimes. But the Chamber's inference of that goes totally against common sense. The Chamber found, in 2586, that Markac's attempt to prevent crimes this way showed that Markac was aware of the possibility that members of the Croatian military forces and special police would perpetrate acts of revenge. That makes no sense. One sentence earlier, the Chamber says: Markac choice these troops "so as to avoid sentiments of revenge against people and to avoid possible conflict." And that is evidence of his mens rea for JCE 3. I submit to you that that is completely contradictory. And that is a crucial part of the Chamber's determination of JCE 3 liability for General Markac. Your Honours, those are my submissions, unless there are any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you very much and good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Helen Brady, and together with Mr. Francois Boudreault, Mr. Todd Schneider, and Ms. Ingrid Elliott, we will be responding now to Mr. Markac's appeal. Your Honours, just to give you a batting order and a road map of this afternoon's presentation, first, I will address the Trial Chamber's conclusion that a joint criminal enterprise existed to permanently remove the Serb civilians from the Krajina through deportation and forcible transfer, unlawful shelling and restrictive and discriminatory measures. This is directly responding to the first ground of appeal, 1A. In the course of my submissions on JCE, Your Honours, they will proceed on the basis of Trial Chamber's conclusion that an illegal artillery attack occurred during Operation Storm; that is, in accordance with the Trial Chamber's finding. However, Your Honours, I will also briefly address the JCE findings on the premise of your question 4; that is, if the Trial Chamber's finding on the illegal artillery attacks were to be found to be erroneous. After me, Mr. Boudreault will then address the conclusion by the Trial Chamber that Markac was a member of that JCE, that he significantly contributed to it and he had the mens rea for the JCE crimes. In relation to the unlawful shelling findings, my colleagues, Mr. Stringer and Mr. Cross, this morning have already dealt at length with this issue, and they've given very complete answers to our position on questions 1, 2, and 3, so we will be fairly short in that regard. We will be adopting the position in our submissions this morning. However, Mr. Schneider will briefly address you on this issue in light of the submissions that were made by Markac Defence. And, finally, Your Honours, Ms. Elliott will respond briefly on some features regarding the deportation findings, and, in particular, that the shelling was the primary and direct cause of the departure of the Serb civilian population from the Krajina. And for the remainder of the grounds we rely on our briefs. I will turn first to the findings about joint criminal enterprise. Only one reasonable conclusion emerges from all the evidence, and that is that by no later than July 1995, a common criminal plan existed to remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina on a permanent basis through forcible displacement, unlawful shelling and restrictive and discriminatory measures and Markac was a member of that JCE. Now, this afternoon, Markac, just as he did in his brief, deconstructs the factual findings. I think his flow chart he -- going so far to say that the factual findings are inverted, and he artificially isolates factual findings and the evidence. Your Honours, that is not how a reasonable fact finder assesses evidence and makes finding, and nor should it guide your review. Instead, just as the Trial Chamber did, this Chamber needs to take a holistic view based on all the evidence considered together and not examine the facts and the evidence in this deconstructed and artificial way and today in this afternoon's submission, what I would like to do is to put this picture, the evidence and the facts, back together again, as they were properly understood by the Trial Chamber. The first point I'd like to make is the critical importance of examining the discussions at Brioni in their context. In light of both preceding and the later events, that's the context in which Brioni needs to be examined. Now, the actual discussion as recorded in the transcript, P461, do form a very important part of the Trial Chamber's findings. I'd like to take Your Honours to key parts of those discussions in just a moment. But it is equally important to stress that these discussions are one component within a much broader complex of evidence and facts and must be considered in that light. And these events confirm that the meeting's true criminal objective. The participants were not merely discussing and planning a military operation designed to defeat the SVK and retake the territory in the -- in that part of the Krajina. They were discussing and planning an operation designed to take back that territory cleansed of the Serb civilians. And this removal of the Serb civilians was to be achieved by force or threat of force, including by forcible displacements and shelling. Your Honours, you cannot properly understand the Brioni transcript, and I want to take you to these before I go to the details of that discussion. You cannot properly under the Brioni transcript and the purpose behind this operation without considering the events preceding that meeting. This operation was, in many ways, the crowning achievement of a policy which Croatian president and supreme commander of the armed forces, Franjo Tudjman, had been pursuing for years, to create an ethnically homogeneous Croatia or as ethnically as possible. Ambassador Peter Galbraith, who -- a man who had frequent contact with Tudjman and his associates over the relevant years, stated that: "Tudjman thought that the Serbs in Croatia were too numerous and constituted a strategic threat to Croatia." That's in his 92 ter statement, paragraph 31, and it's in the Trial Judgement at paragraph 1999. A month before Operation Storm, Tudjman had actually met with his national security council to discuss the settling of Croat emigres from abroad into the tens of thousands of Serb houses which had been abandoned in Western Slavonia during Operation Flash in May 1995. And that comes from Trial Chamber finding 2060. Your Honours, just as importantly, you cannot approach the Brioni discussions without considering them in light of later events, what did unfold after this meeting. And, briefly, within days of that meeting, Croatian forces subjected the towns of Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac, and Gracac to an indiscriminate, unlawful artillery attack causing the mass exodus of 20.000 civilians. This finding is not -- the unlawful attack findings were an important part of the Trial Chamber's analysis but we disagree that it is linchpin in the way presented by Mr. Markac's Defence. In fact, all these pieces of evidence, Your Honour, have to be seen as strands in a cable of evidence which point towards the guilt of the accused rather than links in a chain. Once one falls out, the rest of the house of cards - or however it was put - topples. That is not the case. Your Honours, another factor, apart from the actual indiscriminate and unlawful attacks themselves, is that after this operation, Operation Storm, Tudjman did set about implementing his demographic policy. He and other senior Croatian politicians and military leaders expressed views, promulgated policies aimed at encouraging ethnic Croats to come to the Krajina to re-populate it, while, at the same time, advocated against the Serbs' return. And hand in glove with that vision, policy and legislative measures were taken to prevent their return or at least make it much, much more difficult and therefore unlikely. And I'm referring here to the laws and decrees passed in the ensuing months in August and September imposing very strict, tight 30- and 90-day deadlines for Serb civilians to reclaim their property or risk losing it to the state and given to Croats. And, finally, Your Honours, you must bear in mind that throughout the two-month period after this operation in August and September, Croatian armed forces, the HV and special police, continued to commit further crimes against Serbs and their property on a mass scale, torching houses, looting property, carrying out murders and other inhumane acts against the Serbs who did remain there and this triggered further civilian departures from the area. I'd like to now turn to take a closer look at the discussions at Brioni themselves because, in our submission, the Trial Chamber reached the only reasonable conclusion about these discussions. And, Your Honours, I point out that their finding about the discussions is in paragraph 1995 of the trial Judgement, that the Trial Chamber found that this discussion, this set of discussions, was, in itself, something from which they could infer was a conversation about forcing civilians out, rather than protecting civilians. So that finding, they make that finding about Brioni, independently, as it were, from the other findings. But, of course, because they're making findings in light of their previous findings, it would be very artificial if they tossed their unlawful -- their decision on unlawful attacks out the window and then began to look at Brioni on its own. That would not be a reasonable way of having approached Brioni. But it is important to note that on its own, the Chamber was prepared to make that finding about the import of the Brioni discussions. So I'll turn to have a look now at the discussions themselves. As Tudjman and the others were pouring over maps, and this is in the presence of Gotovina and Markac, their main focus was whether, how, and when to launch an artillery attack against the SVK. That is something the Trial Chamber did find at paragraph 1990. But these operational discussions occurred within discussions aimed not just to take back territory but to take it back cleansed or without the Serbs in it by forcibly displacing them from that area. Your Honours, you'll need to read the whole transcript, of course. And, today, in the time, I'll just highlight four exchanges that we say shed particular light on what the discussions were truly about. I think Mr. Jones said something like there's nothing in there to show that there was this intent to deport. And we think a very different intent arises from these and other parts of -- of the discussions. I will take you to the first one. I think it should be on your screen. It's P461, the transcript of Brioni, and it's page 10. This is relatively early on in the meeting. Tudjman observes that when they undertake a general offensive "even greater panic will break out in Knin than has to date." President Tudjman then reminds them to remember "how many Croatian villages and towns have been destroyed." And makes the remark, "but that's still not the situation in Knin today." After he urges them to resolve the UNCRO matter and by that it is how to avoid hitting it. You can see this in another part of the discussion. Tudjman then says this: "But their counter-attack from Knin and so forth, it would provide very good justification for this action, and accordingly we have the pretext to strike, if we can with artillery, if you can, for complete demoralisation ... not just this ..." And Gotovina replies: "... if there is an order to strike at Knin, we will destroy it in its entirety in a few hours." Your Honours, turning to a second exchange, this one at page 15, Tudjman here is speaking about giving ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Tudjman here is speaking he has just made the comment about giving the civilians a way out and explains his reasoning for this. He says: "Because it is important that those civilians set out and then the army will follow them, when -- then the army will follow them and when the columns set out, they will have a psychological impact on each other." Gotovina responds: "A number of civilians are already evacuating Knin and heading towards Banja Luka and Belgrade. That means that if we continue this pressure, probably for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving." The final set of exchanges or comments during this meeting that I draw Your Honours' attention to are at pages 23 and 29 of the transcript. At this point, the discussion turns to using propaganda, and Miroslav Tudjman has suggested that information be given on the radio and TV as to the open routes. Tudjman agrees with this idea, and he adds, it's on your screens: "Yes, that should be said, not the fact that the routes are open, but that it has been noticed that civilians are getting out by using such and such route." And then at page 29, Tudjman embraces the idea thrown out by Susak of throwing leaflets as a further means of propaganda and suggesting that they report a general chaos and Croatian victory with the world's support. And Tudjman makes a suggestion about what these leaflets should say: "Serbs, you are already withdrawing via, et cetera, ... and we are calling upon you not to withdraw. We guarantee you ...," and there's a space, and he explains to the meeting. This is a meeting at which both Gotovina and Markac are at and participating or making suggestions on how certain parts of the operations should be conducted. He explains, "... so in that way, to give them a road, while ostensibly guaranteeing them civilian rights, et cetera ..." And after which on the tape he is heard to give a laugh, a chuckle. Now, Your Honours, several things stand out from these discussions. In the first exchange, Tudjman notes the large number of destroyed Croatian villages and towns and notes that -- that's still not the case with Knin. He and Gotovina then discuss striking Knin. But unlike other parts of the discussion, when they do actually go on to discuss military strategy and even some targets in -- in -- targets in quite some detail, for other bits and pieces of the operation, when it comes to Knin, the discussants in the conversation say nothing about striking only military targets there. They say nothing about how to protect Knin's civilian inhabitants. Instead the comment is really about using artillery strikes for complete demoralisation. Your Honours, Gotovina's continuing pressure comment that we've heard a bit about already today is also very telling. This comment acknowledges that the -- oh, I see my friend has stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it was perhaps noted this morning, and I sincerely regret interrupting the flow of the Prosecution's presentation, but if we're going to continue to focus on General Gotovina at Brioni with excerpts that were not put during the Prosecution's response this morning to our appeal, and the focus thus far has been on General Gotovina and Mr. Tudjman, then we would request that if it continues at this pace that we be allowed at least five minutes to respond or reply at the end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I believe that Ms. Brady did not cite materials which were not before us already. But I was wondering, you are mentioning in the conversations in which Mr. Gotovina participated, did Mr. Markac take an active part in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I mean, we are now on the Markac part.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that. But, Your Honours, I have to, I guess, describe the conversation as it's going during the course of that meeting, when two major members of that meeting are having discussions of this nature. It's true that Markac, when actually his words are recorded in the discussion, his comments are about what might be called very military matters. He's not the direct discussant. However, in our submission, and Mr. Boudreault will go into this in greater detail, he's present at a discussion where the only clear meaning is one thing. And that's why we need to set the scene, as it were, about what Gotovina says. And just to take the other point that Mr. Misetic has -- has said, actually, this morning, in my colleague's submissions, Ms. Baig and Mr. Stringer, they both referred to this pressure comment by Gotovina. But having said that, if he wishes to have a five-minute reply to what we say, I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. We will let you reply. Five minutes when this is over.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Gotovina's continuing pressure comment is also telling. It acknowledges that the pressure that they be applying - that is, the shelling - would be the cause or the trigger of the Serbs leaving the area. And in our submission, their comments show that the departure of the -- this comment shows that the departure of the Serbs was, indeed, the object of this and not merely an unintended foreseeable but unintended consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- you will have your few minutes to answer. Please so let Ms. Brady continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in other words, in this discussion they are planning to exploit the fact that the Serbs were then in a demoralised state and by their shelling to trigger their departure. The exchanges on propaganda are also very revealing. It makes little or no sense to even discuss this kind of propaganda if the discussants had simply been seeing this Serb departure as merely a temporary measure or even an inevitable consequence of their attack rather than its intended outcome. And Tudjman's comment about giving them a road while ostensibly guaranteeing their civil rights also, as the Trial Chamber found, shows the true intent of this operation: To show the Serbs out, while at the same time giving the impression that they could stay. There would be no place for this sort of cynical comment if the true intent was -- sorry, Your Honours. This cynical comment would have no place unless the true purpose was in fact to forcibly, that is, to push out the Serbs from the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I really have some doubt whether you should -- the gravamen of your argument to such an extent to be things connected to Mr. Gotovina. I did not interrupt you. I listened to the counsel. I think it would be more correct to focus on Mr. Markac now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But as I did explain, the meeting is taking place with various discussants, and he's present and making his contributions towards a certain -- certain angles of that discussion. Markac's interpretations of Brioni are not reasonably plausible. He basically argues that the discussions about leaving civilians a route out simply reflected a recognition that the Serbs were demoralised, they wouldn't stay in the area, if they were once again to be Croatian, and would leave once the shelling began. So he says their comments really -- merely aimed to serve legitimate military goals of further demoralising the enemy and speeding up military victory and reducing their own casualties. This argument lacks evidentiary support and it doesn't stand up to scrutiny. Firstly, his argument calls for an assumption that the discussants were planning a shelling attack against strictly military targets. But in this case, why would the participants assume that the Serb civilians would simply, en masse, up and leave the towns and villages where their families had lived for hundreds of years in the face of such an artillery attack? Witnesses in fact testified that they'd not left during previous shelling attacks. But even accepting for the argument's sake that the discussants could have assumed that a number of civilians would flee the attack, the shelling, we would expect to see in their discussions a concern for civilian protection. But as the Trial Chamber found, there were no such discussions. Instead, the discussions about civilians really focussed or were centred on ensuring that they would have a way out and then using those departures of the civilians to induce the army out and vice versa. Your Honours, while a swift military victory and a reduction in combatant losses may, in theory, be legitimate aims, that is, in a -- when we have a military operation aimed at a military objective, they provide no justification when, as here, the operation is itself aimed at forcibly displacing a civilian population from the territory so that the land can be taken without its inhabitants, a certain -- the Serb civilians. This is a patently illegal purpose. My colleague, Ms. Baig, has already answered question 4, and I won't rehearse what she said there. But, in short, it's impermissible for an army to plan an artillery operation with the aim or purpose of deporting a civilian population. This is the case even if it serves another military purpose. This is a very obvious proposition when an artillery operation with a criminal purpose of deportation is carried out by the criminal means of directly attacking civilians and civilian objects in an indiscriminate shelling attack as the Trial Chamber found in this case. But it remains our case, it remains the case, even if the artillery attacks were not found to be unlawful in the strict sense of Articles 51 and 52 of Additional Protocol II. IHL permits an army to treat only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Additional Protocol I.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Sorry. I meant Additional Protocol I, yes. Sorry, Your Honour. IHL permits an army to treat only the enemy soldiers and military objects as objects of attack, while civilians may be removed from a conflict zone if imperative military reasons demand or for their own protection. This has to be on a temporary basis and follow certain strict conditions. If the true aim of the artillery attack is in fact to deport a civilian population, what may on its surface look like a legal artillery attack, is, in fact, unlawful because of that purpose. And it can amount to deportation and persecution as a crime against humanity, of course, assuming the other elements are met. There's no inconsistency here between these crimes against humanity convictions and the applications of the laws of war. What the Brioni discussions show, Your Honours, is that when you look at these discussions in light of preceding events and later events, is that the participants were -- were aware of the difficult situation facing the Serbs in Krajina and they knew that this could be exploited to force them out. And with this in mind, they planned a military artillery attack with the aim of taking back the land and, at the same time, forcibly displacing the Serbs from it. Your Honours, events after Operation Storm confirm that the true purpose was the removal of the Serb civilian population from the Krajina by forcible means. I won't repeat what's already been said about the shelling attack itself which led the 20.000 civilians to flee in fright nor about the crimes that happened in the ensuing two months against the Serb civilians. But, again, I'll highlight the many speeches, statements and policies made by Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, and others, in high-level positions about repopulating the area with Croats by placing Croats in formerly Serb homes and all measures to prevent the Serbs from returning. When asked in an interview a month after the operation if the Krajina Serbs would return home, Tudjman replied that: "The return of all of them is virtually unthinkable." At the same time, Croatian authorities were passing laws making it very difficult, if not impossible, for the expelled Serbs to reclaim their property and homes given those restrictive time limits and difficulties they faced in re-entering the country from which they had just been expelled. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber rejected these laws were simply aimed at protecting property and solving a temporary housing problem, but were, in fact, passed to provide those Serb homes to incoming Croats and thereby deprive Krajina Serbs of their homes and properties. And the many speeches, the Trial Chamber goes into some detail on the speeches and the statements made publicly by Tudjman in the weeks and months after Operation Storm. I point Your Honours to just two of them. On -- he is speaking -- Tudjman is speaking at a public gathering in Knin on the 26th of August, a few weeks only after the operation, and he refers to Knin and the Serbs who had fled like this. He says referring to Knin: "But today it is Croatian Knin and never again it will go back to what it was before when they spread cancer which has been destroying Croatian national being in the middle of Croatia and didn't allow Croatian people to be truly alone on its own." Later he said of the Serbs who fled: "They were gone in a few days as if they'd never been here. They did not even have time to collect their rotten money and dirty underwear." And on the 5th of August, 1996, this is the one-year anniversary of the operation, when Tudjman was addressing the troops in Knin, he said: "We have returned Zvonimir's Croatian town to the fold of its motherland Croatia as pure as it was in Zvonimir's time." Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's JCE conclusion is firmly based on all of the evidence: Tudjman and others' ideas and policies for Croatia, the Brioni discussions, the indiscriminate attacks which did actually occur after this, the ensuing mass departures, the crime wave in the August/September period, the policies, the speeches, the property laws. From this, only one picture emerges: that there was a common criminal plan to remove the Serb civilian population from the Krajina on a permanent basis by the crimes of forcible displacement, unlawful attacks and restrictive and discriminatory measures. Markac's appeal on this ground must fail. Your Honours, unless you have questions for me, Mr. Boudreault will now address on grounds 1B and C, more specifically on how Markac links to that JCE which I've just shown was the only reasonable conclusion [Overlapping speakers] dealing with membership and contribution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I mentioned, I think, earlier today, that the Trial Chamber concluded that the evacuation orders were not a primary cause for departure. So did it have any role to play? How would you assess the role of the evacuation orders issued by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My colleague Ms. Elliott will briefly address you on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: In effect, it did not -- it was not the cause or the trigger for the departures as a causation [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So it had no impact?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Unless you can read something about that into the intent for the JCE. But in our submission, it would not affect either the mens rea for the JCE, the fact that discussions were going on. If Your Honour is meaning the fact that discussions were going on to evacuate and that's something that the participants knew about, that might have affect the finding on JCE intent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, my question is very simple: Did the evacuation order cause some people to depart in listening, in abiding with the order or not at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Sorry. Not the bulk. The mass, the en masse departure of the Serb civilians was occurring much earlier; indeed, early hours of the morning up through the middle of the day. And this evacuation order came too late, Your Honours, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the answer is: Partially yes. Some people left in response to it. None. Some thousands. Some hundreds?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may leave that for Ms. Elliott --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- she is really the expert on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, slightly out of order, but in order to answer this specific question on evacuation order, perhaps I can very briefly address you now. I think it is helpful to consider a short time-line of a day's events to illustrate and support the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's findings on the cause-and-effect relationship between the shelling and the sudden civilian flight. The shelling attack in Knin, Benkovac, and Gracac started at 5.00 a.m. Civilians initially hid in their basements in fear and panic. At 7.00 a.m., the attack in Obrovac town started. Civilians there immediately fled. Later in the morning, first in Gracac, and then towards noon in Knin, lulls in the intense shelling allowed people to escape from their basements and flee. The mass flight continued during the afternoon, including from Benkovac. By 5.00 p.m., the civilian population was already leaving Knin on a massive scale. And I would refer you to Trial Judgement paragraph 1531. The only escape route from Knin left open by the HV was clogged. Witness describes some of the towns are deserted by evening. So turning to the evacuation order, the existence of this order is not in doubt. However, the time-line shows that the evacuation order revealed only to civilian protection for the first time at 6.00 p.m. could not be the trigger for the mass civilian flight which started 11 hours earlier. As you have already heard, by 5.00 p.m. the population flight was described as massive. The Chamber's extensive and reasonable analysis of the role of the evacuation order also showed that the RSK authorities were panicked, disorganised, and unprepared to effect any evacuation plan. The evacuation request for assistance to the UN were not followed up. The evacuation order was poorly disseminated by the RSK authorities and I would also pause here to note that there was civilian -- there was Croatian propaganda also involved in this point, as planned in Brioni. And I would refer Your Honours to the Trial Judgement at paragraphs 1526 to 1527, and 1538. The order was simply ineffective. The Chamber was reasonable to dismiss the evacuation order as an alternative trigger. That would be our answer on the evacuation order, unless I can assist further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As my colleague, Ms. Brady announced, I will respond to grounds 1B and 1C of Markac's appeal and show that he was reasonably and correctly convicted under JCE. In our submissions, this remains whether the Appeals Chamber agrees with our primary contention that the artillery attack was unlawful or with our alternative submission that the attack was unlawful because it aimed at removing the civilian population in violation of the principles of distinction in humanity. In either case, Markac contributed to the criminal plan to remove the Serb population in the following ways: First, he was involved in the planning of the operation which led to the forcible removal of thousands of Krajina Serbs. Second, he ordered the unlawful shelling of Gracac which triggered the flight of the town's inhabitants. Third, he failed to prevent, punish or report the crimes of his subordinates against Serb civilians and their property. In this climate of impunity, his subordinates were encouraged and continued to commit crimes which led to further forced departures. Markac's participation in the criminal plan was intentional and determined. He was involved from the very beginning in planning and ordering the unlawful attack. He saw the massive flight of civilians this attack caused and knew that only a limited number of vulnerable Serb civilians would remain in the Krajina, those who had no possibility to leave. As the commander of the special police, he should have been protecting those remaining Serbs, but, instead, he gave impunity to his subordinates to continue persecuting them. He was even activity involved in covering up some of these crimes. Given all of this, the Chamber came to the only reasonable conclusion, that Markac had JCE intent. Markac was also aware of the possibility and willingly took the risk that JCE 3 crimes be committed. He knew that the criminal plan was to expel as many Serbs as possible by using force or threat of force. He was aware of the heightened ethnic tensions surrounding the operation, the revenge motivations harboured by Croatian forces and the vulnerable position of the remaining Serbs in the area. The Chamber properly convicted Markac for the JCE 1 and JCE 3 crimes. In grounds 1B and 1C Markac fails to show any legal or factual error in the Chamber's findings, much less an error which would affect the verdict. These grounds should be dismissed in their entirety. Now, today, I will discuss Markac's participation in planning Operation Storm, his order to shell Gracac, and his failure to act against the crimes of his subordinates. For the remainder, and in particular with respect to legal issues, the Prosecution relies on its written submissions. I turn first to Markac's involvement in planning Operation Storm. As explained by my colleague Ms. Brady, at Brioni, the Croatian leadership agreed not just to an operation to retake the Krajina but also to force out the Serb population. Markac actively participated in this meeting. He and President Tudjman discussed the operations on Gracac with Tudjman instructing Markac to enter and report that he has entered Gracac as soon as possible, as this would lead to even greater panic than shelling the town for two days. That's's Exhibit P461 at page 18. Markac proposed accusing the Serbs of having launched a sabotage attack as a pretext for launching Operation Storm. That's Exhibit P461 at pages 19 and 20. Markac also discussed details with Gotovina and Tudjman, including destroying the enemy's communication system to bring about total chaos. It's at pages 24 and 25 of the exhibit. He then met with Gotovina and Rajcic to co-ordinate the artillery attack on the towns. He then ordered the attack on Gracac. That's at Trial Judgement 2583. In these circumstances, the Chamber reasonably found that Markac's participation at Brioni and in the following meeting of the 3rd of August furthered the criminal plan to expel the Krajina Serbs. The Chamber also properly relied on this, together with other facts, to conclude to Markac's JCE intent. I turn next to Markac's order to shell Gracac. The Trial Chamber reasonably found that Markac ordered an unlawful artillery attack on Gracac and that it was a significant contribution to the common plan in and of itself. It also reasonably relied on Markac's order to conclude to his JCE intent. I will highlight four key points that confirm the reasonableness of the Chamber's conclusion. First, Markac knew full well of the criminal plan to use an attack to forcibly remove the Krajina Serbs. He was present at Brioni. He was then involved in the discussions with Gotovina and Rajcic to co-ordinate the use of artillery on the Krajina towns. Second, a report of the special police to Cervenko states that at 5.15 a.m. on 4 August 1995, "on the orders of operation commander Colonel-General Mladen Markac," the chief of artillery launched the artillery attack in the area of the responsibility of the special police. That's Exhibit P614 at page 6, discussed at Trial Judgement at paragraph 2555. It's around that time, 5.15 a.m. on 4 August that shells started landing on Gracac. That's at paragraph 1451 of the Judgement. Third, the unlawful attack on Gracac was perpetrated by the special police and HV assets that had been resubordinated to the special police. That's at Trial Judgement 1452 and 2561. Markac could command and control both these groups. Trial Judgement, paragraph 194 and 196. The fourth point that I want to mention is the fact that the attack on Gracac was a major operation, was carried out in an organised manner, and was reported up the chain of command.
