There's nothing to suggest that the shelling of Gracac was done by Markac's subordinates at their own initiative and without his approval. So the Chamber was faced with an unlawful attack in accordance with the criminal plan known to Markac which fit squarely with the order given by Markac, perpetrated by units controlled by Markac and which was carried out in an organised way and reported up the chain of command. In these circumstances, the Chamber reached the only reasonable conclusion that Markac ordered the unlawful shelling of Gracac. I turn now to Markac's behaviour in relation to the crimes of his subordinates. This is a point that has been completely ignored in Markac's submission today. Markac took no steps to prevent, report or punish crimes committed by his subordinates in Gracac on the 5th and 6th of August and in Donji Lapac on the 7th and 8th of August. He then failed to address the crimes of the special police in Grubori and Ramljane, even participating in their covering up. Markac's conduct contributed to the creation of a climate of impunity. It encouraged the commission of further crimes against Krajina Serbs and led to further Serb departures. The Chamber properly found that these deliberate and repeated failures to address the crimes contributed to the criminal plan to forcibly remove and persecute the Krajina Serbs, and that Markac intended that result. Markac says in his written submissions that he did not know about the wanton destruction by subordinates in Gracac and Donji Lapac. Now, I would simply refer to our submissions in our respondent's brief on this, and say that, first, the special police burned and destroyed Gracac on the afternoon of 5 August and the morning of 6th August while Markac was present in town with them. The Chamber found that he would have seen the burning by his subordinates. Paragraph 2571. This is the only reasonable conclusion given that all the houses in Gracac had been partially or totally burned during that time. That's Trial Judgement 697. Markac was also informed of the wanton destruction in Donji Lapac while his subordinates were there on 7 and 8 of August. The Chamber reasonably inferred this fact because Markac was regularly informed of developments on the grounds by a variety of sources. The destruction of Donji Lapac by the special police was a major event on the 7th of August. Markac's deputy Sacic admitted that he was told on 9 of August, 1995, that Donji Lapac was burning. That's noted at Trial Judgement 611, referring to transcript 27791-27792. This would certainly have been reported to Markac. In fact, the burning of Donji Lapac by the special police was so widely known that it was even discussed at a meeting between Tudjman, Cervenko, Gotovina and other high ranking military officials. That's exhibit 470, pages 53 and 54, Trial Judgement 2039. Markac also argues that he did not cover up the crimes of his subordinates at Grubori and Ramljane but he fails to show the Chamber's findings were unreasonable. In relation to Grubori, the Chamber found that the Lucko Unit of the special police murdered five Serb civilians in the course of an operation on 25 August. The Lucko Unit also burned houses and shot or burned animals without military justification. The murder victims were elderly and vulnerable, exactly the people Gotovina had predicted would not be able to leave the Krajina. They included two elderly men and two women, one of which was aged 89 or 90. That's at Trial Judgement 389-390. Josip Celic, the assistant commander of the Lucko Unit, first reported up the chain of command that nothing particular had happened during the operation. However, Markac and his deputy Sacic soon became aware that something had gone wrong, that persons had been killed. This was also widely known among international observers. Instead of investigating and taking measures to report or punish the responsible persons, Markac and Sacic had Celic change his report to state that the killings and burning had occurred as a result of a clash with "armed Chetniks" or terrorists. That's at Trial Judgement 2297 and 2300. Markac then forwarded this report to Cervenko. He sought to strengthen this false account by ordering renewed reports by the Lucko Unit matching the clash with terrorists story. Markac was also involved in efforts to prevent on-site investigation into these crimes. Trial Judgement 2300. In these circumstances, the Chamber reasonably concluded that Markac participated in the cover-up of the Grubori crimes. Markac simply fails to show any error in those findings. With respect to Ramljane, Markac knew on the afternoon of 26 August 1995 that members of the Lucko Unit had committed arson. That's at Trial Judgement 2302. He learned this from various sources. He was present just outside the village the same day and saw the smoke rising from the building. Trial Judgement 1077, 2297. One of the group leaders in the Lucko Unit admitted to Markac that he had deliberately burned Serb property. Trial Judgement 1077. Markac allegedly declared that there would be investigations and disciplinary matters, but instead on following through on his word, he advanced a false account that the incident was a response to terrorist activity. That's at Trial Judgement 2238 and 2302, and the exhibit is P579, page 3. It's a report of this false account of Markac to Cervenko. Markac also argues that his failures to take actions in relation to his subordinates' crimes and his participation in the cover-ups did not contribute to the criminal plan. The Chamber carefully considered this question. It gave example of how Markac's conduct led to his subordinates committing further crimes and further deportation. That's at Trial Judgement 2581. Markac fails to show this was unreasonable. He also fails to show the Chamber erred in finding that his failure and his involvement in the cover-ups showed his JCE intent. Markac knew that further crimes against Serb civilians would lead to further forced departure; yet, he encouraged those further crimes. This was reasonably found an indication of Markac JCE intent. So to conclude on ground 1B, Markac simply fails to show an error in the Chamber's finding that he significantly contributed to the criminal plan and did so with JCE intent. I will be very briefly on ground -- on ground 1C in relation to the JCE 3 conviction. We submit that the Chamber reasonably found that the crimes were committed were a natural and foreseeable consequences of the JCE and that Markac was aware of the possibility. I would refer you to paragraphs 139 to 156 of our response brief. But I would say this: Markac has argued today that he chose people from outside the region to limit the risk of crimes such as murder, plunder, and wanton instruction. Now the Trial Chamber noted this assertion that Markac had made in his interview with the Prosecution. But it found this purported measure was obviously insufficient to dispel the possibility of crimes being committed against Serb civilians. The measure did not address the broader revenge sentiment held by members of the Croatian forces which were based not only on the specific connection with the local areas but also on the general enmity towards the Serb takeover of Croatian territory. In the past, these ethnic tensions had resulted in crimes on both sides: So, Serb crimes against Croats and Croat crimes against Serbs. Particularly in previous Croatian military operations, such as Medak and Flash, there had been some incidents of deportation of Serb civilians and attacks on them and their possessions. Markac knew that the -- of the accusation of international observers that Croatian forces had destroyed Serb property when withdrawing after the Medak pocket operation in 1993. Now you can find more on this in paragraphs 149 and 150 of our respondent's brief, and we refer to Trial Judgement paragraph 1683, 2003 and 2585. So for these reasons Markac's grounds 1B and 1C should be dismissed. Your Honours, we do not intend to go and address grounds 2, 3, 5, and 6 of Markac's appeal. But I only want to raise an argument -- I want to address an argument that has been raised for the first time in Markac's reply, in relation to ground 6. And I want to deal with a question Your Honour raised a little earlier concerning P82. So concerning ground 6. At paragraph 153 of his reply, Markac asserts that he was not on notice that the Orahovac murders were perpetrated by the special police. However, the Prosecution pre-trial brief at paragraph 124 specifically alleges that the special police was responsible for these murders. In addition, both parties addressed the issue of who murdered the Serb civilians and the uniform they were wearing during Witness Ilic's testimony. As to Markac's cross-examination on this, I would refer you to transcript 7574 to 7578. Now the point about P82. I don't think we need to go into closed session. I will stick to the Judgement. The Trial Chamber was well aware that there were laps of memory and significantly inconsistency that emerged during the testimony of Witness 82, and that's at paragraph 625 of the Trial Judgement. It found that it would rely on this testimony only to the extent it was corroborated by other evidence. Now, it is important to understand corroboration doesn't need to be on every single detail. I would refer you -- Your Honours, in this connection, to the Nahimana Appeal Judgement at paragraph 428. So the Trial Chamber here found that there was corroboration on the story of P82, on all the major elements of his testimony. The Defence today simply failed to show any error in this by referring to vague problems relating to P82. So unless Your Honours have further questions, Mr. Schneider will now show the Chamber properly found Gracac was unlawfully shelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Schneider.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. At General Markac' order, special police and HV artillery units treated the whole town of Gracac as its target when they fired at least 150 rounds into this town on 4 and 5 August 1995. This was an unlawful attack. The Trial Chamber's findings were reasonable and Markac's arguments should be dismissed. In addition to responding to his arguments, I will answer questions 1, 2, and 3 from the Scheduling Order addendum. To be clear, the Prosecution's answers this morning to questions 1, 2, and 3 apply to all four towns, including Gracac. I am just going to highlight a few points specific to Gracac itself that were overlooked by Markac in his answers to these same questions. With regard to the unlawful shelling of Gracac, I will not repeat our submissions this morning on why the attack on all four towns, including Gracac, was unlawful. I am focussing on Gracac but the shelling of this town cannot be examined on its own. It must be considered in the context of the overall unlawful attack and the overall common criminal plan. The Chamber relied on wide range of evidence on finding there was an unlawful attack against Gracac. First, we have the plain text of three orders instructing artillery units to put Gracac itself under artillery fire. This is in Gotovina's order and Exhibit P1125. This is in his chief of artillery Rajcic's attachment to that order, Exhibit D970. And, at this point, I would clarify Prosecution counsel this morning referred to this exhibit as D97. It was D970. Finally the third order was in the order of Marijan First, the Operation Group Zadar chief of artillery. That is Exhibit P1201. In line with the three orders to put the town under artillery fire, we have reports that the artillery units did just that. So we have special police units, artillery units reporting several times they fired simply at Gracac. That's at Exhibit P2436. These units noted other times that there is artillery fire targeting Gracac at Exhibit P2385. Apart from these orders to the units and the reports in response to these orders we have the co-ordination of the unlawful attack of Gracac with the unlawful attacks against the other three towns. On this point, I would first note the 3 August 1995 meeting between Markac and Gotovina, the JCE members, and others, to plan the illegal attack on Gracac. Also, the artillery units that opened fire on Gracac did so at the same time other units were firing into the towns of Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac. This co-ordination was the result of the fact that shelling of Gracac was just one part of the unlawful attack on the four towns, which itself was one part of the common criminal plan to permanently displace the Serb civilian population. All of the evidence I've just discussed demonstrates the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding that there was an unlawful attack against Gracac. I turn now to question 1. The Trial Chamber did not err in applying a 200-metre margin of error in analysing the lawfulness of the artillery shelling in Gracac itself. Special police and Croatian army units fired on Gracac with a specific type of weaponry, 130-millimetre guns, at paragraph 1452. Rajcic had given evidence on the margin of error for these same guns. His calculation for this margin was based on these 130-millimetres guns being 26 kilometres away from Knin. And I refer you to paragraph 1237 of the Judgement. For Gracac, these exact same guns were 3 kilometres closer at 23 kilometres away. Again, paragraph 1452. Prosecution artillery expert Harry Konings explained that the margin of error for a particular weapon goes down as the guns are moved closer to a target. This is in paragraph 1165 of the Judgement. Given this evidence from Konings, the fact that the 130-millimetre guns fired on Gracac were 3 kilometres closer than those of Rajcic's evidence, and, again, recall he had presented a margin of error of 70 to 75 metres front or back, and 15 metres right or left. And this is at Judgement paragraph 1237. His figures should be adjusted lower for the shelling of Gracac itself. Given this, the 200-metre margin of error was reasonable based on the evidence available to the Trial Chamber. As an aside at this moment, I would like to respond to arguments raised today about an alleged inconsistency in the Prosecution relying on certain evidence by Rajcic, such as this, versus his other evidence that there was no order to treat the towns as targets. There is no inconsistency in this regard. Rajcic's testimony on the interpretation of Gotovina's order went not only to that piece of evidence but to Rajcic's own order itself which repeated the same direction to artillery units to put the towns under fire. If Gotovina's order was illegal, so was Rajcic's. In the Judgement, Trial Chamber correctly observed that personal bias or motive to avoid incriminates oneself could affect the credibility of a witness's testimony. This is noted in the Judgement paragraph 31. This consideration fully applied to the Trial Chamber's assessment of Rajcic's strained interpretation of the attack order that he and Gotovina issued. And I would add that this applies with equal force to the evidence of Turkalj relied on today by the Markac Defence. Like Rajcic, Turkalj fell within the class of witnesses who wanted to avoid incriminating themselves because Turkalj was the commander of the special police artillery unit that had fired into Gracac and treated the whole town as target. Trial Chamber reasonably rejected this self-serving account, in light of the other evidence I've already discussed today. As to who called -- and I should have followed up when I was on Rajcic, but to return to Rajcic for a moment as to who called Rajcic as a witness. We note that the Defence submitted a witness statement from this same witness, Rajcic, at D1425. More importantly than that, no party owns or controls a witness. It is for the Trial Chamber to evaluate on its own, regardless of which party called a witness, the credibility of the witness's evidence. Turning to question 2. The Trial Chamber's conclusions about impact sites in Gracac should be upheld even assuming the margin of error used by the Trial Chamber was erroneous. What is important is that the Trial Chamber found that shells landed in locations all over Gracac, all four corners of the town, and in the middle. I refer you to Judgement paragraphs 1456 through 1459 and the map exhibits cited there. This spread of fire across the entire town helped show the town itself was a target. Secondly, the Chamber found that some of these shells landed near homes, civilian objects. Of these, some landed up to 800 metres away from the nearest military target. And to briefly address a point raised today, the Prosecution did establish the civilian nature of these homes that were hit. There was no reversal of the burden of proof. What is instead important is that this large distance up to 800 metres between military targets and shell impact again helps to show an intent to target the town itself and not just military targets within it. Today, you've heard different figures as to the distance between UN observer Hermann Steenbergen's house and the nearest military target. The Markac Defence has asserted it was only 450 metres away from an item on the Jagoda list; Exhibit D1447. However, this was an unsigned, undated list of possible targets from which actual targets might be selected. I refer you to Judgement paragraph 1403. More importantly, the Trial Chamber did not accept that items on this list were actually aimed at during the shelling of Gracac. That is noted in the Judgement at paragraphs 1423 and 1454. Given this, the shells that struck Steenbergen's house were 800 metres away from the nearest military target, no reliance should be placed on the Jagoda list. On related matter as a possible target, the argument today that there were potential targets of opportunity in Gracac being aimed at when the shells hit these houses hit -- at or near these houses has no merit. The Chamber reasonably rejected this possibility based on the following: First, the shells that impact -- did near -- forgive me, Your Honours. The shells that impacted near Gacesa and Steenbergen's houses did so at 5.00 a.m. on 4 August 1995. This is noted in the Judgement, paragraph 1932. The Trial Chamber found there is no enemy troop movement from the SVK at this time in the morning to be possible targets of opportunity and no forward observers is being used at that time to help identify any such targets. Indeed, the town itself had, as the Trial Chamber found, minimal, if any, SVK presence. Given all of this, there was no reversal of the burden of proof as to targets of opportunity or the lack thereof, rather, as the Trial Chamber's reasonable evaluation of this evidence as a whole that led it to reject the possibility of such targets in this particular instance. Turning now to question 3, the Trial Chamber's finding that an illegal artillery attack took place against Gracac should be upheld even assuming any error with impact site conclusions noted in the Judgement for Gracac itself. We have the three orders to put the town itself under artillery fire. We have the corresponding reports from artillery units showing that the town itself was treated as the target. We have JCE members Markac and Gotovina planning this illegal attack. Beyond Gracac itself, we have the unlawful attack on the other three towns occurring at exactly the same time as this attack. In particular, for those other towns, I would refer to the evidence cited this morning by Mr. Stringer and Mr. Cross, but would note in particular the eye-witness accounts of indiscriminate shelling and the disproportionate attack on Martic to show that the unlawful attack on all four towns was a reasonable finding. All of this evidence I've just mentioned does not change based on a margin of error or impact site conclusions. When all this evidence is considered as a whole, it leads to the only reasonable conclusion that Gracac was unlawfully attacked pursuant to Markac's order. This is especially true given the very limited number of known impact sites we had within the town of Gracac itself. That cannot outweigh the other very strong compelling evidence I've just mentioned. At this point I want to note that earlier today Markac Defence accepted that the fact that shells impacted near the two houses in Gracac was the result of error and could have been up to 20 rounds itself. The point here is whatever the margin of error was, it remains that Croatian forces disregarded the risk of civilian casualties when they shelled Gracac. We know this based on the following: The artillery units fired at least 150 rounds into the small town of Gracac in just a day and a half. They did so using artillery that was inaccurate anywhere between 300 and 800 metres. They did so when aiming at a handful, as noted earlier, of military targets that in truth were a limited military advantage. They did so into a town with minimal, if any, enemy troop presence. All of this shows a disregard for civilian casualties, which helps further show the attack itself was unlawful. The Trial Chamber's findings that the special police and Croatian army artillery units at Markac's order treated the whole town of Gracac as a target and thus engaged in an unlawful attack should be upheld. To draw the Prosecution's response to Markac to a close, the Chamber properly found that Gotovina, Markac and others, acted together in a joint criminal enterprise aimed at permanently removing as many Serb civilians from the Krajina as possible. To achieve this, they unleashed a concerted intensive and unlawful attack against the civilians of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, which sparked the terrified flight of at least 20.000 civilians from the region. Further deportations were triggered by the unchecked wave of crimes by HV and special police as they swept through the territory after the initial attack, killing, abusing, looting, and burning. The implementation of discriminatory measures cemented the deportation, making return for the Serb civilians impossible. Markac's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. He has failed to show that the Trial Chamber any error which would invalidate the Judgement or any unreasonable factual findings that would result in a miscarriage of justice. This concludes my submissions, unless you have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions, so therefore we will now have a pause of 15 minutes. We will reconvene at five minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We will now have reply by Markac, 30 minutes, and then the counsel for Mr. Gotovina as agreed will have five minutes or so to respond. After that, Mr. Gotovina will be invited, if he wishes to have ten minutes personal address, and, as well, Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution seems to be under two misapprehensions, if I may put it that way. The first misapprehension is that we're defending President Tudjman. He is not our client, Markac is. We heard about Tudjman's inflammatory speeches on the 26th of August, 1995, three weeks after the alleged artillery attacks, but we have heard very little about General Markac. And I will return to that in a moment. The second misapprehension seemed to be that their response today was simply an opportunity to restate their response brief to respond to our written pleadings. Now, of course, the purpose of their response was to respond to our oral submissions made today, and they said nothing about my submissions, nothing about how it all hangs on an unlawful artillery attack finding. They didn't respond at all. They gave what sounded very much like a closing speech after a trial, punctuated by the mantra that we've shown no error. And they gave no answer because there is no answer. And we're sure that the Appeals Chamber will draw the necessary inferences from their failure to respond. So we're not going to respond to all the points which are not responses at all. We simply refer the Appeals Chamber to our appeals briefs, and especially in regard to crimes in Donji Lapac and at Grubori, we have a full response in our briefs and we won't repeat it. It is completely denied, completely and utterly denied that there was any failure to prevent or punish, and on the contrary, as you've heard today, Markac tried to prevent crimes and yet the Trial Chamber used it against him. And I did want to just refer Your Honours to Blaskic paragraph 602 where the Chamber said this: "In concluding that the Appellant knew of the crimes that were being committed, the Trial Chamber further relied upon orders issued by the Appellant directing personnel under his command to treat the detainees according to the requirements of humanitarian law. This is a finds with which the Appeals Chamber cannot agree. In relying on those orders, the Trial Chamber effectively sanctioned the Appellant for fulfilling his duty as a military officer to prevent and punish violations of humanitarian law. Evidence of the execution of that duty cannot be cited as evidence of the Appellant's prior knowledge of and assent to those violations." And we rely fully on that dictum. Now, the Prosecution rely very heavily on a context approach, a totality approach, and variations on that theme, sometimes described as reviewing the evidence as a whole, and so I intend to tackle that head on. First of all, it is not a totality approach at all. It's a subset of the totality. In fact, the Prosecution, when it refers to the totality, it is referring to the incriminating subset of the totality of evidence minus all exculpatory evidence minus all explanations which are favourable to the Appellant. That's not a totality approach. It doesn't look at all the relevant evidence and interpretations, exculpatory and incriminating, and I will develop that a little. And secondly, the main point of Your Honours' question number 4, as the table, I hope, which perhaps was initially perplexing, shows is that if that is wrong, the unlawful artillery attack finding, then there is no use relying on a totality approach because there is no actus reus. So looking at Brioni, looking at a totality, will not get the Prosecution anywhere. Now, I'd like to touch on General Markac's "participation at Brioni" because that was touched on and it is significant. And I would ask, if possible, if you have Exhibit P461, to look at it, but if not, it doesn't matter. You can look at it later. There were only six pages, I believe, where General Markac is -- where he has any comment at Brioni. Now, can it be maintained as a proposition that everyone present at the Brioni meeting was a member of the JCE? Surely not, because that is pure guilt by association. Right. So if that proposition is wrong, then we have to look at what Markac said and did at Brioni which is incriminating. We've had Tudjman, Tudjman, Tudjman. No. We need to look at what Markac said and did. And the reference is at page 17 of that exhibit. And there, in fact, it is just the president saying, What ask Markac's task here? Who will take Ljubovo? Purely and simply, wondering what his operational task will be in the operation. And then paragraph 18: Markac: "Mr. President, allow me to add something regarding my task in this plan on a micro level related to Mr. Norac. We all head out from Velebit --" In fact there is almost no point in -- I was going to -- there's no point in me reading it apart from what the president says. The president says: "When you say you're going to block Gracac off, bear in mind that there can be a state of panic in Gracac. You have to enter as quickly as possible and report that you have entered, as well as all of you who will be involved, because that will have a psychological effect in such situations. The psychological effect of the fall of a town is greater than if you shell it for two days." That is what Tudjman says to Markac about Gracac. He's saying, Don't shell it, better to march in there and announce that you have taken it. That is the complete opposite of the alleged JCE. That's page 18. Page 19. The president says, We should have a pretext for the military action. And they ask Markac to do that, and he says, We can accuse them of launching a sabotage attack. Nothing to do with the JCE. One may not like the idea of having pretexts, but I imagine every army in the world occasionally uses pretext for attacks. Anyway, nothing to do with the JCE. 19. Sorry, that was page 19. 24, is the next intervention. And he simply says that it will take him four days to get to Gracac because it's 18 kilometres, and there's an argument about why it should take four days to go 18 kilometres. 25, Markac says that in essence he should take down the communications system. That's all sound military tactics, nothing JCE-esque at all. 31 is the final reference, which simply says -- and again -- it is hard to know exactly what's being discussed and that's one of the problems of not having a live witness. And whoever explained this just says, We should give them an hour, just enough to take cover. So who knows what that is about. Absolutely nothing incriminating, nothing JCE-related and that's why they are forced to rely on Tudjman. And as I said, it is not guilt by association. There's nothing by Markac. Moreover, nothing by anyone at Brioni about let's prevent their return. Let's use laws to stop them coming back, and that is absolutely -- that's the other half of the JCE. If there are two halves of this apple, there is displacing them and not letting them return, and you don't see anything of that half of the apple at Brioni. And they have absolutely no answer to that, the Prosecution, as far as Brioni is concerned. Moreover, in relation to that, the Prosecution hasn't answered the fact that the Chamber found, at 2562 to 2563, that neither Gotovina nor Markac were involved in -- in adopting discriminatory measures, which is this second half of the apple. Just to give you a preview of how I intend to proceed at this stage, I want to deal with some further issues and then I will give the floor to my learned colleague Mr. Kuzmanovic to reply on Gracac and, if possible, some extra time for the Gotovina team on evacuation orders because they've had no time to deal with it. Now, failure to prevent or punish crimes. The Prosecution say, well, we didn't deal with that at all. Well, no, not in detail because we, unlike them, were answering your questions. So in fact that shows the Prosecution should not be addressing it in their response to us because of the precise reason that we didn't deal with it. But we did deal with it in the context of the question asked, and if you still have the chart, you'll see that the top-level box to the far left, Markac substantially contributed to the JCE, including failure to prevent/punish. We've dealt with it there and we've dealt with it by showing that that finding depends on finding that he participated in an unlawful attack. You have the paragraph references. And the Chamber did not identify failure to prevent or punish as an independent, separate ground for substantial contribution. And the reference for that is paragraph 2582, and time doesn't allow me to read it so I will simply say this, that that paragraph starts off by saying, "Considering the above," and "the above" refers to paragraph 2580, the first sentences of which deal with unlawful attack. So again, it's considering unlawful attack in trying to determine whether he substantially contributed. And then again it refers to the alleged deportation of Krajina Serbs by virtue of non-artillery crimes and that's also factored in, so that the finding that there was a substantial contribution does not identify as an independent contribution failure to prevent or punish and -- and 2580 to 52582 to make that clear. Moreover, in relation to the alleged failure to prevent and punish, we want to point out the irrationality of the Chamber on this point -- not point out but remind it to the Chamber. As we've said in paragraph 167 of our appeals brief, the Trial Chamber in acquitting Mr. Cermak said, in essence, well, covering up crimes couldn't make a contribution to the JCE because the JCE is about forcibly expelling Serbs. This is what they say at paragraph 2548: "Considering its finding on the objective of the JCE being the permanent removal of the Serb civilian population from the Krajina by force or threat of force, the Trial Chamber finds that Cermak's misleading assurances were not of a magnitude and nature to constitute -- contribute to the JCE. With regard to Cermak's denial and concealment of the crimes committed in Grubori, the Trial Chamber finds, considering the finding on the JCE objective and the nature of Cermak's acts, that they did not constitute a significant contribution to the JCE." And this was a case of putting weapons next to civilians to suggest that, in fact, they were combatants, a much more significant cover-up, if you like. So the Chamber was fully aware when dealing with Cermak, when acquitting him, that the JCE was about permanently removing Serbs, so a cover-up of murders committed weeks later would not have any link, would not constitute a significant contribution, but failed to apply exactly the same point to Markac. On the totality -- I have five minutes. The Prosecution defends the Chamber's totality approach when seeking to salvage its inferences regards Brioni and the JCE, et cetera. The problem is that to have a totality approach you need a Judgement with incontrovertible, unambiguous, reliable or strong evidence, which are the necessary foundations of a totality approach. But claiming to use a totality approach to assess evidence and make inferences when, in fact, it systematically disregarded exculpatory evidence, the Chamber ran foul of the guidance given in this Chamber's previous Judgements. And I refer to Ntagerura. The Prosecution is -- has cited Ntagerura frequently, relies on it for its totality approach. But in fact, if one looks at what the Appeals Chamber said, it's paragraph 174, 175: "Only after the analysis of all the relevant evidence can a Trial Chamber determine whether the evidence upon which the Prosecution relies should be accepted as establishing the existence of the facts alleged, notwithstanding the evidence upon which the Defence relies." Then paragraph 175, it says, and I'm going to paraphrase, the presumption of innocence -- well, I better quote: "... the presumption of innocence requires that each fact on which an accused's conviction is based must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The Appeals Chamber agrees with the Prosecution's argument that 'if facts which are essential to a finding of guilt are still doubtful'" - oh, I don't have time - "'... notwithstanding the support of other facts, this will produce a doubt in the mind of the Trial Chamber that guilt has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt.' Thus, if one of the links is not proved beyond a reasonable doubt, the chain will not support a conviction." So one has the metaphor a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. The Prosecution likes the cable metaphor. Whether you use a metaphor of chains or cables, the fact is if a piece of evidence is half doubtful, half incriminating, half exculpatory, and another piece of evidence is likewise, half incriminating, half exculpatory, you don't just add up the two halves which are incriminating and you say, well, there, we have a strong argument now. The halves -- the doubtful halves multiply as well. Half times a half is a quarter. It's not one. So they overlook the fact that the doubts multiply through the evidence as well, not just the certainties. And that applies to Brioni because it relies on these excerpts, highly selective excerpts from -- from Gotovina's and Tudjman's statements at Brioni, but ignore the context and ignore all the other elements there. So if I can just -- it's dealt it in our appeals briefs, paragraphs 21 to 86, Brioni, we analyse it in detail. But how about all these facts which are also part of the totality? One, that references to leaving a corridor for civilians and military forces to evacuate is in accordance with humanitarian necessity and sound military reasoning. As counsel for Gotovina said, you can't trap civilians in a war zone. And we have UN exhibits, D28 -- UN documents which are exhibits, D28 and D1530, where the UN says -- this is D28: "However, Croatia will allow with full guarantees for security the departure from those areas of all those who expressed desire to do so." The UN is calling on Croatia to allow people to leave, and quite right. And then D1530, and it's at the -- it's a resolution of the Security Council and demand that the government of the Republic of Croatia "respect fully the rights of the local Serb population, including their rights to remain, leave, or return." You have to respect their right to leave and not hem them in. That the Brioni discussions didn't need to be either about deporting civilians or protecting them. As we said in our appeals brief that is a false dichotomy. But there are plenty of other reasons why you might wish them to go. But the ostensible passage on which they place so much reliance is a paragraph full of ellipses, things which haven't been recorded, and subject to many interpretations. Here's one possible interpretation. Tudjman realises the Serbs are not going to stay. He says, well, if they do say, they can have their civil rights. He realises they're not actually going to stay so they're ostensible. They're ostensible civil rights. One simply doesn't know -- the fact is -- if I can perhaps just develop one analogy and I hope it doesn't come across as inappropriate, but in hotels these days, one comes across these signs which say, Consider the environment and don't make us wash your towels too much, and clearly the hotel business has never shown any great concern for the environment in the past. I don't see hotel chains giving money to Greenpeace or showing any other concern about the environment. Clearly they want to save money on detergent and so they say -- you can imagine a board meeting of the hotel chain, saying, Well, let's put up signs saying, Consider the environment, and that way we'll save money and we won't have to wash so many towels. It doesn't mean that they don't care about the environment -- it doesn't mean that the environment isn't going to be protected. It doesn't mean that there will be less towels wastefully washed. And so, it's the same context because -- if someone says, Yes, we can say this and in any event this will happen. I mean, in fact, what it shows, all of this, is that without a witness who actually says, This is what he meant, this is what everybody understood, which would be normal in a criminal trial of this magnitude, we're all guessing at what is meant. Now I don't want to trespass too much on the Chamber's time, so I'm permitted a brief review whether there's -- what I'll do is I'll just cite the page references of Brioni which I would also ask you to look at. In relation to Serb shelling of civilian areas in the town of Osijek, Croatian town, Tudjman, Cervenko, and Gotovina all rejected any retaliatory strike on non-military objectives. And Tudjman explicitly dismissed Serb villages as illegitimate targets. Cervenko concurs, and Gotovina says that there's no target even close to an adequate objective. Tudjman says, We can hit a battery, nothing but that. Pages 20 to 21. Page 25, Gotovina states that the objective of the operation is military of territory, making no reference to any other purpose. Page 27, Tudjman says: "From a military viewpoint, the task is just to attack their batteries." The Gotovina statement that Knin could be destroyed within a few hours should be seen in the context of the preceding paragraphs which can only reasonable be read to be referring to military targets not civilians. And so on. So, none of the above pieces are conclusive, beyond dispute or incontrovertible, and so the totality approach simply doesn't assist. I think to give my colleagues time, I will stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If you don't mind, I will just stay right here rather than shift around. First an observation and then I want to make three or four specific points on the response argument. First observation is: In relation to substantial contribution, the only argument put forth was essentially a recitation of the Trial Judgement. It was not anything that dealt with our brief. It was not anything with our oral argument. On the substantial contribution issue it was: The Judgement at these paragraphs says this, and therefore it is right. That's not an argument. The second thing I wanted to say with regard to the record in one of the arguments that was made regarding artillery. On page 169 of the response referring to -- line 12, referring to Prosecution artillery expert Konings and the margin of error, and also referring to Witness Rajcic and the margin of error, the Prosecution knows this, Rajcic only testified to a 70 to 75 metres range of error as internal margin of error. He did not discuss the additional external factors which Konings discussed, wind speed, air temperature, density, muzzle velocity. Those add to the range of error 240 additional metres for external errors. So Rajcic's margin of error is not 70 to 75 metres because that is simply internal. You have to add all of the external factors, as Konings did, to 240 metres, or up to 315 metres if you accept Rajcic's 70 to 75 metres of internal margin of error. You can't just factor on that alone. So that is a misleading argument to say that the margin of error is only 70 to 75 metres. Second, there was a statement that the shelling caused a disregard for civilian casualties. I noted that on page 173, line 24, in relation to Gracac. My question is: What civilian casualties? There were no civilian casualties. No dead, no wounded. Third, Konings was an expert for the Prosecution. He found absolutely no fault with the special police's use of artillery in Gracac. Transcript 14775 and 76. He was not put the question by the Prosecution regarding the special police's use of artillery. He had no opinions critical of the special police's use of artillery in Operation Storm. Prosecution's own expert. The other thing I wanted to add, on page 171, I think it's lines 10 and 11, where in the record has it been established the civilian nature of the targets or the homes, or whatever it is, in Gracac? The Prosecution certainly didn't establish it, they didn't cite anything to the record. I went through the six -- six -- six, I believe, impact areas. They didn't respond to any of those impact areas that I discussed. Where? There was no expert that discussed any shell impacts at all in Gracac. Finally, I wanted to point the Trial Chamber's attention to, again, Josip Turkalj. Now the comment from the Prosecution is -- for the first time we hear that Turkalj testified the way he did because he didn't want to incriminate himself, even though he was a Prosecution witness. Turkalj testified at trial regarding artillery on several occasions and he was asked: What happened to you, Mr. Turkalj, when the RSK fired into the Republic of Croatia? What was the reaction of the civilian population in Croatian-held territory? Did they flee, did they go into hiding? What did they do? And he answered: "When the ARSK artillery fired upon towns or civilian targets, everyone sought refuge in shelters wherever they could. People did not abandon places where they lived, if that's what you're asking me about. They spent most of the time in shelters, and the situation ... prevailed for years." Then the focus turned to Gracac. Let's talk about the attack on Gracac. When you got to Gracac, there was no civilian population. They had evacuated. That's correct. Yes, there was no civilian population. "... Mr. Turkalj, based on your experience being on the other side of -- in Croatian-held territory receiving an artillery attack, were you surprised that, in fact, the entire civilian population had evacuated with the ARSK?" And Judge Orie reformulated the question: When the RSK fired into it the Republic of Croatia, what was the reaction of the population? That was asked of the witness. And now the comparison is made between the reaction of the civilian population as the witness experienced it being on the receiving side, and now, on arriving at the side that had received the artillery fired by the forces this witness was a part of. And Mr. Kehoe [sic] says: "I will take the liberty to answer Your Honours' and counsel's question this way: I was surprised at the fact that there was no civilian population there. It was already said that the targets engaged in Gracac were engaged with an exceptionally small number of projectiles in view of the number of targets in Gracac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you should conclude in a moment or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. This is my last point. Thank you. "To draw a comparison, I was present in ... the town of Karlovac where hundreds or even thousands of rounds landed on Karlovac, and the population never abandoned it. It was always there. "So the movements of the population can never be correlated with the activities of shelling, or at least I could not when it came to the shelling of towns that came from our side." That's transcript reference number 13772 and 73, Your Honours. With that, I will conclude my submissions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Gotovina. I'm terribly sorry, I forget the promise I made to you, that you would be able to respond. Five minutes, counsel of Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and I appreciate the extra time. With your leave, in the five minutes I would like to address the second topic, which was the evacuation issue. We never really addressed the argument presented by Ms. Elliott and with your leave I'd like to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The first point is concerning Ms. Brady's submissions on General Gotovina's comments at Brioni. We take exception to what appeared be quotation and then insertion of language. She correctly cited that General Gotovina said: "If we continue this pressure," and then inserted the words "meaning the shelling." No such language appears in the Brioni transcript. In fact that was highly contested at trial as to what that language meant. Now, we'd like to draw your attention to what the Prosecution acknowledged in its pre-trial brief as to what the participants meant by continuing this pressure. First of all, it should be noted that continuing this pressure could not have referred to shelling because there was no shelling taking place in the Krajina on the date of the Brioni meeting. Therefore, continuing something that hadn't taken place yet wouldn't make any sense. Instead, the Prosecution correctly in its pre-trial brief explained what the participants were discussing. And this is via Sanction we're showing this. It says -- this is at paragraph 28: "Following discussions regarding the operational plan for the attack, Tudjman observed that the general offensive would create great panic in Knin ..." And that is what we submit, Your Honours. They're talking about that the offensive is going to create a general panic, not particularly using artillery. And as we know, in all places but the four towns, once the offensive was underway, in fact they did leave for reasons that the Chamber found were not the result of unlawful conduct by the Croatian Army. Secondly, with respect to General Gotovina's comments about being able to destroy Knin if the order is given. We note the Prosecution's opening statement which confirmed that the Prosecution itself did not contend that there was a mens rea to destroy Knin. Quite the opposite, according to the Prosecution. This is again on your screens. This is the Prosecution's comment. "Despite the bombardment, Your Honour --" and this is at trial transcript 444. "Despite the bombardment, Your Honour, the Court should not get the wrong impression. This was not Stalingrad or Vukovar, where weeks of shelling reduced the city to rubble. It was not the most destructive shelling of the war. But that is precisely the point. The intention was not to destroy Knin, the city of Zvonimir, into which President Tudjman intended to resettle Croats but to drive out Serbs." So there is no dispute in this case that there was no intent to destroy Knin. Turning our attention to the evacuation orders. The proposition that masses of civilians were evacuating early in the day is simply fantasy. There is no evidence in the record, contemporaneous evidence, to support that proposition. You will not find any evidence from the 4th of August, the 5th of August, the 6th of August, any reports, anything of the like to confirm any mass exodus of civilians prior to the issuance of Martic's evacuation order. Are there claims that were made in the weeks and the months later by individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, counsel, for the intervention. Mr. President, it was under our understanding that Mr. Misetic's five minutes was granted in order to respond to Ms. Brady's specific comments about Brioni and General Gotovina's remarks as made in that meeting. It wasn't our understanding that the five minutes was granted in order to go into other areas that didn't fall within that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked for leave when I got on my feet and you granted it, and that's why I proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please continue, and it is almost up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we turn to two documents to confirm what the contemporaneous records confirm. And this is Exhibit P398, beginning at page 1, and this is the report of -- it's the commander of Sector South, General Forand, it's a transcript. We're showing it via Sanction. And it says towards the bottom concerning -- sorry, towards the top -- the bottom of the first paragraph. He says: "Discussing why the Krajina fell," beginning at line 7, "and this is a bit surprising when you look at it from the military point of view. Another aspect that was critical, I think, in their -- why it went so fast, they decided very early, on the afternoon, on the 4th afternoon to evacuate the civilians from Knin and all the surrounding towns, and as soon as that was done, everybody started to flee away, including the military." General Forand again at trial Exhibit P399. Page 1 -- I'm sorry, page 2. I'll skip over in the interests of time. On page 1, General Forand describes being called to a meeting at 1800 hours where the SVK authorities asked him to assist in the evacuation of the civilian population. On page 2 from lines 2 to 8: "And I told them that when they had a plan, you know, I would come back. So they said, We'll come back in an hour and we'll have a plan. I could not go back in an hour. It was a couple of hours, you know, before we could go back to that location, and when we arrived there, we found out that they had evacuated the location. There was nobody there. And that's when we started to see quite a flow of vehicles getting out of Knin and going direction north."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think -- I really think that you ought to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Your time is up. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I apologise. I just want to tie up one thing from this morning. As Your Honours may recall, I raised a question about the demonstrative aids, the maps and the photographs, and whether the circles on the margin of error corresponded to the legends at the bottom, and I just want to inform the Chamber that Mr. Misetic and I have been in touch about that during the course of the day. He assures us that the circles are the correct size and I take his word for it. It may be that they don't correspond to the legends. But for the limited purpose of these demonstrative aids, they're not in evidence. They relate to the 400 metres which, in fact, was not even accepted by the Trial Chamber. I think Your Honours are aware of that and acceptable to us from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I made it clear that they were -- that we looked at them without prejudice. Thank you very much. And, Mr. Gotovina, you would like to [Microphone not activated] THE APPELLANT GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to address you -- Your Honours, I would like to address you in English [as interpreted] if I may. Your Honours, throughout my military career, I have endeavoured to conduct myself honourably and in a dignified manner. As a soldier and officer, I have always done my best to protect civilians. As an officer, I am proud of the way Operation Storm was conducted. I am proud of that operation, not only because we won the battle but also because civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects were reduced to the bare minimum. As a human being, I am, of course, extremely sorry for the loss of civilian lives and the destruction of civilian objects in the aftermath of the operation. I cannot, however, be held accountable for what others may have done or failed to do while I was engaged in and conducting operations in Bosnia. Throughout the war, I was tasked with difficult duties and responsibilities. To this day, I remain convinced that I fulfilled my duties to the best of my ability. As a man, I know that with hindsight, it is possible to say that things could have been different. But, as a commander, I did not have the benefit of hindsight at the time of the crimes charged. During Operation Storm, we were engaged in a life and death struggle against another military force to liberate our country whilst trying to protect the lives of our men and that of civilians. I lay no claim to perfection and I hope I will not be convicted on that basis. Even though I have made mistakes in my time, such as not surrendering to the Tribunal, you can be sure that I am the first person to regret them. You may find fault with my judgement, but you will be hard-pressed to find any willingness or consent on my part to hurt, abuse, or deny the rights of any man, be he a civilian or a soldier, simply because he is a Serb or is of Serb ethnicity. I know and can live with the fact that the way I acted during Operation Storm was appropriate and my orders bear testimony to that. Your Honours, I'm not asking for any favours, and I'm only asking for what my lawyers have already requested. I know for a certainty that my actions were consistent with those of an honest and diligent military officer who tried to do his best in trying circumstances. If this Chamber were to examine my actions in light of such a context, I would be entirely satisfied and would ask for nothing more. Your Honours, thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gotovina. [In English] Mr. Markac, ten minutes. THE APPELLANT MARKAC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, convinced of the fairness of this Tribunal and my own innocence, nine years ago I appeared before this Tribunal voluntarily. I was surprised at the allegations made about the military and police Operation Storm in the course of these proceedings which are not founded on true facts, and which in many respects misinterpret the actual events on the ground. Motivated by the attempts to alter the facts of the homeland war, I wish to say this in all honesty: I am not a member of any joint criminal enterprise, nor am I a war criminal. Moreover, I first heard of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise in the course of these proceedings. Neither the representatives of the international community who were present in Croatia at the time nor any member of the public in the country had ever indicated to me that such an enterprise existed, to begin with. Likewise, nobody from domestic institutions or the international community, either before, during, or after Operation Storm, has ever drawn my attention to possible unlawful acts committed by the special police of the Ministry of Interior of whose professional conduct I am particularly proud. Consequently, I did not plan, commit, or cover up any crime, because it goes against my outlook on life. I am an officer of the police and army who has, alongside his subordinates, responsibly and professionally carried out the tasks assigned to me by the Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces and the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia. My job was to fight terrorism, to defend and liberate the unlawfully occupied territory, and to restore the legal system of the Republic of Croatia in that territory. As a person and a humanist, I deeply sympathise with all those who have suffered a personal loss during these unfortunate events. Your Honour, I am not guilty. I expect that you will thoroughly examine the material available to you and deliver a fair judgement. I am grateful for this opportunity to address you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markac. The hearing is now concluded, and the Judgement of the Appeals Chamber will be delivered in due course. We'd like to thank the parties, court management, interpretation staff, the court reporter, and other staff for their assistance today. And the Appeals Chamber will rise.
